## DOSSIER 4 — modelscope/ms-swift (Category 2: training + post-training at frontier-model scale)

**What it is.** Alibaba ModelScope's SWIFT: a unified CPT/SFT/RLHF framework covering 600+ LLMs and 300+ multimodal models, with a Megatron bridge for full-parameter training of frontier-class models (its own example scripts run DeepSeek-V4.1, Qwen3-235B MoE, GLM-5.x). The AAAI 2025 paper's codebase. 16,056★, 594 open issues, created 2023-08-01, Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file body verified). Release v4.6.0 (2026-10-13); pushed the day before this pull.

**Architecture, from the code** (1,604 files, 29 top-level modules under `swift/` enumerated; RL core read). The spine: `swift/pipelines` + `swift/trainers` (HF-Trainer-based PT/SFT), `swift/tuners` (PEFT family), `swift/megatron/` (conversion + training bridge to Megatron-LM for tensor/pipeline-parallel full training), `swift/sequence_parallel`, `swift/ray` (distributed rollout placement). The post-training core, read at source level:
- `swift/rlhf_trainers/` — `grpo_trainer.py`, `ppo_trainer.py`, `dpo_trainer.py`, `cpo_trainer.py`, `orpo_trainer.py`, `kto_trainer.py`, `gkd_trainer.py` (generalized knowledge distillation), `reward_trainer.py`, with `rollout_mixin.py`/`vllm_client.py` coupling generation.
- `swift/rl_core/` — the algorithm heart, deliberately framework-free: `grpo_algorithm.py` (144 lines: `compute_rewards_per_func`, `score_completions` — completions scored by a *set of independent reward functions*, combined downstream) and `advantage.py` (483 lines, read: `compute_advantages(rewards_per_func, reward_weights, num_generations, advantage_estimator ∈ {grpo, rloo, reinforce++}, scale_rewards, kl_in_reward, beta)` returns **per-sequence** advantages as a pure tensor function "suitable for all backends (HF, Megatron, Ray)" — with the reference-model KL subtracted from rewards *before* group normalization, dynamic-sampling std computation, and per-token teacher-KL/log-ratio hooks (`compute_teacher_kl_per_token`, `compute_teacher_logratio`) for on-policy distillation signals applied after the base advantage is broadcast).
- `swift/rollout/` — `agent_loop.py`, `multi_turn.py`, `gym_env.py`, `openenv_wrapper.py`: multi-turn agent RL environments, not just single-turn completion RL.
- `swift/infer_engine/` — one protocol over `vllm_engine.py`, `sglang_engine.py`, `lmdeploy_engine.py`, `transformers_engine.py`, plus `grpo_vllm_engine.py`: the same serving-abstraction trick Dossier 1 uses for eval, applied to training rollouts.

## DOSSIER 5 — axolotl-ai-cloud/axolotl (Category 2: fine-tuning orchestration / adapter factory)

**What it is.** The config-driven fine-tuning orchestrator: one YAML file describes base model, data, adapters, optimization, and evaluation; Axolotl compiles it into a correct HF Trainer run. 12,668★, 1,471 forks, created 2023-04-14, Apache-2.0. Release v0.21.1 (2026-10-27); pushed the day of this pull; 250 open issues.

**Architecture, from the code** (sparse clone read). The contract is a giant Pydantic schema (`src/axolotl/utils/schemas/config.py` — one validated field per knob: `sample_packing` with group/bin sizing and a separate `eval_sample_packing`, FSDP config imported from `schemas/fsdp.py`, fp8 toggles, cloud/checkpoint schemas beside it). Execution: `src/axolotl/core/` — `trainers/`, `datasets/`, `builders/`, `attention/`, plus production-hardening pieces most trainers lack: `checkpoint_mirror.py` (a `CheckpointMirrorCallback`), `checkpoint_publisher.py`, `checkpoint_retry.py` — checkpoints mirrored/publisher-retried to object storage as a first-class behavior. `src/axolotl/kernels/` holds fused Triton/CUDA kernels (`lora.py`, `dora.py`, `geglu.py`, `swiglu.py`, `rms_norm_gated.py`, `gemma4_fused_rope.py`) — LoRA math fused rather than composed from primitives. `src/axolotl/monkeypatch/` is the honest price of the ecosystem: patch layers for transformers, peft, xformers, ring attention, tiled MLP, per-model quirks (`monkeypatch/models/`). Data: `datasets.py` + `prompt_strategies/` per training type (`dpo/`, `kto/`, `orpo/`, `ebft/`, `bradley_terry/`, `messages/` — chat-format strategies), `prompt_tokenizers.py`, samplers in `utils/samplers/`, and `evaluate.py` for in-run evals. Preference algorithms are prompt-strategy + TRL-backed; Axolotl's own depth is SFT/adapter/data, not RL numerics.

**How it enters the skeleton.** The **adapter factory for staged candidates**. Prompt 2's promotion system requires every candidate to be explainable — what data, what config, what scores produced it. Axolotl's config-as-code is exactly that audit trail: a candidate IS a YAML file plus a checkpoint; two candidates differ by a diffable config. The near-minute cadence layers use it like this: data refresh (Fuel Line 1/2) → new config revision → short LoRA/DoRA run with sample packing → checkpoint mirrored out → Dossier 1 evaluates → promote or discard. Checkpoint mirroring is the piece that makes candidate generation survivable on preemptible GPU rentals — a killed run resumes from the mirror instead of from zero.

## DOSSIER 6 — arcee-ai/mergekit (Category 3: model merging / zero-training candidate generation)

**What it is.** The standard toolkit for merging pretrained LLMs in weight space: task arithmetic, TIES, DARE, SLERP, model stock, and evolutionary merge search, configured by YAML. 7,436★, 277 open issues, created 2023-08-21, **LGPL-3.0**. Release v0.1.5 (2026-10-20); pushed 2026-10-31.

**Architecture, from the code** (201 files enumerated; core method source read). `mergekit/merge_methods/` is a registry of merge policies over a shared contract (`base.py`: `GroupMergeMethod`, `ParameterSpec`/`ParameterScope`, `TensorGroup`, `InputContract`). The flagship, read at source level: `generalized_task_arithmetic.py` — a frozen dataclass policy composing the whole modern merge family in one method: task vectors (fine-tune minus base) are **sparsified** via `mergekit/sparsify.py` (`SparsificationMethod`, `RescaleNorm` — DARE-style random dropping with norm rescaling, or TIES-style magnitude trimming), combined under a **consensus rule** (`ConsensusMethod`: `count` vs `sum` — sign-consensus is the TIES interference fix), then normalized/rescaled and scaled by `lambda` before being added back to the base. Siblings: `linear.py` (weighted average), `slerp.py`/`multislerp.py`/`nuslerp.py` (spherical interpolation), `model_stock.py` (geometric layer-wise stock), `karcher.py` (Karcher-mean on the manifold), `nearswap.py`, `sce.py`, `arcee_fusion.py`, `task_adapter.py`, `passthrough.py` (layer grafting — Frankenmerge). `mergekit/scripts/` includes `evolve.py` (mergekit-yaml-evolve: evolutionary search over merge hyperparameters, scored by lm-eval — Dossier 1 as the fitness function), `extract_lora.py`, `layershuffle.py`.

**How it enters the skeleton.** The **cheapest candidate generator in the promotion pipeline**. When two staged adapters each win on different suites (one on GSM8K-style reasoning, one on forecasting calibration), a TIES/DARE merge is a new candidate that costs RAM-minutes, not GPU-hours — it enters shadow eval like any other candidate and lives or dies by the same promotion bar. `evolve.py` closes the loop automatically: merge-config search with harness scores as fitness, bounded by the regression budget. This is also the cold-start compensation from Prompt 2: at zero user traffic, merges of public-data adapters still generate improving candidates.

**License / maintenance / limits.** LGPL-3.0 — fine as a build-time tool; get a license review before embedding mergekit code inside any shipped product (tool use vs library linking is the distinction that matters). Maintenance is steady but not fast (two releases in a year). Hard limits: (1) merges require the same base model and tokenizer family — merging across bases is undefined behavior, not a technique; (2) merged models can silently lose calibration while gaining benchmark points — for a forecasting system, every merge candidate must pass the calibration gate, not just the accuracy suites; (3) evolutionary search will happily overfit the eval it scores on — hold out a confirmation split.

### 3. RRSI — Google Research's Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement
- **Post:** https://www.instagram.com/reel/Dd83Jx1jUd-/ ("Google open-sourced RRSI", text-on-black explainer)
- **What it is:** RRSI = Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Harnesses (Google Cloud AI Research with UNC-Chapel Hill, Stanford, WashU; released Sep 21, 2026). A frozen model's harness — prompts, tools, memory, control flow, sub-agents — is rewritten by an improvement loop, while five rules regularize the *search* rather than the harness: annealed edit budget, evidence ledger, **leakage critic** (screens every candidate edit for task names, benchmark entities, answers, suite-specific logic BEFORE evaluation), noise-adjusted acceptance floor (gain must clear the bootstrapped eval-noise band), and a cost rule (added tokens must be paid for by measured gain) plus pruning of non-contributing components.

Poster's "74 → 80" framing matches the paper.
- **Verdict:** TEST — highest-priority import in this lane. The leakage critic + noise-adjusted floor + cost rule are exactly the promotion gate the skeleton's near-minute improvement loop needs, and the repo ships them as working code (critic.py, calibrate.py).
- **Engine-training value:** The evidence ledger is a labeled dataset of (edit → measured delta) pairs — a training signal for predicting which harness changes generalize. Noise-band calibration data per benchmark suite.

The paper's own Section 5 limitation — sequential self-edits cause catastrophic forgetting — is shown in the post's slide 2 and is the key caveat.

### 6. TTPO — Test-Time Policy Optimization (Zhejiang University / Alibaba)
- **Posts:** https://www.facebook.com/MontrealAI/posts/pfbid03SVnp22Xg1DnhkvRWXAojwA3QozQsjFBZEmfJNTrw814gpz5WgMDNPyDPbMQP7xtl and mirror https://www.facebook.com/groups/Montreal.AI.Academy/permalink/1948738702458248/ (same paper, two group shares — counted once)
- **What it is:** Test-time training for math reasoning **without ground-truth labels**. Majority-vote pseudo-labels are fragile because a wrong vote corrupts the teacher; TTPO's asymmetry observation: rollouts that *disagree* with the pseudo-label are usually wrong whether or not the vote is right. So agreeing rollouts get OPSD distillation, disagreeing rollouts get GRPO penalties, with token-level selection in both branches.
- **Provenance:** Group-share posts are recreators; the paper image they carry is genuine. Primary source: arXiv:2608.27448 (Wang et al., submitted Aug 27, 2026); code https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/TTPO. Verified results [verified]: label-free TTPO matches or exceeds label-supervised OPSD across Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B on AIME 2025/2026, HMMT 2025/2026, BRUMO 2025; pure-TTT setting raises 1.7B base 38.0% → 45.2%; +25.2% to +36.4% in no-thinking mode. Fine-tuning in the paper is LoRA r=64.
- **Verdict:** TEST — this is the cleanest published recipe for learning from *unlabeled* live traffic: user inputs arrive without labels, and TTPO shows how to extract a training signal anyway. Directly on-brief for the consent/input-learning line.
- **Engine-training value:** Pseudo-label agreement rate per prompt is itself a difficulty/uncertainty feature; agree/disagree rollout split produces preference-style pairs without human labels.
- **Skeleton value:** consent/input-learning (primary), brain.

### 8. SIA — Self Improving AI with Harness & Weight Updates (Hexo Labs)

- **What it is:** SIA is the first open framework whose feedback agent updates **both** levers in one loop: the task agent's harness (prompts/tools/logic) AND its weights (LoRA r=32 on gpt-oss-120b). A Feedback-Agent (Sonnet 4.6 in the paper's runs) reads trajectories + reward metrics each generation and chooses the next move — scaffold edit, weight update, or both — and even selects the RL algorithm (PPO+GAE, GRPO, or Entropic Advantage Weighting) from reward shape. Standing caveat from secondary analysis: both levers optimize the same fixed verifier → coupled Goodhart risk.
- **Verdict:** TEST — closest existing open implementation of the skeleton's promotion loop; run it on a disposable task before designing our own loop controller.

### 13. AIA Forecaster — Bridgewater AIA Labs technical report
- **Post:** https://www.facebook.com/0xSojalSec/posts/pfbid08SeuZRPdSc3hdm57BpahY9oGnS2m67DXwnCTdwoeDZ5jx9FJRT1H36hJ4wyw1HLQl (paper first-page broadcast)
- **What it is:** The most operationally complete published recipe for LLM forecasting: M independent agentic forecasters with full search discretion over high-quality news sources → a supervisor agent reconciling divergent forecasts via targeted fact-checking → statistical calibration (Platt scaling, proven equivalent to generalized log-odds extremization) to counter LLM hedging toward 50%. Plus an exhaustive foreknowledge-bias (information-cutoff leakage) analysis.
- **Provenance:** Broadcaster is a recreator; the paper is primary. Source: arXiv:2511.07678 (Alur, Stadie, Kang et al., Bridgewater AIA Labs, Nov 2025). Verified numbers [verified]: ForecastBench market subset Brier 0.0753 vs superforecasters 0.0740 (statistically indistinguishable); new harder benchmark MarketLiquid (1,610 liquid-market questions): AIA 0.1258 vs market consensus 0.1106 standalone, but a 67/33 market/AIA blend scores 0.106 — better than either; **search ablation: removing search collapses Brier 0.1002 → 0.3609** (worse than always answering 50%); ensemble of many runs is essential (single runs unstable); Platt scaling beats isotonic regression in the small-calibration-data regime (Brier 0.1076 calibrated vs 0.1140 raw in the operational-recipe summary).
- **Verdict:** TEST — the forecasting-side architecture for the skeleton's ForecastBench entry: multi-forecaster ensemble + supervisor reconciliation + Platt calibration + strict cutoff discipline. Every piece is specified enough to implement.
- **Engine-training value:** Resolved binary questions with (forecast, outcome) pairs = calibration training set; Platt coefficient √3 ≈ 1.73 as the extremization prior; foreknowledge-bias test protocol as a data-hygiene feature (leakage flag per retrieval result).
- **Skeleton value:** brain (forecasting head), benchmark program, data pipeline.

### 14. ForecastBench itself — the dataset and submission protocol (via Jheng-Hong Yang's post + FRI sources)
- **Post:** https://www.facebook.com/yang.d.mie/posts/pfbid02cA1yDUPk4nQ8d7jHTn6rE33P8BWhxxVH8Zhyedkm3yuVWCd7z5D7UhsVciyibYsSl (consultant's share with difficulty-adjusted Brier scatter + parity projection)
- **What it is:** ForecastBench (Forecasting Research Institute; ICLR 2025 paper, Karger et al. 2024) is a dynamic, contamination-free benchmark: questions concern future events with no known answer at submission time. Current protocol: rounds every two weeks; question set published 00:00 UTC on the due date; **500 questions** (250 market-sourced from Kalshi/Manifold/Metaculus/Polymarket + 250 dataset-generated from ACLED, DBnomics, FRED, Wikipedia, yfinance); forecasts due 23:59:59 UTC same day; ≥95% coverage of both halves required for leaderboard inclusion; two boards — Baseline (out-of-the-box) and Tournament (any scaffolding allowed).
- **Provenance:** Yang's post is a competent recreator summary of the FRI paper; figures verified against FRI's paper and submission wiki. Primary sources: paper (ICLR 2025 proceedings), datasets repo https://github.com/forecastingresearch/forecastbench-datasets (CC-BY-SA-4.0, updated nightly), HF mirror https://huggingface.co/datasets/forecastingresearch/forecastbench-datasets, submission wiki (github.com/forecastingresearch/forecastbench/wiki). Registration: register.forecastbench.org; next public round called out by FRI for **November 9, 2026**. Funding note: Open Philanthropy funds the benchmark until mid-2027.
- **Verdict:** TEST — entering the Tournament leaderboard is the skeleton's public forecasting proof; the submission spec is fully documented and the question/forecast/resolution datasets are downloadable today for offline rehearsal.
- **Engine-training value:** The datasets repo is a growing labeled corpus: questions + submitted forecasts (with reasoning text, consulted URLs, searches) + resolutions. Labels: yes, resolved binary outcomes. Location: GitHub repo + HF mirror. Features: forecaster reasoning traces per question are distillation material for our own forecasting head.
- **Skeleton value:** benchmark program (primary), data pipeline.

### 15. Semantic Calibration — Apple paper (Nakkiran et al.)
- **Posts:** https://www.facebook.com/cecile.tamura/posts/pfbid07JB7tnPh3HfMJDSfgTV17YpW1pYvTPX1tZFJgbfVQM6ysB2MyR4vG7SMDVExGBpBl (paper share with commentary thread) and two further shares of the same paper in the corpus (facebook.com/eruciform post; "The World of Data" post) — counted once.
- **What it is:** "Trained on Tokens, Calibrated on Concepts" (Apple; ICLR 2026) introduces B-calibration: calibration parameterized by equivalence classes (semantic classes of answers). Findings: base LLMs are remarkably semantically calibrated on open-domain QA (smECE ≈ 0.030–0.036 on their reliability plots) despite never being trained for it; **RL instruction-tuning systematically breaks it; chain-of-thought also breaks it** (the model can't predict its final answer class before generating). Mechanism: calibration emerges from local loss optimality in next-token prediction.
- **Provenance:** Paper shares are faithful. The lead post's commentary goes beyond the paper — its caption argues "RLHF causes hallucinations by rewarding confident answers," which is the commenter's inference, not the paper's claim; comment thread extends further into information-theory speculation. Paper itself: arXiv:2511.04869 (v1 Nov 10, 2025; Apple, Aug 24, 2026 revision in the arXiv HTML); OpenReview ICLR 2026 record.
- **Verdict:** TEST — gives the skeleton a measurable calibration target and a warning with teeth: our post-training recipe (RLHF/DPO/GRPO + CoT) can be expected to *degrade* native calibration unless the benchmark program tracks semantic calibration (B-calibration / smECE) as a first-class metric alongside Brier.
- **Engine-training value:** Metric: smECE under semantic collapsing of sampled answers; feature: pre-generation distribution over answer classes (the paper's predictor of when calibration will hold). Data: sampled answer sets per question (self-generated, no external labels needed beyond correctness).
- **Skeleton value:** benchmark program (primary), brain (confidence reporting).

## X3 — @karansdalal — TTT-E2E: LLMs that continue training during deployment (Stanford/NVIDIA/Astera)
Post: https://x.com/karansdalal/status/2010774529120092481 (Jan 12, 2026 announcement; surfaced via Blockchain.News coverage quoting the Stanford AI Lab announcement; PRIMARY SOURCE VERIFIED: arXiv:2512.23675, "End-to-End Test-Time Training for Long Context," Tandon, Dalal et al., submitted 29 Dec 2025; code public at github.com/test-time-training/e2e)
1. WHAT IT IS — A continual-learning mechanism, not a claim: long-context modeling reframed as continual learning. A standard Transformer with sliding-window attention keeps training at test time via next-token prediction on the context it reads, compressing context into MLP weights; the initialization is meta-learned at training time so the model is good AFTER its test-time updates. Verified results from the abstract: at 3B scale / 164B training tokens, TTT-E2E scales with context like full attention (Mamba 2 and Gated DeltaNet do not), with constant inference latency — 2.7× faster than full attention at 128K context. Coverage adds a LongBench recall claim (+15% after 100K tokens of experience) — that figure is the coverage's, not the abstract's; treat as CITED.
2. WHERE TO FIND IT — The post above; paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.23675; code github.com/test-time-training/e2e (JAX, per the deep-context research doc that cites it).
3. HOW TO USE IT — This is the leading public candidate mechanism for Prompt 2's "honest minute": weight-level learning from incoming context at inference, with a meta-learned initialization — the design question for the skeleton is whether user-context TTT updates stay session-local (safe, ZDR-compatible) or feed the staged-candidate pool (needs the Fuel-Line-2 consent architecture before any of it trains anything shared).
4. WHICH SYSTEM — Skeleton continual-learning loop (Fuel Line 3 mechanisms) and serving layer (constant-latency long context changes the provider's cost math).
5. CREATIVE ANGLES — For GSE specifically: a game-week context (usage, health, matchup notes) compressed into weights at inference is a "the model read the week" mechanism that retrieval alone does not give — the reasoning layer could run TTT over the week's verified corpus per game window, then discard the session weights, keeping the improvement ephemeral but real.
6. ## X4 — @koustavagoswami — "Spurious Advantage Hidden in GRPO": your GRPO model may be learning to guess (SignBalance fix)
Post: x.com status ID NOT exposed by the mirror (read verbatim via Instalker profile mirror, crawled 2026-11-07; post links arXiv:2609.04063 — PRIMARY SOURCE VERIFIED: "Spurious Advantage Hidden in GRPO," Wang, Basu, Goswami, Yu, Tao (RIT / Adobe Research), submitted 3 Sep 2026)
1. WHAT IT IS — A defect in GRPO's advantage estimator, with a one-line fix. GRPO's per-rollout magnitude is a pure function of within-group correct/wrong counts, so a rollout that guesses a bounded answer gets the same gradient as one that reasoned to it — the "spurious advantage." A zero-reasoning policy that always outputs "2" scores 2.69% on MATH, so the guessable floor is real even on open-ended-looking benchmarks. The fix, SignBalance: make the magnitude composition-free — keep the verifier sign, use a global scale, restore zero-mean via a stop-gradient per-class rescale. Parameter-free, no extra model, drop-in. Results as posted (Qwen2.5-0.5B): +6.26 SAT-Math, +5.90 AQuA over GRPO; on par on open-answer math; ahead on average for multi-turn search agents. Paper abstract confirms the three spurious cases (bounded-answer tasks, bounded sub-cases inside open sets, search agents with many paths to one answer) and that code "will be released."
2. WHERE TO FIND IT — The mirror above; paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04063.
3. HOW TO USE IT — Anywhere the skeleton (or the GSE reasoning layer) uses GRPO/RLVR with verifiable rewards on bounded-answer tasks — which includes multiple-choice-style benchmark items and pick/pass decisions framed as bounded choices: swap the advantage estimator, or at minimum measure the guess-floor of the task set before trusting GRPO gains.
4. WHICH SYSTEM — Skeleton post-training (RLVR/GRPO stage) and benchmark program (guess-floor auditing of MMLU/ARC-style items).
5. CREATIVE ANGLES — The lens generalizes past GRPO: any group-relative reward in the crowd-RLHF queue (Prompt 2, Fuel Line 2) inherits the same failure — preference pairs built from within-group comparisons can reward lucky/verbose/sycophantic responses indistinguishably from good ones. The guess-floor measurement (run a zero-reasoning policy, score it) is a cheap audit for every bounded task the program touches, including GSE's own bounded market questions.
6. RISKS — Results at 0.5B scale in the post (paper says "different scales," details in-paper); code not yet released per the abstract; single-paper result, not yet replicated.

The mathematics of forecasting: a frontier map (October 2026)
Forecasting mathematics in 2026 is defined less by new forecasting methods than by sharp boundaries: iff-theorems saying exactly which processes, spectra, distribution families and reliability notions are learnable, matched by impossibility theorems saying what no procedure can do. Across eleven clusters and 768 verified works, the same pattern recurs. The classical object, the conditional law L(Xt+h∣Ft)L(Xt+h​∣Ft​), is no longer studied only through its formulas, which are the Wiener–Kolmogorov projection, the filtering equations and the Boltzmann limit. It is studied through four questions. Can it be learned from one history? Can it be certified (calibration, coverage, anytime-valid comparison)? Is it valid over a given horizon (predictability limits, kinetic validity horizons, blowup)? And how should several versions of it be combined (pooling, markets)? The decisive 2024–2026 results sit at the boundaries between these questions, and the most contested claims concern machine-learned forecasters that perform well empirically but sit outside every existing theorem.
The document has six parts before the reviews: the map with its figures, nine cross-cutting theses, a hypothesis ledger with evidence status, ranked reading lists, open problems and an audit of the starting document. Part VII answers a follow-up question: what forecasting theory implies for scaling, and whether mainstream ML training is aligned with it. Part VIII contains the eleven cluster reviews and a review of 2025–2026 preprints from strong research groups, followed by a methods note. Inline links point to the DOI or arXiv record. "Preprint" means not refereed as of 23 October 2026, and "announcement" means a non-refereed release by a company or institution.

full_text:
📷
Figure 1. Each point is one verified work, placed by publication year. The year axis is logarithmic in years before 2027, which expands the frontier. Bubble area scales with citation count, so recent work appears small because citations have not yet accrued, not because it is less important. Labels mark the two highest-scoring works per cluster; for the two new clusters below the dashed line, they mark the top two expert must-reads.
📷
Figure 2. Number of records in one cluster tagged as connecting to another, summed in both directions; tags were assigned by the cluster reviewers. The map splits into a statistical block and a dynamical block, and ML forecasting is the main bridge between them (63 links to evaluation, 51 to dynamics). Learning & scaling connects mainly to foundations (26) and ML forecasting (23). ML alignment connects mainly to evaluation (21), ML forecasting (20) and calibration (18). Neither new cluster has any tagged links to filtering, and PDE limits has none to evaluation or calibration. These empty cells are gaps in the literature (thesis 9; Part VII).
Part II. Nine cross-cutting theses
1. Forecastability is now a characterized property
The oldest negative result, Bailey's theorem that no procedure consistently estimates the next-step conditional probability for every stationary ergodic binary process (Györfi et al. 1998), has turned into a programme of exact characterizations. Distribution-dependent learning curves fall into three regimes: exponential, linear, or arbitrarily slow (Bousquet et al. 2021). The processes that admit optimistically universal online learning, meaning a single rule that succeeds whenever any rule can, are now characterized for arbitrary binary concept classes (Hanneke & Wang 2025). The capstone is Blanchard, Shetty & Rakhlin 2026 (COLT 2026; the seed called it a preprint). A family of adaptively chosen distributions permits VC-dependent regret if and only if it is generalized smooth, and the same condition characterizes private learnability. The dynamical analogue appeared the same year. Colbrook, Mezić & Stepanenko 2026 give convergent, certified Koopman spectral algorithms under explicit conditions. Without those conditions, they build adversarial systems on which no single-limit procedure can succeed, so the task requires nested limits. Even the closed-form classical solution has a computability boundary: the Wiener–Kolmogorov MMSE is computable for strictly positive computable spectral densities, but #P1#P1​-complete to compute, and not Turing-computable for some differentiable ones (Boche et al. 2024). The common lesson is that the question "can this be forecast?" has no answer until the class and the success criterion are fixed. The most important open direction is rates: nearly all of these characterizations are qualitative (consistency, or an iff for a regret order), and the log-loss, real-valued versions most relevant to probabilistic forecasting are missing.

title: topic-forecasting-full.txt
full_text:
2. Reliability splits into a hierarchy, each level with its own price
Statistics and theoretical computer science have converged on the same conclusion: "calibrated" names a family of guarantees with distinct costs. For binary sequential forecasting in ℓ1ℓ1​-ECE, the long-standing T2/3T2/3 barrier fell (Dagan et al. 2025, STOC 2025). The current bracket is Ω(T0.54389)Ω(T0.54389) against O(T0.662942)O(T0.662942), the upper bound from a preprint (Dai & Fishelson 2026). Changing the measure changes the answer. Distance to calibration admits O(T)O(T​) (Qiao & Zheng 2024), and calibration decision loss admits O(log⁡T/T)O(logT/T​) on average (Hu & Wu 2024). Groupwise guarantees cost strictly more. Online multicalibration is Θ(T2/3)Θ(T2/3) up to logarithmic factors (Collina et al. 2026a), and batch multicalibration needs Θ~(ε−3)Θ~(ε−3) samples against ε−2ε−2 for marginal calibration (Collina et al. 2026b, to appear at SODA 2027). Exact truthfulness of calibration measures is impossible sequentially, while approximate truthfulness is attainable (Gokul et al. 2026). Conformal prediction has the matching pattern. Distribution-free conditional coverage is impossible (Barber et al. 2021), coverage over a class of covariate shifts is the strongest achievable relaxation (Gibbs et al. 2025), and a Neyman–Pearson argument identifies the efficiency-optimal valid set (Tibshirani et al. 2026, preprint). On the statistics side, TT-calibration hierarchies (Gneiting & Resin 2023) organize the same distinctions for distributional forecasts. Synthesis. These are not competing definitions but a lattice of guarantees, priced in rounds or samples. The unanswered question is which point in the lattice a given downstream decision needs. The decision-calibration line (Hu & Wu 2024; Roth–Shi; Noarov et al.) is the only programme answering that question directly.
3. Proper scoring rules are the common currency
Strictly proper scores (Gneiting & Raftery 2007, 5,749 OpenAlex citations and the top-ranked work in this map's importance score) now appear in five other places. Robust aggregation pairs each proper score with a max-min optimal pooling rule: Brier with linear pooling, log with logarithmic pooling (Neyman & Roughgarden 2023). Cost-function prediction markets are exactly dual to follow-the-regularized-leader expert algorithms (Chen & Vaughan 2010). Operational ML weather ensembles are trained by minimizing (almost) fair CRPS (Lang et al. 2026) and evaluated by CRPS (Price et al. 2024). LLM event forecasting is ranked by Brier score (Karger et al. 2025). Signature-kernel scores extend strict propriety to laws of whole trajectories (Issa et al. 2023). Elicitability theory sets the limits of this currency: (VaR, ES) is jointly but not separately elicitable (Fissler & Ziegel 2016), tail properties cannot be ranked by expected scores (Brehmer & Strokorb 2019), and evaluating only on extremes causes the forecaster's dilemma (Lerch et al. 2017). The unifying open problem is discrimination: propriety is necessary, but finite-sample power against relevant misspecification, especially of multivariate dependence, has no general theory. Practice built on CRPS-only training and evaluation therefore rests on an untheorized step (thesis 7).

title: topic-forecasting-full.txt
full_text:
4. Evaluation has become sequential and anytime-valid
The most consequential methodological shift in evaluation is from fixed-sample tests of Diebold–Mariano and Giacomini–White type to e-values and test martingales. These are valid under optional stopping and continuous monitoring, without stationarity assumptions. The foundations are the e-value calculus (Vovk & Wang 2021) and the game-theoretic synthesis (Ramdas et al. 2023). The forecasting-specific results are e-values for comparing probability forecasts (Henzi & Ziegel 2022), confidence sequences for score differences between sequential forecasters (Choe & Ramdas 2024), and e-backtests for VaR and ES (Wang, Wang & Ziegel 2025). The game-theoretic view also reconnects evaluation to foundations, since Ville's inequality, Shafer–Vovk probability and defensive forecasting are one theory seen from different sides. The main limits are bounded-score assumptions (the log score and heavy-tailed CRPS are not covered) and power loss against a prespecified horizon.

5. Predictability limits: intrinsic versus practical, and AI is inside the limit

Lorenz's 1969 multiscale result, where the horizon stays finite as initial error tends to zero, was restated as a precise PDE question by Palmer, Döring & Seregin 2014. The best quantitative estimate for midlatitude weather is about two weeks, and a tenfold reduction in initial error adds at most about five days (Zhang et al. 2019). The 2023–2026 evidence does not support the popular hypothesis that AI breaks this barrier. The measured gains of ML weather models amount to roughly one day of practical lead time, inside the intrinsic limit. Deterministic emulators misrepresent small-perturbation error growth (Selz & Craig 2023), which would falsely imply unlimited predictability. The often-cited "23-day" improvement (Vonich & Hakim 2024) is computed through a model whose error growth is suspect for exactly this reason. Skill beyond two weeks comes from slow, boundary-forced components that physics ensembles also exploit. Underneath, the mathematics is moving. Positive Lyapunov exponents are now proved for Galerkin truncations of 2D stochastic Navier–Stokes (Bedrossian & Punshon-Smith 2024). Spontaneous stochasticity, the idea that deterministic equations with deterministic data yield an intrinsically random but universal law, has one ODE theorem (Drivas, Mailybaev & Raibekas 2023) and a renormalization-group framework for discrete models (Mailybaev & Raibekas 2023). It remains a conjecture for Navier–Stokes. If it holds, the positive side of the real butterfly effect is that individual realizations are unpredictable while their law is predictable and universal. That would make probabilistic forecasting the only well-posed kind at long horizons.

title: topic-forecasting-full.txt
full_text:
6. Validity horizons of statistical descriptions
A second sense of "how far ahead" asks for how long a statistical description, rather than a trajectory, remains a valid forecast. The landmark is the hard-sphere theorem of Deng, Hani & Ma 2024 (Annals of Mathematics, forthcoming). The Boltzmann equation is the correct forecast for as long as its regular solution exists, so the kinetic forecast's validity horizon equals the lifespan of the limit PDE. Its continuation to fluid equations, in iterated limits (Deng, Hani & Ma 2025, preprint), is the strongest current claim on Hilbert's sixth problem. Uncertainty quantification lags the mean forecast: fluctuation and large-deviation theory is still short-time out of equilibrium (Bodineau et al. 2023). For long-run statistics under parameter change, linear response is proved for Axiom A, noisy and some intermittent systems (Ruelle 2009; Hairer & Majda 2010; Dragičević et al. 2025). It remains unproved for any open class of deterministic non-uniformly hyperbolic flows, which is the setting of climate response forecasting. Berger's emergence adds a third failure mode, distinct from chaos and from non-differentiable response. The set of statistical descriptions that orbits settle into can be super-polynomially complex. The Annals construction of analytic pseudo-rotations (Berger 2026) disproves Birkhoff's 1941 conjecture and gives examples with maximal local emergence, and whether high emergence is typical is open (Berger 2026b, preprint).
7. Machine-learned forecasters work in practice but sit outside existing theorems
ML forecasting has the most empirical success and the least theorem coverage of any cluster. Probabilistic ML ensembles beat the ECMWF physics ensemble on marginal scores: GenCast was better on 97.2% of 1,320 targets (Price et al. 2024), and ECMWF's AIFS ENS has been operational since July 2025. Four theoretical gaps stand out. First, FGN trains only on per-location marginal CRPS yet reproduces joint spatial structure (Alet et al. 2025, preprint). A marginal score cannot identify a joint law, so the structure must come from the architecture, and no theorem says when this suffices. Second, operator learning faces a curse of parametric complexity: smoothness alone forces parameter counts exponential in 1/ε1/ε (Lanthaler & Stuart 2025). Whatever structure emulators exploit (dissipativity, attractor dimension, locality) is unidentified. Third, extrapolation fails at the edge of the training support, which is where warnings matter: models trained without Category 3–5 cyclones cannot forecast Category 5 storms (Sun et al. 2025). Fourth, time-series foundation models lead curated benchmarks, but reusing LLM weights adds nothing (Tan et al. 2024). For chaotic systems, a context-parroting baseline matches foundation models, and accuracy scales with the attractor's fractal dimension (Zhang & Gilpin 2025, preprint). Apparent in-context forecasting may therefore be nearest-neighbour analog forecasting. On the filtering side, guided diffusion for data assimilation cannot be both exact and efficient in general, assuming one-way functions exist (Gupta et al. 2024). The only positive theorem linking ML surrogates to assimilation needs strong inflation (Sanz-Alonso & Waniorek 2025). A related line treats large sequence models as approximate Bayes or Solomonoff mixtures. Supporting evidence comes from compression (Delétang et al. 2024) and linearly decodable belief states (Shai et al. 2024). Against it, LLMs violate martingale properties that any Bayesian predictor must satisfy (Falck et al. 2024). That hypothesis is contested and active.

title: topic-forecasting-full.txt
full_text:
8. Aggregation: simple rules win for statistical reasons; markets aggregate only under idealizations
The forecast-combination puzzle, where equal weights beat estimated weights, is understood as a bias–variance trade-off, and simple quantile ensembles were the most reliable forecasters in the COVID-19 hubs. The pooling theorems are sharp. Linear pools of calibrated forecasts are miscalibrated (Ranjan & Gneiting 2010), which motivates extremizing. Extremizing after averaging has a worst-case justification under "projective substitutes" (Neyman & Roughgarden 2022), but no scheme beats a trivial benchmark with many conditionally iid experts (Arieli et al. 2018). Market aggregation holds for separable securities and idealized traders (Ostrovsky 2012). It breaks under ambiguity aversion, and no security aggregates for every information structure (Galanis et al. 2024). The first large-scale evidence from Polymarket and Kalshi is still mostly in working papers, and it points both ways. Prices track realized frequencies (Reichenbach & Walther 2025), but identical contracts diverged across venues in 2024 (Clinton & Huang 2025), and wash-trading-like activity makes volume an invalid proxy for crowd size (Sirolly et al. 2025). In asset returns, out-of-sample predictability is weak (Welch & Goyal 2008). The "virtue of complexity" (Kelly, Malamud & Zhou 2024) is contested by the argument that P≫TP≫T random-feature forecasts reduce to volatility-timed momentum (Nagel 2025, working paper). That dispute is itself about implicit aggregation over a huge ensemble. LLM forecasters enter as highly correlated experts. ForecastBench showed superforecasters ahead in 2024 (Karger et al. 2025), and the Forecasting Research Institute's July 2026 update reports several systems statistically indistinguishable from superforecasters (FRI 2026, blog post). Leakage critiques (Paleka et al. 2025) keep this contested.
9. Three structural gaps, and AI-generated proofs as a new kind of evidence
Three weak links appear in Figure 2. First, filtration-sensitive evaluation. Adapted optimal transport gives the right geometry for comparing forecasting models that differ in when information is revealed (Bartl, Beiglböck & Pammer 2026; Backhoff-Veraguas et al. 2020). Every proper score in use, including signature scores, is blind to filtrations, so no evaluation method yet measures what adapted OT measures. Second, single-path estimation. Adapted-distance estimation, Koopman rates and universal-prediction rates are proved mostly for iid paths or reversible stochastic dynamics, whereas forecasting usually observes one long nonstationary trajectory. Third, PDE results and statistical evaluation do not meet. Validity-horizon theorems say nothing about calibration of the resulting forecasts, and no evaluation theory targets kinetic or fluid forecasts.

title: topic-forecasting-full.txt
full_text:
Separately, 2026 brought AI-generated mathematics into the evidence base. In September 2026 OpenAI released a manuscript and Lean formalization claiming smooth, finite-energy, forced blowup for 3D Navier–Stokes on R3R3 and T3T3, which corresponds to Clay alternatives (C) and (D) (OpenAI 2026, announcement). A companion manuscript claims unforced 3D Euler blowup. Clay described the problem as apparently settled, announced a deliberately unhurried evaluation, and has awarded nothing. The unforced alternatives (A) and (B) are untouched. Independent checking is partial. A Part I reconstruction of the profile construction has appeared (Lei & Ren 2026, preprint). An audit documents mismatches between the prose and the Lean code and argues that a compiling formalization certifies the formal statement, not the paper (Bastounis, Circelli & Hansen 2026, preprint). There is also a priority dispute with the Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa and Alpöge–Buckmaster line (Alpöge et al. 2026, preprint). ML-assisted discovery of unstable singular profiles (Wang et al. 2025, preprint) belongs to the same shift. These are results whose verification standard is itself under debate, and this map labels them accordingly.

full_text:
## PART 1 — The 18 inventoried-only posts

### #24 — @sfdata9ers — missed-tackle team rankings through Week 7 (data: @pfref)
- Post: https://x.com/sfdata9ers/status/2115844929247166692
- **WHAT IT IS:** a full-league ranking of team missed tackles through Week 7. The timeline text exposes the endpoints: 1. DET, 2. TEN, 3. MIN at the top (fewest) … 30. PHI, 31. DEN, 32. CLE at the bottom (most). The middle of the table lives in the post's image, which could not be read this pass — gapped, not guessed.
- **SOURCE CHECK (the payload this post actually carries):** the attribution is real. Pro Football Reference publishes missed tackles as **MTkl** (and MTkl%) in its player-level Advanced Defense tables, publicly, updated Wednesdays — PFR's own pages state the advanced stats run through Week 7 of 2026 as of today. An independent PFR-sourced republication (BetMGM's missed-tackles table, updated Oct 28) reproduces the same shape: DET fewest by a wide margin (12), DEN most (56), CLE (51) and PHI (49) the next-worst cluster. Two mid-table swaps vs the post (TEN/MIN order, DEN/CLE order) are consistent with a one-week window difference between the post's Week 7 cut and the republication's later update — the post's endpoints are **CITED and cross-checked at headline level**, not scraped cell-by-cell.
- **HOW TO USE IT:** PFR does not publish a ready-made team ranking; the table is the sum of player MTkl on each team's Advanced Defense page. That is a summing job, not a data purchase — GSE can build the identical table in-house, weekly, for free, and timestamp it.
- **WHICH SYSTEM:** GSE engine, **matchups layer** (defensive tackling quality is a real YAC/explosives input) and it interlocks with the first run's #16: Minnesota's missed-tackle rank is the other half of the Flores profile — a defense that both manufactures negative plays and rarely whiffs is a different projection than either trait alone.
- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** missed-tackle rate against is an *offensive* stat too — the same PFR table, read from the ball-carrier side via player rushing/receiving advanced stats, identifies which RBs/WRs gain hidden yards against sloppy-tackling defenses. Nobody posts that version.
- **RISKS:** missed tackles are a charted stat; PFR's charting standard is consistent but single-source. Small counts early-season (DET at 12 is a 7-week sample).
- **FIRST TEST / VERDICT:** build the W1–7 team MTkl table from PFR and diff it against the post's visible endpoints; if it matches, the table becomes a standing weekly pull. **LEARN-ONLY.**

- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** funnels are two-sided — a defense that funnels to RBs is telling you its coverage removes WRs/TEs *or* that its pass rush forces checkdowns; separating those two causes (pressure rate vs coverage shell) turns a descriptive chart into a predictive one. That decomposition is the version worth building.

### #34 — @_avichawla (Avi Chawla) — prefix-aware LLM routing, explained
- Post: https://x.com/_avichawla/status/2115748674903130471
- **WHAT IT IS (mechanism):** an explainer of KV-cache-aware request routing for multi-GPU LLM serving. Production prompts share long prefixes (system prompt, tool definitions, conversation history); the GPU that served the last turn holds that prefix's KV cache. A cache-blind router sends the next turn to a cold GPU, which recomputes the whole prefix before generating a token. A prefix-aware router hashes the prompt block-by-block (each hash chained over everything before it), keeps a block-to-worker index of *locations* (never the tensors), routes to the worker holding the most matching blocks — Worker B with 4/4 blocks in his worked example — weighs load alongside locality so the warmest GPU doesn't get the longest queue, and updates the index from cache events so the next turn lands warm too. A small edit early in the prompt invalidates every block after it — the fragility is part of the mechanism.
- **THE BENCHMARK CLAIM — TRACED TO SOURCE:** the post's figures (p90 time-to-first-token 0.54s vs 92.5s random on 8 vLLM pods / 16 H100s) are a faithful retelling of **llm-d's own published benchmark** ("KV-Cache Wins You Can See," Sept 2025, engineers from IBM/Red Hat/Google/Alibaba/DaoCloud): precise prefix-aware scheduling hit p90 TTFT of 0.542s vs 31.1s for llm-d's earlier approximate scheduler and ~92s for random routing; throughput roughly doubled vs cache-blind routing. The post's "170x sooner" = 92.5 / 0.54. **Status: the post's numbers are VERIFIED as an accurate reproduction of the llm-d project's published results — and those results are a backer-run benchmark on a workload built to reward the technique**: 150 simulated tenants with 6,000-token shared contexts, total KV demand at ~73% of cluster capacity (6× any single pod). Independent commentary on the same benchmark is blunt: gains collapse toward zero when prefix share is low or cache is plentiful; llm-d wins exactly when cache is scarce and workload is skewed.
- **WHERE TO FIND IT:** llm-d (llm-d.ai, open-source Kubernetes distributed-inference project) for the system; Chawla's linked article covers the four caching layers (KV / prefix / prompt / semantic) from first principles.
- **HOW TO USE IT — AT GARRETT'S SCALE, HONESTLY:** he does not run multi-GPU vLLM clusters; fleet inference is API-based plus Kaggle jobs. The mechanism still transfers one level up, twice: (1) **stable-prefix discipline** — system prompts, tool definitions, and doctrine files kept byte-stable and front-loaded is what makes both provider-side prompt caching and tools like Headroom (this morning's Instagram find) pay; an early-token edit to a system prompt silently forfeits the cache everywhere. (2) **Session affinity in his own routing layer** — his gateway (OmniRoute/OpenRouter path) should pin a continuing conversation to the same provider/model endpoint for the same reason the router pins to Worker B: the warm cache lives there, and a mid-conversation provider hop is a cold-prefill tax on every turn.

### Deep dive A — #14 @DFSArmy / Kevin "Geek" Alan, "Cracking the DFS Code"

**What the public record actually contains (all mined free, per free-first routing):** the book — *Cracking the DFS Code: Revealing the Secrets to Winning Large-Field DraftKings NFL Tournaments* (Amazon; promo code "BOOK" gives 20% off DFS Army subscriptions, which tells you the book is also a funnel) — and the author's own long-form video walkthroughs on DFS Army's channels ("I Studied 230,000 NFL DFS Lineups" for main slate; a separate 350-lineup showdown study), whose published summaries expose the study's structure and headline results.

**THE SAMPLE — STATUS UPGRADE, STATED PRECISELY:** the post's "34,856 top lineups over 4 seasons" can now be traced to the publisher's own study description: **232,000 lineups analyzed across 376 major tournaments over four seasons, of which 35,000+ were top-100 finishing entries.** The post's 34,856 is evidently the exact count of that top-100 subset, and the discrepancy between "34,856" and "over 35,000" is rounding in the publisher's own summary, not invention. Status: **the figure is now corroborated by the publisher's primary public description of the study** — it is still publisher-stated, not independently reproduced (the underlying lineup-level data is not public, so no third party *can* reproduce it), and "top lineup" = top-100 finisher in a major tournament, which is now a *known* definition rather than an unknown one. That is as verified as this claim can get without buying the book and re-auditing — and it resolves the first run's open question about what "top" meant.

**The construction rules, with their stated evidence (author's published summaries):**
- **Stacks:** 87% of top-100 lineups used QB+1 or QB+2 (QB+1 ~50%, QB+2 ~38%, naked QB ~10%, concentrated in the expensive-rushing-QB era). **45% of winning stacks did not include the WR1** — the partner was a WR2/WR3/TE. Bring-backs appear in only ~50% — optional, not mandatory.
- **Ownership:** the "two sub-10%" rule — at least two skill players (RB/WR/TE) under 10% owned — held in **94%** of top-100 lineups. Average winning total ownership ≈ 126%: winners eat real chalk and differentiate surgically. Shape: ~2 sub-5% punts, ~2 sub-10%, ~3 in the 10–20% band, 1–2 pieces over 20%.

### #11 — @run_the_sims — the pass-rate Nash equilibrium
- Post: https://x.com/run_the_sims/status/2115788393728880945
- **WHAT IT IS (mechanism):** a game-theory argument about play-calling. Offense and defense are in a mixed-strategy game: if passing is under-used relative to its value, defenses that sell out against the run get punished until they rebalance; the equilibrium pass rate is the rate at which the defense is *indifferent* — where the marginal value of a pass equals the marginal value of a run against an adjusted defense. The post, citing **@SumerSports** data in a Kollmann/Tice quote chain, puts the equilibrium at ~55% against the NFL's actual ~54% — i.e., the league is already essentially at equilibrium, and "just pass more" is not a free lunch, because the observed rate is the *defense-adjusted* outcome.
- **LOGIC CHECK:** the argument's structure is sound — it is the standard indifference/minimax logic, correctly applied: an equilibrium rate is set by the opponent's best response, not by the offense's preference, and situational mix (score state, down-and-distance) explains small residuals. The digits (~55% vs ~54%) are cited to SumerSports and NOT reproduced this run — UNVERIFIED at the digit level; the range is directionally consistent with publicly known neutral-situation pass rates, which this run also did not re-derive.
- **WHERE TO FIND IT:** the post and its quote chain (@SumerSports is the data attribution).
- **HOW TO USE IT:** as a prior inside reasoning, not as a stat to quote: treat league pass rate as an equilibrium outcome; treat *team-level deviations* — a team passing far above/below its equilibrium given its personnel — as the actual signal (exploiting a defense, or leaking value).
- **WHICH SYSTEM IT PLUGS INTO:** GSE engine, **situations layer with matchups-layer consequences** — it disciplines two reasoning habits: (1) never credit/blame an offense for a play mix the opponent's defense induced (see #16 — Flores manufactures exactly this), and (2) when a team's mix moves, ask what changed in opponents' responses before crediting a coaching decision.
- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** invert the lens for content: "the defense chose this offense's play mix" is a publishable, non-obvious frame for a weekly piece, and it is *true* in a way most coverage never states. Pair with #7's beater catalog: equilibrium thinking says why the beater works — it reprices the defense's indifference point.

# Reproduce-or-refute checks — 2026-10-29

Two public analytics claims from today's X sweep, tested against public data computed in-house. Method and verdicts below; scripts and intermediate tables are in `~/workspace/x-for-you-sweep/raw/repro-koalaty/`.

---

## Check 1 — @KoalatyStats defensive target funnels (X, Oct 29)

Source post: https://x.com/KoalatyStats/status/2115811766294757392 — "2026: Where are NFL defenses allowing targets to go?" Headline claims: Green Bay allows the 2nd-highest target share to WRs; Detroit allows the 3rd-most pass attempts, the highest PROE, and the 2nd-highest target share to TEs; San Francisco and Atlanta funnel targets to RBs.

title: Reproduce-or-refute checks — 2026-10-29
full_text:
### Method
- **Data:** nflverse public releases, downloaded 2026-10-29 — `play_by_play_2026.csv.gz` (pbp) and `roster_2026.csv`.
- **Data vintage / completeness:** the current nflverse release contains **Weeks 1–7 only** (107 games, 18,738 plays). Week 8 is not yet in the release, so a through-Week-8 reproduction is **not computable from nflverse today**. All verdicts below are for the through-Week-7 window — which turns out to be the window the chart itself was almost certainly built on (see the pattern of exact rank matches).
- **Targets faced:** plays with `pass_attempt == 1`, excluding QB spikes and two-point attempts, with a non-null `receiver_id` → **6,805 targets** league-wide.
- **Position attribution:** `receiver_id` (GSIS) joined to `roster_2026.csv` on `gsis_id`, using the roster `position` field. **Zero unmapped receivers** (0 of 6,805). Distribution: WR 3,941 / TE 1,629 / RB 1,228 / QB 4 / OL 3. Target share allowed = targets to that group ÷ all targets faced (the 7 QB/OL trick-play targets stay in the denominator as OTHER). The roster file holds one row per player (no duplicate GSIS IDs) and lists no FBs in 2026, so RB needs no FB fold-in.
- **Pass attempts faced:** primary = count of `pass_attempt == 1` (excluding two-point attempts); cross-checked against dropbacks faced (`qb_dropback == 1`).
- **PROE allowed:** nflverse pbp carries `xpass`/`pass_oe` on 99.5% of dropbacks. PROE allowed = mean `pass_oe` of opposing dropbacks vs that defense. Six alternative definitions were also computed (per-attempt, per-game averaged, spikes excluded, pass-rate − xpass, win-probability 5–95% filter, single-week and Weeks 4–7 windows).
- **Mapping error modes (documented, not hidden):** roster position is the player's official listing, not his alignment on the play — hybrid players (a listed TE split wide, a listed WR in the backfield) are counted at their listed position; using nflverse participation data (actual alignment) would be the refinement. Listed position (`position`) was used rather than `depth_chart_position`. Neither choice is rank-material here: re-running target shares **including** two-point attempts leaves every claimed rank unchanged.

title: Reproduce-or-refute checks — 2026-10-29
full_text:
### Claim-by-claim verdicts

| # | Claim | Computed (W1–7) | Verdict |
|---|-------|------------------|---------|

| 2 | DET allows 3rd-most pass attempts | DET **279**, rank **3** (ATL 303, DEN 285); also rank 3 by dropbacks (288) | **REPRODUCED** (both definitions) |
| 3 | DET allows the highest PROE | DET **+29.3**, rank **7–11** across all six definitions; **MIA #1 (+34.7) under every season-long definition** | **NOT REPRODUCED** |
| 4 | DET allows 2nd-highest TE target share | DET **30.0%**, rank **2** (KC #1, 31.0%) | **REPRODUCED** |
| 5 | SF and ATL funnel targets to RBs | SF **23.7%** RB share, rank **2**; ATL **22.2%**, rank **3** (MIA #1, 24.1%) | **REPRODUCED** (both top-3; only MIA ahead of SF) |

Extract of the computed table (full 32-team table: `raw/repro-koalaty/defense_funnel_2026_w1-7.csv`):

| Defense | Att faced | Dropbacks | Targets | WR share | TE share | RB share | PROE allowed |
|---------|-----------|-----------|---------|----------|----------|----------|--------------|
| PHI | 252 | 265 | 229 | .673 | .188 | .140 | +30.6 |
| GB | 259 | 275 | 233 | **.657** | .180 | .163 | +26.6 |
| ATL | 303 | 307 | 270 | .552 | .226 | **.222** | +27.3 |
| DET | 279 | 288 | 243 | .551 | **.300** | .144 | +29.3 |

| MIA | — | — | — | — | — | **.241** | **+34.7** |

**On the PROE miss:** the gap is not a rounding or definition artifact. Miami leads Detroit by ~5.5 points under the baseline definition, and Detroit never ranks above 7th in any variant tried (per-attempt: 11th; per-game: 7th; WP-filtered: 10th; Week 7 only: 16th; Weeks 4–7: 7th). Either the chart's PROE column came from a non-standard formula the post doesn't disclose, or it is simply wrong. Everything else in the post reproduces *exactly* at Week 7 under the standard nflverse pipeline — which is what makes the PROE number stand out: the same pipeline that nails four of five claims refutes the fifth.

full_text:
## What this proves about borrowing charts vs computing in-house

1. **The public-chart ecosystem is reproducible almost for free.** Four of five KoalatyStats headline claims and both sfdata9ers endpoints rebuild exactly from two public files (nflverse pbp + rosters; one PFR page) in a few minutes of compute. Nothing in either chart required proprietary data — GSE's warehouse can generate both tables weekly, on its own schedule, with its own definitions written down.
2. **The one wrong number was invisible until reproduced.** The PROE claim sat in a chart whose other four numbers are exactly right. A borrowed chart imports its author's errors with no flag attached; the in-house table is what let the error be isolated to a single column. That is the doctrine in miniature: the reasoning is the product, and reasoning you cannot recompute is reasoning you are renting.
3. **Definition choices are the whole game.** Every verdict above turned on stated definitions (spikes and two-point plays out, roster position over alignment, per-dropback PROE). The borrowed charts state none of theirs. In-house, the definitions live next to the numbers, so a claim can be re-run when the definition is challenged.
4. **Known limits of the in-house route, honestly:** position attribution by roster listing rather than on-play alignment (participation data is the upgrade path), and nflverse's release lag — Week 8 was complete on the field before it existed in the public pbp file, so a borrowed chart can occasionally be *fresher* even when it is less checkable.

**Bottom line:** @KoalatyStats — 4 of 5 claims REPRODUCED exactly, PROE claim NOT REPRODUCED (Miami, not Detroit, allows the most over-expectation passing). @sfdata9ers — endpoints REPRODUCED (DET fewest) with two adjacent-order swaps (CLOSE). Both tables now exist in-house and can be regenerated weekly from `raw/repro-koalaty/repro.py` plus the PFR scrape.

*Run completed 2026-10-29 ~12:07 CT. Data: nflverse releases and pro-football-reference.com as of that date.*

- **What it is:** The canonical public explanation of the seam-shifted wake (SSW): a pitch's seams, held in a fixed orientation, trip the boundary layer asymmetrically and produce a wake that pushes the ball sideways — movement **not** explained by the Magnus effect, which is why some changeups and sinkers break "the wrong way" relative to their spin.

- **Transfer beyond sports:** Boundary-layer tripping by surface texture is general aerodynamics — the same physics governs any spinning or non-spinning projectile with surface features (industrial sprays, sports projectiles, drone rotors at low Reynolds number).
- **Autonomy + structure:** A flight-model ingest schema needs seam orientation as a state variable alongside spin axis/rate; without that field, SSW movement is unexplainable residual forever.
- **Second-order:** Pairs with A3/A4 (the notes and the fitted model) into a complete stack: phenomenon → rigid-body explanation → fitted detector.

## A. Headline method finds (full dossiers)

### A1. Pressure-rate vs blitz-rate gap decomposition — @PocketContext (2116263789272432641) — LEARN-ONLY ★

- **What it is:** For each 2026 QB (33 charted, 29 with ≥150 dropbacks), plot pressure rate faced against blitz rate faced (Next Gen Stats) and read the **gap** between them. Pressure exceeds blitz most for Justin Herbert (+15.9 pts), Geno Smith (+12.1), Bryce Young (+11.8) — QBs getting pressured without blitzes, i.e. losing to 4-man rush/coverage. Blitz exceeds pressure for Michael Penix Jr. (+15.2), Caleb Williams (+13.9), Bo Nix (+2.9) — QBs beating the blitz or escaping it.
- **Construction (as-posted, author-stated):** rate gap = pressure% − blitz% per QB, season to date. The author states the bounding logic explicitly: the gap does **not** yield a true non-blitz pressure rate (some blitzes also produce pressures), but it bounds and ranks where pressure is coming from structurally. Author concedes the limit in-post — a rare, honest construction note.
- **Primary source:** NGS pressure/blitz splits. GSE computes this today from nflverse + NGS feeds it already pulls; no new data needed.
- **Engine layer:** matchups (OL vs front, QB vs pressure structure) — feeds directly into the Flores/pressure work already in the corpus (S108 family).
- **Companion post (2116178423458734457):** Herbert vs Love worked example — Herbert 42.1% pressure rate / 26.2% blitz faced (93/221 pressures, 21 sacks, 2.81s time to throw); Love 37.5% / 35.7% (123/328, 14 sacks, 2.58s). Same construction, two QBs, full counting stats in text.
- **Creative angle:** gap sign flips the coaching question — positive gap = fix protection/answers vs 4-man rush; negative gap = the QB is the pressure answer, blitz him less. Pre-game: rank the week's QBs by gap to find which defenses must blitz to get home (and are therefore exposed deep).
- **Risk:** NGS pressure attribution is model-based; single-season sample to Week 8; as-posted values unverified until reproduced.
- **Verdict:** LEARN-ONLY, **register-worthy**.

- Deserved margin: **GB +9.61**. Actual margin: GB +8. Luck gap (actual − deserved,

title: Repo dossier + reproduction — dgrifka/nfl_simulator ("Deserve-To-Win-O-Meter")
full_text:
## 1. WHAT IT IS

One deserve-to-win number per finished NFL game, computed only from the plays each
team ran. It is a **retrospective verdict, not a prediction and not a replay
engine** — the author says all three plainly.

The repo holds two different models, and telling them apart is the whole story of
this dossier:

**v1 (2026-08-31 → 2026-09-16, RETIRED; code only at tag `v1.4.3`, no longer in
`main`).** The event re-pricing engine the method post describes: for every play
whose outcome contained a coin flip — a fumble on the ground, a field-goal or
extra-point attempt, a dropped interception, a receiver drop — it replaced the
realized EPA with its expectation and bootstrapped the flips into a margin
distribution. It needed FTN charting (`is_interception_worthy`,
`is_catchable_ball`, available only from 2022), so its coverage changed by season.
The general-reader write-up is on Medium ("Who Deserved to Win? Pricing Luck in
NFL Games", @dmgrifka_64770) and describes v1 only.

**v2 — the "process meter" (shipped as library v2.1.0, 2026-09-23; current tag
v2.1.2) — the model of record, and the one that produced the CAR@GB post.** No
event re-pricing, no charting, no special teams. Each team-game is reduced to two
numbers from its scrimmage plays (pass/run with EPA, regular season, garbage time
kept, two-point tries out):

- **Success rate with the takeaway fold:** (K + T_s) / (N + T) — a team's own
  successes K over its own plays N, plus its takeaways T (interceptions + lost
  fumbles forced), each takeaway counting as one more play for the *taking* team,
  successful when the offense lost EPA on it (99.4% of takeaways qualify).
- **Yards per play with the asymmetric fold:** (Y + R) / N — takeaway return yards
  R are credited, but a takeaway is *not* a play in this denominator. That
  asymmetry is the entire difference between v2.0 (unreleased) and v2.1.

Likely points come from one OLS fit on 2016–2023 team-games (4,190 rows):
**points = −16.829 + 35.126 × success rate + 4.178 × yards per play** (in-sample
R² = 0.609). The weights ship as a committed 1 KB `weights.json` and are
pin-checked at load (`WEIGHTS_PIN` refuses any other fit); the library never
refits at score time.

The percent: per game, a dedicated RNG seeded from SHA-256(seed 0 ‖ game_id)
draws 40,000 times from three closed-form posteriors — weights ~ Normal(β̂, Σ̂),
each team's true rate ~ Beta(K+T_s+1, N−K+T−T_s+1), each team's true yards/play ~

title: Repo dossier + reproduction — dgrifka/nfl_simulator ("Deserve-To-Win-O-Meter")
full_text:
Normal(ȳ, s_y/√N) — forms the margin draw, and reports
**p_home = mean of Φ(margin draw / 5.4528)**, where 5.4528 is a "noise-once"
scale: the margin regression's residual SD (8.875) with the sampling noise the
draws themselves carry removed again, so noise is not counted twice. A game
scored alone reads identically to the same game inside a batch — verified by
design and by the stage-0 test suite (six reference percents pinned to 4
decimals; CIN_CLE 0.7488 is one of them, and this run hit it exactly).

Repo shape: `src/nfl_simulator/` (ingest, validate, paths, figure layer, and
`process_meter/` — plays/features/posterior/record/score/fit/readiness/weights),
`research/` (~100 numbered scripts — v1's evidence base, byte-frozen at v1.4.3),
`docs/research/` (76+ numbered decision documents; every gate pre-registered
before the fit that had to pass it), `tests/` (pytest; all but `-m slow` run
network-free), `docs/writeup/figures/`. The research record is unusually honest:
it publishes its failures, a known-defect register, and the components it
*refused* (special teams, field position, penalties, opponent adjustment,
dropped picks in v2) with the measurements behind each refusal.

This run's actual path (equivalent, documented in `run_repro.py`): the loaders
were pointed at a hand-built cache in the library's own layout
(`cache/pbp/pbp_<season>.parquet` + `cache/schedules.parquet`, built from the
same nflverse release files nflreadpy serves), frames were built with the
library's `team_game_features_foldn` + `production_posterior_foldn`, and scoring

title: Repo dossier + reproduction — dgrifka/nfl_simulator ("Deserve-To-Win-O-Meter")
full_text:
## 4. WHICH SYSTEM IT PLUGS INTO

**Primary: postgame grading — the results/ledger layer, not pick formation.**

- The meter answers "did the play deserve the result?" for a game already
  played. That is exactly the question GSE's official ledger and results posts
  need answered honestly: which wins were process and which were variance. Run
  it over every spotlight game after the final, store `p_home`, deserved points
  and the luck gap beside the graded card in the vault package.
- **Situations layer (descriptive context only):** a team's trailing luck gap
  (actual − deserved margin, summed over recent weeks) is a clean, reproducible
  "running hot/cold" descriptor for the reasoning trail. It must stay
  descriptive — see the author's own evidence in §6 before anyone treats it as
  a signal.
- **Not the matchup/usage/health layers, and never side selection.** The meter
  reads a finished game; it has no pregame form. Matchup-first doctrine already
  keeps post-hoc luck out of pick formation, and the author's testing agrees
  (§6). It also cannot price a market: its "likely points" are
  scrimmage-production points from a two-input regression, not a score
  projection — special-teams points are structurally absent from both sides.

title: Repo dossier + reproduction — dgrifka/nfl_simulator ("Deserve-To-Win-O-Meter")
full_text:
## 5. CREATIVE ANGLES

1. **Grade GSE's own card against deserve-to-win — worked example, this game.**
   The margin draws behind the percent are a full deserved-margin distribution,
   so any spread can be graded from the same run (extension beyond the author's
   claims — labelled as such): for CAR@GB, P(deserved margin > 3.5) = **84.2%**
   — the GB −3.5 position was process-backed, not a lucky cover. The points
   draws give a deserved-total distribution: mean **35.2**, P(deserved total <
   46.5) = **97.1%**, 89% interval [25.6, 44.7] — the Under 46.5, which survived
   the actual total landing on 46, was overwhelmingly the process side. A
   postgame card graded this way separates "we were right" from "we got away
   with one" in the ledger, in units language Garrett already uses.
2. **A weekly luck ledger as content.** The meter scores every game from free
   data in seconds. A Monday "who actually deserved it" table — deserved
   winner, luck gap, the poster's own "luck merchant" flag (won the game with a
   share ≤ 47%) — is a repeatable results-week content surface for the site,
   and it is settled-fact postgame material, not pick leakage.
3. **Cross-check for the engine's verdict JSON.** Where GSE's five-stage
   verdict and the meter disagree sharply on a finished game (verdict loved a
   side the process says was outplayed), that game goes on the review list.
   Two independent process reads disagreeing is a research lead; agreeing is a
   receipt.
4. **Benchmark harness for GSE's own luck ideas.** The repo's refused-component
   record (docs 09, 33, 61–62, 68) is a pre-registered graveyard of luck
   adjustments that did not survive measurement — fumble luck, sequencing,
   possession caps. Before GSE builds any luck adjustment of its own, this is
   the checklist of what already failed and why.
5. **The takeaway fold as a defensive-credit pattern.** The asymmetric fold
   (takeaway = a play in the rate, return yards but no play in yards/play) is
   a reusable way to credit defenses in GSE's own per-game team sheets without
   double-counting — it is the one modelling idea in v2 worth lifting even if
   the meter itself were not adopted.

title: Repo dossier + reproduction — dgrifka/nfl_simulator ("Deserve-To-Win-O-Meter")
full_text:
## 6. RISKS AND LIMITS

- **The description gap is the headline risk.** The account's method story
  (loose balls / field goals / drops re-priced) is v1's. The shipped v2 — the
  one producing today's numbers — contains **no field-goal, extra-point, drop,
  punt, kickoff, penalty or field-position component at all**. In this very
  game it never saw: Carolina's two made FGs (6 of their 19 points), Green
  Bay's missed XP, or Green Bay's lost kickoff-return fumble. Anyone citing
  the 88% as "the sim re-ran every bounce" is citing a model that no longer
  exists. v1's code survives only at tag v1.4.3 and additionally needed paid
  FTN charting.
- **Two inputs is a deliberate, severe compression.** Success rate + yards per
  play, no opponent adjustment (measured, found to be shrinkage), garbage time
  counted, no drive context. Two teams with identical rate/ypp get identical
  likely points wherever their drives started. "Deserved" means "deserved by
  scrimmage production volume/efficiency" — nothing more.
- **Scoreboard lean (author's own defect #4, accepted).** In 69.6% of games
  the percent moves toward the team that actually won. The meter partly
  ratifies the scoreboard it claims to audit; treat extreme agreement with
  the result as expected, not as independent confirmation.
- **Never held out, by design.** Brier 0.1436 / log loss 0.4376 on the 543
  gate games are descriptive statistics about a verdict on its own game. The
  author tested the forward-looking version and reports it plainly:
  **stripping luck did not improve next-game prediction** (the v2.1 arm's
  next-game log-loss gain was −0.0007 with a 95% interval straddling zero;
  adopted on definition, not on forecast gain). Any GSE use as a predictive
  input starts from that negative result, not from the headline percent.
- **EPA is the foundation, and EPA is nflverse's model.** "Success" = EPA > 0.
  nflverse occasionally revises historical pbp values; the repo carries a
  whole manifest-drift apparatus (doc 73) because a re-pull once moved numbers
  at the 1e-6 scale. A number quoted from a post is pinned to the author's
  pull; a later re-pull can move the third decimal. (This run pulled pbp on
  2026-10-30 and hit the published values exactly.)
- **The percent hides the interval.** CAR@GB's deserved-margin 89% interval
  is [−0.07, +18.98] — it nearly touches zero. The Φ-smoothing that produces

## The 20 dossiers

### #1 — @sfdata9ers — Defensive EPA/play allowed by quarter (FOOTBALL — full dossier)
- Post: https://x.com/sfdata9ers/status/2115963896129597592 · CATCH-UP TARGET CLOSED.
- **WHAT IT IS:** a 32-team table of defensive EPA/play allowed split by quarter (Q1/Q2/Q3/Q4/Overall), 2026 Weeks 1–7. Read from the chart: Minnesota is the league's best defense overall (−0.220) and collapses games late (Q4 −0.540); Seattle −0.115, Tampa Bay −0.108, Denver −0.049, Kansas City −0.043, Pittsburgh −0.041 overall; Buffalo is worst (+0.148) and uniformly bad across all four quarters (+0.121/+0.156/+0.149/+0.154). The method is plain nflverse-class EPA aggregated by quarter — the *split* is the contribution: it separates script/pace effects (Q1), halftime-adjustment quality (Q3), and closer strength (Q4) into four numbers per defense.
- **WHERE IT COMES FROM:** @sfdata9ers, powered by @FantasyPtsData per the account bio. The EPA values are CITED from the chart, not reproduced this run — but the construction is fully reproducible from nflverse play-by-play GSE already holds (EPA by posteam/defteam × quarter), and this account's earlier tables were reproduced in-house in the AM repro pass (missed tackles) and ON-CORPUS.
- **HOW TO USE IT:** one group-by on the warehouse pbp (defteam × qtr, EPA mean, Weeks 1–7). No new data source. The Q4 column is the one with prop/grading use: a defense at −0.540 in Q4 is a live-betting and 2H-card fact, and the 1H/2H split is exactly the breakout the 360° card standard already demands.
- **WHICH LAYER:** GSE engine **matchups layer** (defense quality by game phase), feeding the **situations layer** (halftime/2H releases) and the vault's 1H-subset breakout.
- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** (1) Pair the defensive quarter split with an offensive quarter split (the corpus already holds @sfdata9ers' QB EPA/play by quarter, ON-CORPUS) to build a phase-matrix per matchup — four mini-games instead of one. (2) Buffalo's flat-bad profile vs Minnesota's late-clamp profile are different *kinds* of bad/good: flat profiles price full-game markets, sloped profiles price half markets — the slope itself is a publishable reasoning line.
- **RISKS:** 7-week samples per quarter-cell are ~150–250 plays; Q4 EPA is score-state contaminated (leading defenses face pass-heavy scripts — which cuts both ways and must be stated, not hidden). Chart-read values carry reading error.

- Post: https://x.com/sfdata9ers/status/2115935459167940886 · CATCH-UP TARGET CLOSED.
- **WHAT IT IS:** throwaway rate per QB (throwaways as a share of attempts; min 70 attempts; data @FantasyPtsData), Weeks 1–7. Top: Bryce Young 12.7%, Bo Nix 11.5%, Jayden Daniels 11.2%, Caleb Williams 10.5%, Jalen Hurts 8.4%. Middle read from the chart: Murray 7.2%, Mahomes 6.8%, Darnold 6.8%, Maye 6.5%, Rodgers 6.5%, Allen 6.4%, Ward 6.2%, Jones 5.4%, Penix 4.9%, Stroud 4.9%, Herbert 4.4%, Cousins 4.3%, Brissett 4.3%, Prescott 4.0%, Lawrence 3.8%, Love 3.7%, Goff 3.1%. Bottom: Purdy 2.8%, Mayfield 2.8%, Winston 2.5%, Stafford 2.3%, Burrow 1.9%, Willis 1.3%, Lamar Jackson lowest at 1.0%. (A few mid-list ranks were partially legible in the capture; the endpoints and named values above were legible.) Throwaway rate is a *decision* stat: it prices how a QB resolves a dead play — throw it away, eat a sack, force it, or run.
- **WHERE IT COMES FROM:** charted data (@FantasyPtsData) — throwaways are a charting judgment, not a pbp field; nflverse pbp does not carry a reliable throwaway flag. Values CITED, not reproducible from public pbp — this is the boundary of the in-house repro program, and the dossier says so plainly.
- **HOW TO USE IT:** as a cited input with source pinned (FantasyPtsData definition), in combination: throwaway rate × pressure rate ≈ sack-avoidance profile. Young at 12.7% with GB's pressure night (see #15: 24 pressures, 2.29s time-to-pressure) is the same story told from both sides — he was throwing away because the alternative was sacks, and his −22 net passing yards under pressure is the cost side.
- **WHICH LAYER:** **matchups layer (QB behavior vs pass rush)** — the QB-behavior track that the corpus's two-clock TTT split (#21 PM run) and pocket-state EPA (#16 below) also feed. Direct prop relevance: high-throwaway QBs suppress INT props but also suppress completion volume; low-throwaway QBs (Jackson 1.0%) resolve dead plays by running or forcing — different prop shapes entirely.
- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** the list inverts a lazy narrative — the top of the list (Young, Nix, Daniels, Williams) is young QBs coached to live for the next down; the bottom is veterans who extend. As content, "who refuses to throw it away, and what it costs/earns" is a clean explainer with a real table behind it.

### #7 — @dair_ai — WM-Basin: black-box detection of distilled LLMs (Meta FAIR)
- Post: https://x.com/dair_ai/status/2115808882434158851 (pass-2 capture; payload from the opened post)
- **WHAT IT IS (VERIFIED at secondary coverage of the paper):** a spotlight on *Watermark Basins: Black-Box Detection of Distilled LLMs* (Meta FAIR / Meta Superintelligence Labs; arXiv:2610.37266 as reported; published Oct 27, 2026). The method, WM-Basin, detects whether a suspect model was trained on outputs from a watermarked teacher — using only the suspect model's generated text, no weights or logits. It passes that text through a clean probe model and reads gradient representations (how training on the text would move the probe's parameters); a student trained on watermarked traces leaves a measurable basin in that space. Reported results: **79% true-positive rate at 0.1% false-positive rate across 1,200 student models (135M–8.2B params, six architecture families, trained on OpenR1-Math reasoning traces), vs 29% for the best prior black-box token-level detector**; the signal survived quantization, pruning, and post-distillation RL, and weakened under clean-data fine-tuning and paraphrasing.
- **WHERE TO FIND IT:** arXiv:2610.37266 (as reported by the coverage); post at the URL above.
