- **HOW TO USE IT:** no install path assessed (paper-stage); the technique needs a probe model and gradient access to *it* (not to the suspect), so a Kaggle-GPU-lane replication on small students is conceivable but not scoped here.
- **WHICH SYSTEM IT PLUGS INTO:** Garrett's **model-routing stack and the NGS/arXiv research program** — provenance is a live question for a stack that routes across many third-party models (is this "new" model a distilled copy of a teacher?) and for eval hygiene generally (the same lab's watermark-radioactivity line detects benchmark contamination). - Post: https://x.com/The_Coach_A/status/2116135289852748090 (6:49 AM, Oct 30 — the newest post in this run)
- **WHAT IT IS:** A scheme post (MatchQuarters; full breakdown paywalled at matchquarters.com, linked) on Steelers DC Patrick Graham: as Big Nickel/base usage rises, Pittsburgh's slot defenders are sub-200 pounds, so Graham attacks *early downs* with a **37% run-blitz rate** — interior pressures on Mike "Cross" and Will "Dog" insert paths, paired with Fire Zone (3-under/3-deep) rotations behind them, *instead of* stunting the front. The pressure is a "forced fit": penetration cuts off the zone track while dropping safeties vise the box, guaranteeing a low-yardage down. The blitz is not primarily a pass weapon — it is run-fit insurance for a personnel weakness.
- **WHERE IT COMES FROM:** Cody Alexander (@The_Coach_A), film-based; the 37% figure is his charting, CITED. The graphic ("THE VISE") diagrams the funnel between the hashes vs the Saints.

# PART 1 — FULL DOSSIERS (football method first)

## D1 — @Timo_NFL — Playoff-leverage selection bias in dynamic-rating simulations (10-post thread, Oct 23)

**WHAT IT IS.** A methodological correction to a chart genre the whole industry publishes. Season simulations often update team ratings *inside* the simulation (a simulated Week 7 win raises the team's rating for simulated Weeks 8–18). If "playoff leverage" for this week's game is then computed by comparing playoff odds across sims filtered to wins vs sims filtered to losses, the number is inflated: the win-filter doesn't just select the game outcome, it also selects sims where the team drew a higher rating path — so the team wins more *future* games for reasons that have nothing to do with this game. His measurement for Week 7 games: the filter method inflates leverage by a factor of **1.3–1.6× per team**, with ~1.3 as the floor for any team still in the hunt. His published leverage chart corrects for this and shows the single-game effect only. His test: if a game truly doesn't matter, its leverage should be 0 — the filter method returns a positive number anyway, which proves the contamination.

**WHERE IT COMES FROM.** Timo Riske — verified as the author of PFF's playoff-picture series (PFF, 2021–2025), where playoff leverage is his signature chart and where his documented causal method is the *paired simulation*: copy each sim, flip only the game in question, and difference the outcomes. The thread is the same author explaining why the dynamic-ratings variant of the chart — used by other sim publishers — cannot be read at face value. Dynamic ratings exist for real reasons (they keep the sim from being overconfident off extreme current ratings, and the update factor K is a tuning lever), but they "do not necessarily reflect reality," and they poison the leverage filter.

**HOW TO USE IT / INPUTS.** Any Monte Carlo season sim with team ratings. Rule: compute leverage from paired/flipped sims or with ratings frozen at their pre-game values; never by outcome-filtering a dynamic-rating sim. The 1.3–1.6× factor is his measurement on his setup — the *mechanism* (conditioning on a post-outcome variable) is not in doubt, the exact factor is UNVERIFIED independently.

**WHICH LAYER.** Everything-else (season context / playoff picture) — and a standing audit question for any third-party sim output GSE cites, including the LineOfEvidence Sim Lab class of tools: *which leverage construction produced this number?*

## D2 — @PattonAnalytics — Play-Caller Evaluation Model v3.0 (Substack article read in full)

**Posts.** "Play Caller Tendencies 🎮" (Oct 22 — Declan Doyle 9th, Brad Idzik 11th ranked as first-time callers; David Blough 21st, Sean Mannion 29th), the tendency-vs-design follow-up, and the two "full breakdown of v3.0" posts linking the article (Oct 22).

**WHAT IT IS (verified at the primary source — pattonanalytics365.substack.com/p/evaluating-play-callers, "Evaluating Play Callers," Part III — Offense, published 2026-10-22).** A process-only play-caller rating built from six tendency components, deliberately *not* built from outcomes:
1. **Personnel diversification** — for every play, a model predicts the probability of 11/12/21/other personnel from the game situation; the component is the **Shannon entropy** of that distribution. Credit goes not for using many packages but for using them *without the situation giving them away*.
2. **Play-sequencing predictability** — whether the previous few calls predict the next call beyond what down/distance/score already explain.
3. **Play-sequencing volatility** — drive-to-drive variance of (2); two offenses can average the same predictability with very different shapes.
4. **PROE Plus** — pass rate over expectation combined with offensive pace (aggressiveness × tempo profile).
5. **Motion rate.**
6. **Play-action rate.**
The six are transformed, **oriented by their historical relationship to offensive EPA** (the "Y-aware" step — EPA is a compass, not an input), passed through **PCA**, weighted by variance explained, and combined into the rating. Callers are also grouped into four *style clusters*, explicitly not quality tiers. An "Easy Button %" (RPO + screen + play-action share) is computed but kept out of the score as a descriptive stat. Top of the board through Week 6: Shanahan and Reid; Payton near the top despite Denver's negative EPA/play — the author names that process/outcome gap as the model's point, not its flaw. His own limits, on the record: it is not a pure estimate of coaching value above replacement, it cannot see reads/protection adjustments/wrong routes, and the defensive version is exploratory only.

**HOW TO USE IT / INPUTS.** Play-by-play with personnel groupings (nflverse pbp carries personnel fields), down/distance/score state, and play-action flags (in nflverse). Motion rate is the one component needing charted data (Fantasy Points Data class) — five of six components are computable from public pbp. The sequencing components need a situation-conditioned call-prediction model (a multinomial model on state features; the residual predictability from recent-call features is the metric).

## D3 — @MagicSportsGuy — aDOT is six different numbers (measurement-provenance post, Oct 20)

## D5 — @jmthrivept — injury prognosis by mechanism + historical comps (Batch D; method posts Oct 20–23)

**WHAT IT IS.** A physical therapist's injury-analysis practice, and the pull captures its two working methods:
1. **Historical-comp prognosis tables.** On Terry McLaurin's confirmed torn patellar tendon (Oct 20), he posts the comp set: David Boston (24 — next season 70-880-7 in 14 games, then tore the *other* patellar tendon in year 2), Victor Cruz (28 — missed the next season entirely to a calf injury during rehab, returned year 2 at 39-586-1 in 15 games), Jimmy Graham (29 — next season 65-923-6 in 16 games, year 2: 57-520-10), framing McLaurin at 31 against them.
2. **Mechanism reasoning.** Calf strains elevate Achilles-rupture risk through faulty force transmission (applied to the Rams' conservative RTP handling and Puka Nacua); a prior core/groin injury can make the nervous system redistribute load and alter activation timing, suppressing distal (calf) peak output — with the practical distinction that a neural re-activation problem can play this week while a true strain cannot (examples cited: Marshawn Lloyd, Christian Watson); plus a reporting-epistemics post: an initially mislabeled injury type propagates through the insider telephone chain and corrupts every downstream expectation (the Lamar Jackson case).

**VERIFICATION.** The comp table checks out where independently verifiable: Cruz's 2016 return line (39-586-1) and Graham's 2016 line (65-923-6) match the historical record as republished in SI's own Oct 2026 McLaurin history pieces and the standard comp tables; SI's coverage of the same injury cites a 2025 *Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine* study (45 NFL patellar-tendon tears; 57.8% returned to play; median return 11.4 months) — the account's method is the published clinical-historical method, executed accurately. His week-level availability leans (e.g., Lamar plays, Puka misses Week 7) are his stated opinion, labeled by him as "best medical education guess," and are graded as opinion here.

**WHICH LAYER.** Health — this is the input class the health layer actually needs: not in/out status but *mechanism, expected timeline, and reinjury pathway* per named player. The comp-table format is directly reusable as an engine artifact: injury → age-matched historical comps → distribution of outcomes, including the year-2 second-injury pattern (Boston) that a simple "returns in ~11 months" line hides.

## D8 — @FantasyProsLabs — two first-party studies: ECR deviation cost, and absence-effect asymmetries (Oct 21–23)

**STUDY 1 — deviating from consensus costs more than it gains.** From millions of real synced lineups, Weeks 1–6: over half of all lineups differed from the "optimal" lineup implied by Expert Consensus Rankings. Of the start/sit decisions that went off-script, **55% lost points** versus the ECR choice (after removing lineups with injured/bye starters), and the asymmetry is in the magnitudes: losses averaged **−8.8 points**, gains **+7.1**. Status: FIRST-PARTY STATED — FantasyPros owns the lineup data and the ECR; the design is stated plainly and the numbers were not independently reproduced.

**STUDY 2 — "Fantasy Mythbusters Ep. I," every case 2018–25.** Three absence myths tested: (a) the star WR being out does **not** symmetrically boost the WR2 (no hypertargeting windfall in reverse); (b) without the WR2, the star WR1's target share rises only modestly — stars are already near their ceilings; (c) a backup QB does **not** hyper-target his WR1 — the WR1 keeps his share but scores **1.2 fewer points per game** because the whole offense degrades (worked example: CeeDee Lamb 2022 with Cooper Rush — share rose 26%→37% and he *still* lost 2.5 ppg).

**WHICH LAYER.** Usage — this is the correction term for the engine's role-shift logic (Session 3's C-301 role shift alerts): the naive adjustment "absent player's share flows to the next man" is empirically wrong in both directions; the offense-level degradation term dominates the share-transfer term for QB changes.

## Additional dossiers (A1–A7)

### A1 — @N01ennn — harness2: Google Research's self-improving agent harness (TOOL — full dossier)
- Post: https://x.com/N01ennn/status/2116233378215411919 (feed item F35)
- **WHAT IT IS:** An open-source framework that improves an AI agent by rewriting everything *around* the frozen model — its harness. The loop as posted and as verified: the agent runs a task with its current harness; a Harness Editor proposes edits (one general, one domain-specific) across 8 editable components (system prompt, guardrails, memory, skills, plugins, tool guidance, scripts, subagents); each edit is probed on the same task; a Harness Composer merges what the behavioral contrast supports; an Experience Reflector writes lessons into a persistent Improvement Harness that guides future tasks. No ground-truth labels are used — improvement is contrastive (before vs after behavior), which the authors call Propose-Probe-Compose.
- **WHERE TO FIND IT:** Verified by Motif this run via web sources: code at **github.com/google-research/harness2** (Apache-2.0; repo screenshot in the post matches — docs/, harness2/, scripts/, LICENSE, README.md, pyproject.toml); paper at **arXiv:2610.14224**; project page harness2.github.io. Released by Google Cloud AI Research + Northwestern (lead: Tomas Pfister's team; first author Ruiyao Xu). README states it is not an officially supported Google product.
- **HOW TO USE IT:** Local demo runs on Linux with Python 3.12 + uv and needs no AI account or API key (deterministic editors). Real benchmark runs need model API access (the paper's executors were Gemini 3.5 Flash and GLM-5 under OpenCode/Codex harnesses, with Claude Opus 4.8 as editor). Reported gains from one refinement step: up to +11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench (GLM-5/OpenCode 64.2 → 75.7), +4.5 JobBench, +11.8 on Harvey's LAB — vendor/paper-reported, labeled as such.
- **WHICH SYSTEM IT PLUGS INTO:** **Agent fleet infrastructure** — this is the first credible, open, verifier-free recipe for the exact thing Garrett's fleet does by hand: improving agent scaffolding (prompts, skills, memory, subagent configs) from experience. It maps one-to-one onto the fleet's skill/AGENTS.md layer and the claude-ds/OpenCode harness setups. It would not replace the fleet bus; it would sit above individual agent harnesses as an offline improvement loop.
- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** Run harness2's loop against a *single* bounded fleet job first (e.g., a sweep's own dossier-writing harness — this very task's prompt scaffold), with Garrett's hard gates untouched: the loop edits scaffolding, never permissions. The lessons-file mechanism ("Improvement Harness") is also a design pattern worth stealing even without the code: a persistent, structured lessons artifact that future runs must read — AGENTS.md already plays this role manually.

### #6 — @PattonAnalytics — SCRACK defined: SCRAMBLE + SACK (FOOTBALL — full dossier)
- Post: https://x.com/PattonAnalytics/status/2116264185013137658 (3:21 PM CDT, Oct 30)
- **WHAT IT IS:** The definition post for a composite QB metric: **SCRACK = scramble EPA + sack EPA** — the total expected-points value a quarterback produces on the two play types where the called pass play breaks down into QB improvisation or QB failure. Per the post, the metric's major proponent is @schwartzsteins. Construction: sum (or per-dropback rate — the chart post, dossier #9, presents it as a bar value per QB) of EPA on scrambles plus EPA on sacks taken.
- **WHERE IT COMES FROM:** @PattonAnalytics attributing the metric to @schwartzsteins; the source bar chart was reposted the same evening (dossier #9). EPA and play-type flags (scramble vs designed run vs sack) exist in nflverse play-by-play, so the metric is in-house computable in principle; the author's exact denominator is UNVERIFIED.
- **HOW TO USE IT:** From warehouse dropbacks: filter QB scrambles (qb_scramble flag) and sacks, sum EPA, normalize per dropback. Needs care separating designed QB runs from scrambles — nflverse carries that flag.
- **WHICH LAYER:** **Matchups layer (QB breakdown-play value vs pressure defenses)** — SCRACK is the trait that decides how much a blitz-heavy defense (e.g., Minnesota's menu, dossiers in prior runs) actually gains against a specific QB.
- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** SCRACK is the mirror image of dossier #1's pressure split: the pressure split measures the whole offense under pressure; SCRACK isolates the QB's personal rescue/damage plays. Publishing both separates "his line fails him" from "he fails himself" — the exact attribution question the sack-EPA QB-fault chart on Garrett's catch-up list asks.
- **RISKS:** Scramble EPA is high-variance and opponent-dependent; sack EPA assigns all sack blame to the QB by construction (coverage sacks included); small samples swing it (dossier #7 is literally about that swing).
- **FIRST TEST / VERDICT:** Compute SCRACK per dropback for 2026 Weeks 1–7 from the warehouse and compare the ranking's extremes to dossier #9's chart. **TEST.**

### #10 — @The_Coach_A — Nub-Trips and the "shove" call (FOOTBALL — full dossier)
- Post: https://x.com/The_Coach_A/status/2116304150019654125 (6:00 PM CDT, Oct 30; link resolved by Motif: https://www.matchquarters.com/p/defending-trips-nub-shove-call)
- **WHAT IT IS:** A scheme mechanism, from the post text: offenses use nub-Trips (tight end alone on the nub side) to make the defense "buy low" on the TE side — Houston adds play-action to the nub TE so the secondary bites — while the real stress is multiple vertical routes from the Trips side. Every split-field defense therefore needs a "shove" mechanism to cap those verticals. - WHAT IT IS: Four single-week descriptive instruments from one pipeline (data: @FantasyPtsData). (1) PGWE — Post-Game Win Expectancy: a win-probability read computed from final game stats (the post names yards per play, success rate, and 3rd-down conversions as drivers); KC graded 74% in a game Kansas City lost, Arizona 60% in its win at Dallas — i.e., a "who should have won" audit in the same family as @nfl_simulator's DTW, but built from box-score aggregates rather than play-by-play resimulation. (2) Pressure-faced vs off-target throw rate per QB — separates protection failure from accuracy failure. (3) Target depth (aDOT) against catchable-throw rate — depth-adjusted accuracy; Geno Smith flagged as the week's standout (rocket emoji is the author's). (4) EPA per target leaderboard with a 32-target floor; Mike Evans #1, then Tee Higgins, Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Sam LaPorta, TJ Hockensen (text-readable; the rest is chart-locked).
- WHERE IT COMES FROM: @sfdata9ers, data @FantasyPtsData (paid charting suite). PGWE's exact model is not published by the author — inputs named, weights not. Chart values for posts 1–3 are image-locked on the x_search route.

EPA/target is straight nflverse play-by-play with a target floor.
- WHICH LAYER IT PLUGS INTO: Matchups layer (QB-vs-pressure and receiver efficiency), with PGWE feeding the situations layer as a second, independent luck audit beside DTW.
- CREATIVE ANGLES: (a) PGWE-vs-DTW disagreement is itself a signal — when the box-score audit and the resimulation audit disagree, the disagreement localizes to high-variance plays, which is exactly what the published reasoning should name. (b) The pressure/off-target split is the cleanest public answer to "was it the line or the QB" — a weekly content card GSE can own with its own numbers. (c) EPA/target with a stated floor is a better public leaderboard than raw EPA because the floor is disclosed; steal the disclosure habit.

## W2 — @Timo_NFL — "Dire situations" drive metric, explained in-thread (FOOTBALL — full dossier; 4 posts)

- Posts (a single explanatory thread, Mon Nov 2, 21:20–22:10 GMT):
  - Per-play vs per-drive divergence note — https://x.com/Timo_NFL/status/2117366376306286946
  - Metric definition: lowest conversion chance in a series vs field-position baseline — https://x.com/Timo_NFL/status/2117367047080599627
  - Seahawks defense: +4.5pp more dire situations on converted series — https://x.com/Timo_NFL/status/2117367392527659054
  - Goal-line weighting / yards-to-points translation explainer — https://x.com/Timo_NFL/status/2117369009515417777 (with companion 2117368621139968242)
- WHAT IT IS: A drive-level defensive (and offensive) efficiency metric built on series outcomes instead of plays. Construction, from the author's own thread: for each series, find the lowest probability of converting to a new first down reached at any point in that series; compare it against a baseline expectation for the series' starting field position; aggregate the difference. The companion posts define the sibling drive-efficiency measure: yards gained relative to yards available, translated into points so the goal line carries its proper weight — the author claims it is "much more predictive than points per drive" (claim, UNVERIFIED). The worked example: Seattle's defense puts opponents into dire situations 4.5 percentage points more often than baseline even on series the opponent eventually converts — pressure that per-play EPA hides (the author notes a defense can rank #20 per play and #10 per drive on the same games).
- WHERE IT COMES FROM: @Timo_NFL, computed from play-by-play (nflverse-class data; the thread does not name a dataset or publish code — the conversion-probability model behind "lowest chance to convert" is the author's).
- HOW TO USE IT: Fully computable in-house: 1st-down conversion probability by down/distance/field position is fittable from settled nflverse history; the per-series minimum and the field-position baseline are deterministic aggregations on top. No external dependency.
- WHICH LAYER IT PLUGS INTO: Matchups layer (defensive quality that survives opponent conversion luck) — and it directly patches a known blind spot: per-play EPA punishes defenses for splash plays allowed even when the drive was strangled.
- CREATIVE ANGLES: (a) Pair with W1's pressure family: a defense that creates dire situations without pressure is a coverage defense; one that needs pressure is fragile — two different matchup stories from one extra column. (b) The per-play/per-drive rank gap (e.g. #20 vs #10) is a publishable "the box score is lying about this defense" content hook. (c) On offense, the same metric grades red-zone-adjacent stalls that EPA smooths over.

## W2 — @run_the_sims — The Nash correction: "55% was NOT a Nash equilibrium" (FOOTBALL — full dossier; 2 posts; primary source fully read this run)

- Posts:
  - Correction TL;DR + full analysis link — https://x.com/run_the_sims/status/2117639201764131312 (Tue Nov 3, 15:25 GMT), linking https://thesidequest.com/newsletter/2026-10-30-i-called-it-a-nash-equilibrium/
  - "Hand up" self-correction post — https://x.com/run_the_sims/status/2117639188401058194 (15:25 GMT): optimal early-down run-pass mix now put at 56–75%.
- WHAT IT IS: A public, worked retraction and rebuild of the pass-rate equilibrium claim this corpus first filed on 2026-10-29 ("Equilibrium: about 55% pass. The NFL: 54%"). VERIFIED at the primary source this run — the full Side Quest article was read end to end. The corrected method, in the author's own construction: (1) The defense's "call" is redefined from raw box count (8+ vs 6 or fewer, which skipped the 7-man box — about a third of early downs) to box advantage (Tej Seth's definition: blockers in the box, from SumerSports charting, minus defenders in the box, from nflverse; Defense+ 34% of early downs, Even 48%, Offense+ 18%; 87,000 first/second-down plays, 2022–2025). (2) With payoffs measured per box advantage, the pass beats the run against every box (e.g., Even: pass +0.06 vs run −0.06 points per play against a situation-adjusted baseline, Kovash–Levitt style), so passing is a dominant strategy and the original line-crossing was never a Nash equilibrium — it only made the defense indifferent. (3) The fix that produces an interior optimum: pass value decays as the defense's certainty of a pass rises (measured with Ben Baldwin's expected-pass model as the certainty proxy): pass payoff falls 0.027 EPA per 10 points of certainty against Defense+, 0.019 against Even, 0.014 against Offense+, while run payoff holds roughly flat. The mix-value curve therefore bends (a negative quadratic term) and peaks before 100%: by box, 58% (Defense+), 63% (Even), 77% (Offense+); against the defense's best response the best mix is about 71% pass, with a resampling range of roughly 57–75% and the author's stated overall range 56–75% — all above today's ~52%. The author correctly renames the object: a Stackelberg equilibrium (the offense commits to a season tendency; the defense responds), not a Nash equilibrium.
- WHERE IT COMES FROM: @run_the_sims (Nick, The Side Quest), data SumerSports + nflverse, framework after Brian Burke (2008) and Kovash & Levitt (2009); tendency-response checked across 128 team-seasons (defenses shift to light boxes at 1.15× and two-high at 1.02× the situational rate). The article names its own limits plainly (below).

Links a MatchQuarters clinic (t.co, unresolved this run).
  - "Know thy enemy…" — https://x.com/The_Coach_A/status/2117970209420046489 (13:20 GMT): a teaser line with an image; payload is in the image/clinic, not the text.
  - 2-Man "Robber" red-zone coverage, the construction post — https://x.com/The_Coach_A/status/2117968408838881353 (13:13 GMT): in the low red zone the defense tags a 2-Man Robber bracket conversion — underneath defenders stay sticky and play trail technique to box out targets, both hash safeties anchor on the goal line to cap vertical stems, and the compressed spacing forces contested throws.
  - The companion clinic pointer — https://x.com/The_Coach_A/status/2117968411426730302 (13:13 GMT): links the MatchQuarters piece at matchquarters.com/p/2-man-robber-red-zone-coverage (the one fully resolved outbound link in this set).
- WHAT IT IS: Two mechanisms and their pointers. (1) The read-out blitzer is a conditional rusher: his path is not fixed at the snap, it is a read — attack the declared gap, and if protection slides to you, abandon it and wrap to the gap the slide vacated. Functionally it turns one blitzer into a stunt without a second rusher being assigned the twist; the interior rush picking for him is what makes the wrap lane real. This extends the PM run's pressure-construction trilogy (NOT stunts, trailer blitz, double-mug) with the individual-technique layer underneath those structures. (2) The Robber conversion is the red-zone answer to compressed spacing: man underneath with trail technique (stay on the hip, undercut the break) plus safeties anchored at the goal line converts the red zone's missing vertical space from a defensive problem into the coverage's premise — there is no deep ball to protect, so both safeties become bracket players.
- WHERE IT COMES FROM: @The_Coach_A (MatchQuarters), the corpus's standing scheme source. Full clinic text is paywalled; the construction posts carry the core mechanics in their own text, as this account's better posts do.

Five stat families get a chart each: combined EPA/play, combined pass yards per dropback, combined RB yards-before-contact per rush, combined pressure rate, and combined explosive-play rate (big pass 15+ yards, big run 10+). Data: 2026 season, sourced to TruMedia per the manifesto post. Named reads in text: Packers–Patriots flagged as probably the best game of the week on combined EPA; Jared Goff noted as playing his last outdoor game until Week 17 (situational note attached to the pass-yards chart).

# COUNTED 20 — FEED DOSSIERS (9 posts)

## F1 — @azulgarza_ — FoundationForecast: conformal prediction on time-series foundation models (TimeCopilot)
Post: https://x.com/azulgarza_/status/2118030744283152415 (feed #68)
1. WHAT IT IS — A library announcement, verified at the primary source: FoundationForecast (by the TimeCopilot crew; the poster is on that team) puts time-series foundation models — Chronos, TimesFM, Moirai, Toto, TiRex, TimeGPT and more — behind one Python API (forecast / cross-validation / anomaly detection), and its headline feature for this post: conformal prediction intervals on any of those models via a ConformalIntervals wrapper that calibrates interval levels from cross-validation errors, so coverage is not limited by a model's native quantile outputs. The post's install line is `uv add foundationforecast`.
2. WHERE TO FIND IT — VERIFIED: github.com/TimeCopilot/foundationforecast (Apache-2.0), docs at docs.timecopilot.dev/foundationforecast, PyPI package `foundationforecast` (v0.1.15 listed; Python 3.10+, some models need specific Python versions). Poster is a recreator-announcer of her own team's library — the repo is the original source.
3. HOW TO USE IT — `pip install foundationforecast` (or uv add); one FoundationForecast class takes a list of model wrappers (e.g. Chronos with an HF repo_id), a long-format dataframe, horizon and level; conformal intervals are passed as prediction_intervals=ConformalIntervals(...). Their published replication: full GIFT-Eval (16 models × 97 dataset configs) for about $37 of compute.
4. WHICH SYSTEM — GSE prediction engine, calibration layer — the exact seam where GSE's adopted conformal stack (Romano CQR / Barber weighted conformal, per the standing corpus verdicts) meets player/game time series: rolling player usage, team scoring rates, and any series the engine forecasts weekly. It does not replace the engine's conformal work; it offers a benchmark harness and a second opinion on series the engine currently handles with simpler models.
5. CREATIVE ANGLES — Use it as the benchmark opponent: run Chronos-Bolt zero-shot on team points and player targets series and publish (internally) where a foundation model beats GSE's reasoning-informed numbers and where it loses — the loss map is the interesting half. Also a Kaggle-GPU-lane fit: the $37 full-benchmark replication says evaluation is cheap.
6. RISKS — Young library (0.1.x, created Aug 2026 per the repo page); model licenses vary by checkpoint (one listed model carries a modified-MIT license with a revenue threshold — read each model card); conformal coverage from CV errors assumes exchangeability the season-ordered NFL data violates — the corpus' own conformal verdicts (weighted/CQR variants) still govern.

The pairing is the method: depth alone rewards reckless QBs, catchable % alone rewards checkdown artists; together they separate "accurate because conservative" from "accurate while aggressive."
2. WHERE TO FIND IT — The post above. Catchable/on-target charting is a FantasyPtsData / PFR advanced-passing class field; depth is computable from nflverse air yards.

Together they triangulate a QB: accurate-at-depth AND efficient is the only quadrant that should move a number.

title: Core NFL Schemes & Systems + Fourth & Film
authors: Garrett / Fourth & Film / GSE Coaching Intelligence
full_text:
# Core NFL Schemes & Systems (Extracted Source)

Core Offensive Schemes & Systems
West Coast Offense (Bill Walsh):
Core Concept: Short, high-percentage horizontal passes (slants, quick outs, shallow crosses) released under 2.5 seconds on 3- to 5-step drops. Passing sets up the run rather than the other way around.
Personnel & Demands: Requires high-accuracy passers and high yards-after-catch (YAC) receivers/backs.
Weaknesses: Vulnerable to tight press-man coverage jamming routes at the line.
Air Coryell (Don Coryell):
Core Concept: Deep, aggressive vertical passing requiring a route tree designated by numerical codes (e.g., 989 = go, post, go).
Personnel & Demands: Needs an offensive line capable of sustaining long pass-protection blocks, a big-armed quarterback, and receiving tight ends working intermediate seams.
Weaknesses: High sack risk and lower completion percentage.
Air Raid (Hal Mumme, Mike Leach):
Core Concept: Passing 70–80% of snaps out of shotgun/empty sets with 10 personnel (1 RB, 4 WR). Built around only 10–20 core concepts executed at high tempo (e.g., Mesh, Four Verticals, Shallow Cross, Y-Cross, Stick).
Weaknesses: Poor clock control; susceptible to relentless pass rush if one-dimensional.
Erhardt-Perkins (Ron Erhardt, Ray Perkins / Bill Belichick):
Core Concept: Concept-based play calling (single words like Ghost) rather than formation/route-tree codes. Any concept can be run out of any formation or personnel grouping, allowing fast no-huddle audibles.
Demands: High mental processing demand on receivers and quarterback to recognize coverages pre-snap.
Shanahan / McVay Outside Zone & Bootleg:
Core Concept: Marries wide-zone run blocking (linemen moving laterally to create vertical cutback lanes) with play-action bootlegs. Uses pre-snap jet motion and identical backfield footwork so runs and passes look indistinguishable.
Demands: Highly agile offensive linemen (often lighter athletes around 290 lbs) and disciplined running backs who read leverage cuts.
Power & Gap Run Schemes:
Core Concept: Creates a designated point of attack by down-blocking with the line, kicking out the edge with a fullback, and pulling the backside guard.
Demands: Massive road-grader linemen and heavy personnel (21 or 22 personnel).
Run-Pass Option (RPO):
Core Concept: Puts a conflict defender (usually an overhang linebacker or safety) in a bind. If he crashes down on the run fit, the quarterback throws behind him; if he drops into coverage, the back gets the handoff.

title: Core NFL Schemes & Systems + Fourth & Film
authors: Garrett / Fourth & Film / GSE Coaching Intelligence
full_text:
Demands: 0.8-second decision window from the quarterback.
Heavy Personnel Sets (12 & 13 Personnel):
Core Concept: Forces defenses into a mismatch dilemma: keep light nickel/dime DBs on the field and get overpowered in the run game, or substitute heavier linebackers and surrender speed in space.
Passing Route Concepts & Counters
Mesh: Two shallow crosses from opposite directions crossing closely to create natural traffic/picks against man coverage. Counter: Zone drops or man-switch assignments.
Levels: Two or three receivers running crossing/in-breaking routes across the field at staggered depths (short, intermediate, deep) to force zone defenders into high-low dilemmas. Counter: Pattern matching and cloud coverage.
Flood: Three receivers overloading a single sideline at three distinct levels (deep corner, intermediate out, flat). Stresses Cover 3 and Cover 4 by placing 3 receivers on 2 zone defenders. Counter: Cover 2 (safety over the corner route) and backside pressure.
Smash: Outside receiver runs a short hitch/curl while the inside receiver runs a corner route behind it. Attacks the void in Cover 2 between the flat corner and deep half safety. Counter: Tampa 2 (middle linebacker running deep middle).
Four Verticals: All four eligibles run vertical routes to stress single-high safeties (Cover 3) or divide two-high safeties down the seam (Cover 2). Counter: Quarters (Cover 4) coverage.
Stick: Quick 3-receiver triangle read featuring an outside fade, a 5-yard option/stick route, and a flat route. Designed to defeat blitzes and soft Cover 3 zone. Counter: Press-man and robber/buzz defenders.
Dagger: Inside vertical clear-out route that clears the deep safety, opening a deep 15-yard dig route underneath for the outside receiver. Destroys standard Cover 2. Counter: Tampa 2 or robber safety dropping into the hole.
Pass Protection Schemes
5-0 / Big on Big (BOB): Linemen lock up man-to-man against defensive linemen. Easy to install, but highly vulnerable to stunts and twists.
Full Slide: The entire offensive line slides one gap in a single direction (e.g., left or right), leaving the backside rusher for the running back. Vulnerable if a defensive end isolates the running back.
Half Slide (Jet / Turnback):
The most standard NFL protection.
One side plays man-to-man (guard and tackle), while the center and other side slide into gap zones starting from the identified "Mike" linebacker.

title: Core NFL Schemes & Systems + Fourth & Film
authors: Garrett / Fourth & Film / GSE Coaching Intelligence
full_text:
Running back checks the remaining linebackers on a "one you, two me" rule.
Weaknesses: Overloads sending four rushers to the weak side or four to the strong side require hot routes or sight adjustments.
Play-Action & Boot Protections:
Boot Action: Offensive lineman or tight end travels back across the formation to protect the quarterback's backside.
Naked Boot: Entire line flows with the run fake; quarterback rolls out unblocked and must beat or hold the edge defender with the fake.
Defensive Coverage Shells & Mechanics
Cover 1 (Man Free):
Structure: Single high safety in the deep middle; 5 defenders locked in man-to-man coverage; four-man rush.
Assignments: Linebackers split the running back via banjo rules (whoever the back releases toward covers him) while the free linebacker acts as a "plugger" (spies QB, adds on blitz, or cuts crossers).
Strength / Weakness: Puts 7+ men in the run box to stop the run. Demands elite cornerbacks who can hold up on islands.
Cover 2 (Two-Deep, Five-Under Zone):
Structure: Two safeties split deep halves ("wider than the widest, deeper than the deepest"). Five underneath defenders: 2 flat corners, 2 hook/curl linebackers, 1 middle hook.
Key Mechanic: Outside corners must jam/re-route receivers at the line to prevent free releases into the deep vertical seams.
Weaknesses: Light 6-man run box; vertical seams and deep hole between safeties.
Cover 3 (Three-Deep, Four-Under Zone):
Structure: Corners defend deep outside thirds; single high safety takes the deep middle; four underneath defenders (two buzz to the numbers/flats, two take hook zones 1 yard outside the hashes).
Strength / Weakness: Strong against the run with 7–8 men in the box. Vulnerable in the flats to quick outs/hitches ("free access") and against 4-vertical attacks.
Cover 4 / Quarters (Pattern Match):
Structure: Four deep quarters. Corners play man on the #1 receiver; safeties read the #2 receiver (tight end or slot).
Pattern Match Rules: If #2 goes vertical, the safety covers him man-to-man. If #2 goes shallow, outside, or blocks, the safety triggers down aggressively into the run fit (giving the defense an 8-man box).
Weaknesses: Post routes behind squatting safeties; free access throws underneath.
Split-Field Concepts (Cover 6 / Cover 9):
Divides the field down the middle: Cover 4 to the passing strength and Cover 2 to the weak side (Cover 9 flips this). Eliminates deep boundary passing while bracketing star receivers.

Shows 7 or 8 defenders walked up on the line of scrimmage to guarantee an unblocked rusher or force quick hot throws. Defenses either send pure heat or drop several defenders out into intermediate passing lanes (rat zones / Tampa 2 / drop-8) to muddy reads.

NFL personnel groupings are designated by two digits totaling the 5 skill eligibles:

Defensive Fronts, Box Counts & Gaps
Gap Alignments & Techniques:
A-Gaps: Space between Center and Guards.
B-Gaps: Space between Guards and Tackles.
C-Gaps: Space outside the Tackles.
Technique Coding: 0-Tech is head-up on the Center; counts outward through wide-9 (wide outside the Tight End).
The Box Definition: 2 yards outside the widest offensive linemen/tight ends to 8 yards past the line of scrimmage.
Heavy Fronts & Run Packages:
6-2 Front: 6 DL, 2 LBs, 3 DBs. Plugs all A, B, and C gaps to eliminate running lanes. Corners are on total islands with zero deep safety help; vulnerable to quick slants or anything over 10 yards.
5-3 Front: 5 DL, 3 LBs, 3 DBs. Standard goal-line personnel. Extra linebacker provides underneath hook/flat support against play-action, but vulnerable if an offense deploys 4 or 5 receivers.
5-2 Eagle: 5 DL, 2 LBs, 4 DBs. Run-first front with improved DB numbers, but 5 down linemen focus on gap control rather than rushing the passer, allowing quarterbacks extended pocket time.
4-4 Defense: 4 DL, 4 LBs, 3 DBs (8-man box). Linebackers spill to control both edges outside the tackles. Hard counter to RPOs and triple-option/sweeps because all 3 phases (give, keep, pitch) are accounted for. Weak against spread sets with 4+ wideouts.
46 Bear Front: 5 DL, 3 LBs, 1 Safety, 2 CBs. Features the "Bear front" with 3 interior defensive linemen directly over the center and both guards (covering both A-gaps and B-gaps). Linebackers walk up to the line of scrimmage showing 8 rushers. Single high safety frequently blitzes to send 6–7 rushers. Vulnerable to quick 3-step passing, bubble screens, and 4-receiver packages.

Base & Sub-Packages:
3-4 Defense: 3 DL, 4 LBs, 4 DBs. Multiplicity-driven front anchored by a 2-gapping 0-tech Nose Tackle who occupies the center and draws double-teams. Allows 4 linebackers to rush or drop from ambiguous pre-snap alignments.
4-3 Base Defense: 4 DL, 3 LBs, 4 DBs. Provides a 4-man organic pass rush while linebackers fit gaps and match tight ends. Weakness occurs when facing 11 personnel (3 WRs), as the Will/Sam linebacker is forced to match a slot receiver in space.
Nickel Defense (4-2-5): 4 DL, 2 LBs, 5 DBs. Replaces a base linebacker with a Nickel corner to cover slot receivers. Nickel corners utilize jam techniques at the line or sit in passing lanes in robber coverage. Susceptible to inside power runs due to having only 2 linebackers in the box.
Dime Defense (4-1-6): 4 DL, 1 LB, 6 DBs (often 4 CBs, 2 Safeties or 3 CBs, 3 Safeties). Used in 3rd-and-12+, 2-minute drills, or against empty backfields. Drops 7 into coverage relying entirely on a 4-man pass rush; gives up inside runs willingly to burn clock.
In-Depth Secondary Coverage Rules & Matchups
Field Math (Zone Geometry):
NFL field is 53 1/3 yards wide by 100 yards long.
If a defense rushes 2 and drops 9, each deep defender covers approximately 13 yards of width, with 5 underneath defenders covering 5 discrete underneath zones.
Standard rush (4 down linemen) leaves 7 coverage defenders: either 3-Deep / 4-Under or 2-Deep / 5-Under.
Cover 1 Plug (Man-to-Man):
Shell: 1 Free Safety deep in the middle (shading 60/40 to the passing strength). Corners play press-man with outside leverage, funneling receivers inside toward help. Nickel plays man on the slot; Strong Safety plays man on the Tight End.
Linebacker Banjo & Plug Rules: Linebackers read the running back's release direction.
If the running back flows to Linebacker A, Linebacker A locks him in man-to-man ("Me, me, me!").
Linebacker B becomes the "Plugger" and executes one of three roles:
Disrupts and collision-checks inside crossing routes.
Spies a mobile scrambling quarterback.
Adds on as a 5th rusher (green dog blitz).
Pre-Snap Recognition (Rat vs. Lab Motions):
Rat (R): Running back motions wide right outside the boundary receiver.
Lab (L): Running back motions wide left outside the boundary receiver.
Read: If a linebacker tracks the back out wide, it is Man coverage (Cover 1). If an outside cornerback widens to take the back and the linebacker only slides/bumps inside, it is Zone coverage (Cover 3).

title: Core NFL Schemes & Systems + Fourth & Film
authors: Garrett / Fourth & Film / GSE Coaching Intelligence
full_text:
Cover 2 (Two-High, 5-Under Zone):
Shell: Safeties split deep halves ("wider than the widest, deeper than the deepest").
Underneath Zones: 5 underneath players: 2 Cornerbacks in the flats, 2 outside Linebackers in hook-curl zones, 1 Middle Linebacker in the middle-hook zone.
Jam Technique: Cornerbacks must physically jam and re-route the #1 outside receiver inside to disrupt timing and protect the vertical seam; free releases allow offenses to split the deep half safety.
Variations: Firmer Cover 2 (corners lock in the flat regardless) vs. Floated Cover 2 (corners sink underneath intermediate routes based on boundary releases).
Cover 3 (Three-Deep, 4-Under Zone):
Shell: Free Safety takes the deep middle third (leaning 60/40 to passing strength); both outside Cornerbacks defend deep outside thirds, keeping all vertical threats in front.
Underneath Landmarks: 4 underneath defenders:
2 Flat/Curl-Flat defenders buzz to the field numbers at 6 to 8 yards depth (if the QB looks away, they "melt" inside).
2 Hook defenders drop to landmarks 1 yard outside the NFL hash marks, reading the quarterback's eyes.
Weaknesses: Vulnerable in the flats to quick outs/hitches ("free access" because corners bail to deep thirds) and 4-vertical concepts stretching 3 deep defenders across 4 zones.
Cover 4 / Quarters (Pattern-Match Rules):
Setup: 4 deep quarters, 3 underneath defenders (2 quarters-flat defenders and 1 Mike linebacker).
Corner Responsibilities: Play man-to-man against the #1 receiver unless #1 runs underneath/shallow. Corners align inside-out (trusting DB speed on outside routes while protecting the inside) or outside-in (preventing deep outs).
Box & Triangle Match Structure:
The Box (Passing Strength):
Apex/Overhang Defender: Reads #2 receiver. If #2 goes out, matches to the flat; if #2 goes vertical, carries him to the safety; if #2 goes in, delivers him to the Mike.
Safety: Reads #2. If #2 goes vertical, locks him man-to-man. If #2 goes out, anticipates #1 coming deep/inside and brackets the post/dig. If #2 goes in, shades middle to rob crossers.
Mike Linebacker: Takes #3 (often RB). If #3 goes vertical, matches vertically; if #3 goes out, makes a "push" call to slide the Apex to #3 in the flat while Mike takes #2.
The Triangle (Weak Side):
Will Linebacker: Part of the run fit. Cannot chase routes into the flat.
Corner: Traps down on #2 if #2 breaks to the flat; if #2 is vertical, carries #1 deep.

title: Core NFL Schemes & Systems + Fourth & Film
authors: Garrett / Fourth & Film / GSE Coaching Intelligence
full_text:
Weak Safety: If #2 is vertical, takes him deep. If #2 breaks out, traps #1 deep over the top.
Split-Field Concepts & Pressure Formations:
Cover 6 (Quarter-Quarter-Half): Plays Cover 4 (Quarters) to the passing strength and Cover 2 (Half-field safety and flat corner) to the weak side. Mike/Will carries the #3 receiver if he goes vertical.
Cover 9: Inverted Cover 6. Plays Quarters to the weak side (neutralizing isolated elite receivers like stacked weak-side threats) and Cover 2 to the strong side.
Cover 0 (Bluff & Amoeba Pressures): Puts 7 or 8 defenders walked up on the line of scrimmage with DBs backed off. Guarantees a free rusher if all rush. Teams often execute "Drop-8" or bail into Tampa 2 / Cover 3 post-snap with interior defenders dropping into "rat zones" to muddy throwing lanes.
Offensive Line Mechanics & Protection Rules
Pass-Blocking Technique & Fundamentals:
Tempo in the Set: Reading pass rusher's pre-snap stance. If the rusher is standing straight up, he must "load and go," giving the tackle time to pace his kick-slide; setting too wide or over-setting leaves the inside B-gap vulnerable.
Hand Placement & Punch: Bisect the defender's frame, then bisect his inside half again to target the armpit. Thumbs up, locking hands inside the chest plate to avoid holding penalties while anchoring against bull rushes.
Protection Schemes & Slide Rules:
5-0 / Big on Big (BOB): 5 offensive linemen lock in man-to-man matchups on 5 rushers. Susceptible to defensive line games, stunts, and twists.
Full Slide: Entire line slides one gap in a single direction; running back or fullback takes the backside edge rusher. Easiest to install for 3-step drops and play-action, but exposes running backs against physical edge defenders.
Half Slide (Jet / Turnback / 2-Jet & 3-Jet):
2-Jet: Slide protection to the left.
3-Jet: Slide protection to the right (slide moves away from the call number).
Guard and tackle on the man side lock up man-to-man on interior DL. The center and backside linemen slide into gap-zone assignments starting from the identified "Mike."
The first uncovered offensive lineman initiates the slide.
"One You, Two Me" Rule: Running back checks the Mike first. If Mike rushes, the back takes him; if a second linebacker blitzes, the quarterback must throw "hot."
Overload Pressure Adjustments:
4-Weak Blitz: 4 rushers come from the weak side. Addressed via:
Tom Call: Tells the running back to cross the formation to the weak side (leaves Mike/Sam unaccounted for).

title: Core NFL Schemes & Systems + Fourth & Film
authors: Garrett / Fourth & Film / GSE Coaching Intelligence
full_text:
Fan Call: Pushes the offensive tackle out wide to take the edge rusher while the back fills the interior gap.
Hot Routes & Sight Adjustments: Receiver automatically alters route into vacated blitz space.
4-Strong Blitz: Addressed via:
Joker / Opposite Call: Flips the slide direction so linemen slide strong.
Stay Call: Keeps an extra blocker (Tight End or Fullback) in the protection, sacrificing an eligible receiver.
Play-Action & Rollout Mechanics:
Fake Power Protection: Pulls a backside guard to sell run-action to freeze linebackers while opening clean throwing lanes behind them.
Boot Action vs. Naked Boot:
Boot Action: An offensive lineman, tight end, or back crosses the formation against the fake to secure the edge for the rolling quarterback.
Naked Boot: The entire line flows in one direction; the quarterback rolls out with zero backside protection and must freeze the edge defender with the fake.
Sprint / Rollout Protection: Linemen slide toward the sprint side; backside tackle hooks the defensive end to prevent pursuit from behind.
Offensive Formations, Terminology & Route Systems
Personnel & Route Lettering:
Letter Designations:
H: Halfback / primary running back.
Y: Primary inline tight end.
Z: Flanker / play-side receiver (usually lines up off the line of scrimmage).
X: Split end / weak-side receiver (lines up on the line of scrimmage, away from the call).
F: Multi-purpose skill player (Fullback, slot receiver, or second tight end).
21 Personnel Formations (2 RBs, 1 TE, 2 WRs):
Backfield Sets:
Split Right/Left: H behind the weak tackle, F behind the strong tackle.
I Right/Left: F and H aligned in a straight line behind the QB (F at 4 yards, H at 8 yards).
Strong Right/Left: F offsets to the strong side between guard and tackle.
Weak Right/Left: F offsets to the weak side away from the tight end.
Receiver Modifiers (Moving Z and X away from the call):
Slot: Z aligns inside X on the weak side.
Zoom: X aligns inside Z on the weak side.
Star: X takes a tight 3-yard split from the tackle; Z aligns inside X.
Sun: X takes a tight 3-yard split; Z aligns outside X.
12 Personnel Formations (1 RB, 2 TEs, 2 WRs) – The "S-Words":
In S-words, Y and Z go to the call; F and X go away from the call.
Solo Right: Y inline to the right with Z split wide; F inline to the left with X split wide.
Classy Tag: Reduces splits of X and Z to tight 3-yard alignments.
Snug Right: Both Y and F align off the line of scrimmage; Z and X compress inside into 3-to-4-yard splits.

title: Core NFL Schemes & Systems + Fourth & Film
authors: Garrett / Fourth & Film / GSE Coaching Intelligence
full_text:
Special Right: Y aligns 1 yard deep and 1 yard outside Z; F aligns 1 yard deep and 1 yard outside X.
Sink Right: Both Y and F sink into the backfield as fullbacks, creating a 3-back set.
Sprout Right: Y flexes wide outside Z; F flexes wide outside X.
Trips Formations (3 Receivers to the Call) – The "T-Words":
In T-words, Y, F, and Z go to the call; X goes away from the call.
Trips Right: Y is inline on the ball; F is in the slot off the ball; Z is outside off the ball.
Trough Right: "TE Get Off" – Y aligns off the line of scrimmage; Z aligns on the ball.
Trout Right: Y detaches from the offensive line into a 3-to-4-yard split with F and Z.
Trump Right: "M = Middle" – Y aligns in the middle between F and Z.
Trio Right: "O = Outside" – Y aligns as the outermost receiver with F and Z inside.
Passing Concepts & Progression Architecture:
Air Coryell Route Numbering: 3-digit calls dictate routes for X, Y, and Z on the route tree (e.g., 8 = Post, 9 = Go/Fade, 6 = 8–12 yard Dig). Mills concept runs a post from the outside receiver paired with a dig from the tight end to hold the deep safety.
Mesh (Air Raid / West Coast): Two receivers cross at 3–5 yards depth, setting natural rub picks against man coverage; running back releases into the flat as a checkdown.
Smash Concept: Outside receiver runs a 5-yard hitch/curl while the inside slot receiver runs an 8-to-12-yard corner route. High-lows the Cover 2 flat cornerback.
Dagger Concept: Inside receiver runs a vertical seam to clear deep safeties; outside receiver breaks on a 15-yard dig into the vacated middle.
Y-Cross: Inside receiver/tight end runs a 15–18 yard deep crosser behind linebackers; cleared by vertical clear-out routes outside.
Double China: Both outside receivers run 5-yard "China" in-routes while an inside receiver runs a corner route; creates inside-out conflict for red-zone defenders.
Ghost (Erhardt-Perkins): Independent route concept featuring a Go (Z), Flat (H), and Hitch (Y). Can be run out of Trips, Bunch, or Doubles by coaching route rules by position rather than formation diagrams.
Situational Down & Distance Football Metrics
1st Down Operations:
1st & 10: Goal is 4–6 yards to establish 2-down series management. Offenses convert on 1st down immediately 20–25% of the time, but convert the full series ~75% of the time. Defenses remain in base looks.
1st & Short (1–5 yards): Immediate conversion rate is ~60%; overall series conversion rate jumps to ~90%. Prime down for deep play-action shots due to minimal penalty for incompletion.

title: Core NFL Schemes & Systems + Fourth & Film
authors: Garrett / Fourth & Film / GSE Coaching Intelligence
full_text:
1st & Long (15+ yards): Often resulting from penalties. Immediate conversion drops to 10–12%; series survival rate falls to 30–35%. Heavy reliance on quick screens and safe checkdowns to regain field position.
2nd Down Operations:
2nd & Short (1–3 yards): Highest offensive flexibility. Low-risk/high-reward deep shots or perimeter runs.
2nd & Medium (4–6 yards): Playbook completely balanced between inside runs and quick game. Conversion on the down sits around 40%; full-series conversion rate is ~75%.
2nd & Long (7–12 yards): Damage control. Goal is recovering at least 50% of needed yardage to create manageable 3rd downs; series survival rate sits at 55–60%.
2nd & Very Long (13+ yards): Often triggered by sacks. Defenses bring heavy heat; counter-punished with draw plays and screen passes.
3rd Down Operations:
3rd & Short (1–3 yards): Power football. ~70% run frequency against loaded 8-to-9-man fronts.
3rd & Medium (4–6 yards): Heavy zone-blitz down. Offenses utilize quick slants, rub-crossers, and option routes.
3rd & Long (7–12 yards): Long-developing route trees against exotic pressure looks; conversion rates fall to 20–25%.
3rd & Very Long (13+ yards): Sub-10% conversion rate. Offenses emphasize ball security and field position over aggressive conversion attempts.
4th Down Operations:
4th & Inches: Dominated by quarterback sneaks and power wedge runs; high analytical conversion rate.
4th & Short (1–4 yards): Offenses counter stacked run fronts with quick slants and RPO flat releases.
4th & Medium (5–9 yards): ~40% conversion rate; relies on pre-snap shift/motion to diagnose coverage shells and deliver timing-based throws.
4th & Long (10+ yards): 15–20% conversion rate; maximum blitz defense against deep protection structures.
Non-Football News Segments (CNN 10 & Science / Trivia)
CTE & Head Trauma Study:
Study Data: Researchers examined 878 deceased former NFL players (died between 2016 and 2021) and found at least 1 in 4 had CTE.
Selection Bias / Context: Only 235 brains were actually donated to science by family members, and 215 of those tested positive for CTE (families who observed cognitive symptoms prior to death were significantly more likely to donate).
Historical Context: Players studied competed largely in the late 1980s and 1990s.
Rule & Safety Changes: Over 50 rule changes in the past two decades; the modified kickoff rule (preventing coverage players from moving until the ball is in play) reduced concussions by approximately 43%.

Player Roster Positions & Core Roles
Offensive Positions:
Quarterback (QB): Captain, receives the snap, makes pre-snap/post-snap reads, hands off, scrambles, or passes.

title: Core NFL Schemes & Systems + Fourth & Film
authors: Garrett / Fourth & Film / GSE Coaching Intelligence
full_text:
Running Back (RB): Carries the football, reads running lanes, catches passes out of the backfield.
Fullback (FB): Lead run blocker in the hole against linebackers; occasionally runs or catches.
Wide Receiver (WR): Speed/agility perimeter or slot route runner creating separation to catch passes.
Offensive Tackle (OT): Edge protector against pass rushers; sets edge in run blocking with footwork and length.
Offensive Guard (OG): Interior protector against defensive tackles; pulls and opens interior run lanes.
Center (C): Snaps the ball, anchors the line, calls out protections and defensive fronts.
Tight End (TE): Hybrid offensive lineman and wide receiver lining up inline, flexed, or in the slot.
Defensive Positions:
Defensive Tackle (DT): Interior lineman penetrating interior gaps to stop inside runs and collapse the pocket.
Defensive End (DE): Edge lineman rushing the passer and setting the edge against outside runs.
EDGE: Hybrid designation combining 4-3 Defensive End and 3-4 Outside Linebacker responsibilities.
Linebacker (ILB / OLB): Second-level defenders filling run gaps, covering tight ends/running backs, and blitzing.
Cornerback (CB): Perimeter coverage specialist matching outside wide receivers in man or zone.
Free Safety (FS): Deep middle centerfielder; typically positioned to the weak side to read the quarterback's eyes.
Strong Safety (SS): Positioned toward the tight end / strong side to provide box run support and match tight ends.
Special Teams:
Kicker (K): Field goals (3 points), extra points (1 point), and kickoffs.
Punter (P): Punts on 4th down to pin the opponent deep and minimize return yardage.
Holder: Catches the long snap and places/spins the ball for the kicker (almost always the punter or backup QB).
Long Snapper (LS): Snaps the football accurately over extended distance under pressure.
Return Specialist (KR / PR): Fields kickoffs/punts; usually an active cornerback, running back, or wide receiver.
Historical Formations & Play-Design Case Studies
The T-Formation (1940 Bears vs. Redskins):
Chicago demolished Washington 73–0 in the 1940 NFL Championship Game, ending the single-wing era and establishing modern under-center play.
Structure: Quarterback under center with 3 backs aligned behind him in a horizontal line forming a "T" (Fullback centered, two Halfbacks flanking).
Options: Hand off to the fullback up the middle, pitch to either halfback outside, or QB keeper.

# Core NFL Schemes & Systems (Extracted Source)

Core Offensive Schemes & Systems
West Coast Offense (Bill Walsh):
Core Concept: Short, high-percentage horizontal passes (slants, quick outs, shallow crosses) released under 2.5 seconds on 3- to 5-step drops. Passing sets up the run rather than the other way around.
Personnel & Demands: Requires high-accuracy passers and high yards-after-catch (YAC) receivers/backs.
Weaknesses: Vulnerable to tight press-man coverage jamming routes at the line.
Air Coryell (Don Coryell):
Core Concept: Deep, aggressive vertical passing requiring a route tree designated by numerical codes (e.g., 989 = go, post, go).
Personnel & Demands: Needs an offensive line capable of sustaining long pass-protection blocks, a big-armed quarterback, and receiving tight ends working intermediate seams.
Weaknesses: High sack risk and lower completion percentage.
Air Raid (Hal Mumme, Mike Leach):
Core Concept: Passing 70–80% of snaps out of shotgun/empty sets with 10 personnel (1 RB, 4 WR). Built around only 10–20 core concepts executed at high tempo (e.g., Mesh, Four Verticals, Shallow Cross, Y-Cross, Stick).
Weaknesses: Poor clock control; susceptible to relentless pass rush if one-dimensional.
Erhardt-Perkins (Ron Erhardt, Ray Perkins / Bill Belichick):
Core Concept: Concept-based play calling (single words like Ghost) rather than formation/route-tree codes. Any concept can be run out of any formation or personnel grouping, allowing fast no-huddle audibles.
Demands: High mental processing demand on receivers and quarterback to recognize coverages pre-snap.
Shanahan / McVay Outside Zone & Bootleg:
Core Concept: Marries wide-zone run blocking (linemen moving laterally to create vertical cutback lanes) with play-action bootlegs. Uses pre-snap jet motion and identical backfield footwork so runs and passes look indistinguishable.
Demands: Highly agile offensive linemen (often lighter athletes around 290 lbs) and disciplined running backs who read leverage cuts.
Power & Gap Run Schemes:
Core Concept: Creates a designated point of attack by down-blocking with the line, kicking out the edge with a fullback, and pulling the backside guard.
Demands: Massive road-grader linemen and heavy personnel (21 or 22 personnel).
Run-Pass Option (RPO):
Core Concept: Puts a conflict defender (usually an overhang linebacker or safety) in a bind. If he crashes down on the run fit, the quarterback throws behind him; if he drops into coverage, the back gets the handoff.

title: Core NFL Schemes & Systems (Extracted Source)
full_text:
Demands: 0.8-second decision window from the quarterback.
Heavy Personnel Sets (12 & 13 Personnel):
Core Concept: Forces defenses into a mismatch dilemma: keep light nickel/dime DBs on the field and get overpowered in the run game, or substitute heavier linebackers and surrender speed in space.
Passing Route Concepts & Counters
Mesh: Two shallow crosses from opposite directions crossing closely to create natural traffic/picks against man coverage. Counter: Zone drops or man-switch assignments.
Levels: Two or three receivers running crossing/in-breaking routes across the field at staggered depths (short, intermediate, deep) to force zone defenders into high-low dilemmas. Counter: Pattern matching and cloud coverage.
Flood: Three receivers overloading a single sideline at three distinct levels (deep corner, intermediate out, flat). Stresses Cover 3 and Cover 4 by placing 3 receivers on 2 zone defenders. Counter: Cover 2 (safety over the corner route) and backside pressure.
Smash: Outside receiver runs a short hitch/curl while the inside receiver runs a corner route behind it. Attacks the void in Cover 2 between the flat corner and deep half safety. Counter: Tampa 2 (middle linebacker running deep middle).
Four Verticals: All four eligibles run vertical routes to stress single-high safeties (Cover 3) or divide two-high safeties down the seam (Cover 2). Counter: Quarters (Cover 4) coverage.
Stick: Quick 3-receiver triangle read featuring an outside fade, a 5-yard option/stick route, and a flat route. Designed to defeat blitzes and soft Cover 3 zone. Counter: Press-man and robber/buzz defenders.
Dagger: Inside vertical clear-out route that clears the deep safety, opening a deep 15-yard dig route underneath for the outside receiver. Destroys standard Cover 2. Counter: Tampa 2 or robber safety dropping into the hole.
Pass Protection Schemes
5-0 / Big on Big (BOB): Linemen lock up man-to-man against defensive linemen. Easy to install, but highly vulnerable to stunts and twists.
Full Slide: The entire offensive line slides one gap in a single direction (e.g., left or right), leaving the backside rusher for the running back. Vulnerable if a defensive end isolates the running back.
Half Slide (Jet / Turnback):
The most standard NFL protection.
One side plays man-to-man (guard and tackle), while the center and other side slide into gap zones starting from the identified "Mike" linebacker.

title: Core NFL Schemes & Systems (Extracted Source)
full_text:
Running back checks the remaining linebackers on a "one you, two me" rule.
Weaknesses: Overloads sending four rushers to the weak side or four to the strong side require hot routes or sight adjustments.
Play-Action & Boot Protections:
Boot Action: Offensive lineman or tight end travels back across the formation to protect the quarterback's backside.
Naked Boot: Entire line flows with the run fake; quarterback rolls out unblocked and must beat or hold the edge defender with the fake.
Defensive Coverage Shells & Mechanics
Cover 1 (Man Free):
Structure: Single high safety in the deep middle; 5 defenders locked in man-to-man coverage; four-man rush.
Assignments: Linebackers split the running back via banjo rules (whoever the back releases toward covers him) while the free linebacker acts as a "plugger" (spies QB, adds on blitz, or cuts crossers).
Strength / Weakness: Puts 7+ men in the run box to stop the run. Demands elite cornerbacks who can hold up on islands.
Cover 2 (Two-Deep, Five-Under Zone):
Structure: Two safeties split deep halves ("wider than the widest, deeper than the deepest"). Five underneath defenders: 2 flat corners, 2 hook/curl linebackers, 1 middle hook.
Key Mechanic: Outside corners must jam/re-route receivers at the line to prevent free releases into the deep vertical seams.
Weaknesses: Light 6-man run box; vertical seams and deep hole between safeties.
Cover 3 (Three-Deep, Four-Under Zone):
Structure: Corners defend deep outside thirds; single high safety takes the deep middle; four underneath defenders (two buzz to the numbers/flats, two take hook zones 1 yard outside the hashes).
Strength / Weakness: Strong against the run with 7–8 men in the box. Vulnerable in the flats to quick outs/hitches ("free access") and against 4-vertical attacks.
Cover 4 / Quarters (Pattern Match):
Structure: Four deep quarters. Corners play man on the #1 receiver; safeties read the #2 receiver (tight end or slot).
Pattern Match Rules: If #2 goes vertical, the safety covers him man-to-man. If #2 goes shallow, outside, or blocks, the safety triggers down aggressively into the run fit (giving the defense an 8-man box).
Weaknesses: Post routes behind squatting safeties; free access throws underneath.
Split-Field Concepts (Cover 6 / Cover 9):
Divides the field down the middle: Cover 4 to the passing strength and Cover 2 to the weak side (Cover 9 flips this). Eliminates deep boundary passing while bracketing star receivers.

NFL personnel groupings are designated by two digits totaling the 5 skill eligibles:
