Defensive Fronts, Box Counts & Gaps
Gap Alignments & Techniques:
A-Gaps: Space between Center and Guards.
B-Gaps: Space between Guards and Tackles.
C-Gaps: Space outside the Tackles.
Technique Coding: 0-Tech is head-up on the Center; counts outward through wide-9 (wide outside the Tight End).
The Box Definition: 2 yards outside the widest offensive linemen/tight ends to 8 yards past the line of scrimmage.
Heavy Fronts & Run Packages:
6-2 Front: 6 DL, 2 LBs, 3 DBs. Plugs all A, B, and C gaps to eliminate running lanes. Corners are on total islands with zero deep safety help; vulnerable to quick slants or anything over 10 yards.
5-3 Front: 5 DL, 3 LBs, 3 DBs. Standard goal-line personnel. Extra linebacker provides underneath hook/flat support against play-action, but vulnerable if an offense deploys 4 or 5 receivers.
5-2 Eagle: 5 DL, 2 LBs, 4 DBs. Run-first front with improved DB numbers, but 5 down linemen focus on gap control rather than rushing the passer, allowing quarterbacks extended pocket time.
4-4 Defense: 4 DL, 4 LBs, 3 DBs (8-man box). Linebackers spill to control both edges outside the tackles. Hard counter to RPOs and triple-option/sweeps because all 3 phases (give, keep, pitch) are accounted for. Weak against spread sets with 4+ wideouts.
46 Bear Front: 5 DL, 3 LBs, 1 Safety, 2 CBs. Features the "Bear front" with 3 interior defensive linemen directly over the center and both guards (covering both A-gaps and B-gaps). Linebackers walk up to the line of scrimmage showing 8 rushers. Single high safety frequently blitzes to send 6–7 rushers. Vulnerable to quick 3-step passing, bubble screens, and 4-receiver packages.

title: Core NFL Schemes & Systems (Extracted Source)
full_text:
Base & Sub-Packages:
3-4 Defense: 3 DL, 4 LBs, 4 DBs. Multiplicity-driven front anchored by a 2-gapping 0-tech Nose Tackle who occupies the center and draws double-teams. Allows 4 linebackers to rush or drop from ambiguous pre-snap alignments.
4-3 Base Defense: 4 DL, 3 LBs, 4 DBs. Provides a 4-man organic pass rush while linebackers fit gaps and match tight ends. Weakness occurs when facing 11 personnel (3 WRs), as the Will/Sam linebacker is forced to match a slot receiver in space.
Nickel Defense (4-2-5): 4 DL, 2 LBs, 5 DBs. Replaces a base linebacker with a Nickel corner to cover slot receivers. Nickel corners utilize jam techniques at the line or sit in passing lanes in robber coverage. Susceptible to inside power runs due to having only 2 linebackers in the box.
Dime Defense (4-1-6): 4 DL, 1 LB, 6 DBs (often 4 CBs, 2 Safeties or 3 CBs, 3 Safeties). Used in 3rd-and-12+, 2-minute drills, or against empty backfields. Drops 7 into coverage relying entirely on a 4-man pass rush; gives up inside runs willingly to burn clock.
In-Depth Secondary Coverage Rules & Matchups
Field Math (Zone Geometry):
NFL field is 53 1/3 yards wide by 100 yards long.
If a defense rushes 2 and drops 9, each deep defender covers approximately 13 yards of width, with 5 underneath defenders covering 5 discrete underneath zones.
Standard rush (4 down linemen) leaves 7 coverage defenders: either 3-Deep / 4-Under or 2-Deep / 5-Under.
Cover 1 Plug (Man-to-Man):
Shell: 1 Free Safety deep in the middle (shading 60/40 to the passing strength). Corners play press-man with outside leverage, funneling receivers inside toward help. Nickel plays man on the slot; Strong Safety plays man on the Tight End.
Linebacker Banjo & Plug Rules: Linebackers read the running back's release direction.
If the running back flows to Linebacker A, Linebacker A locks him in man-to-man ("Me, me, me!").
Linebacker B becomes the "Plugger" and executes one of three roles:
Disrupts and collision-checks inside crossing routes.
Spies a mobile scrambling quarterback.
Adds on as a 5th rusher (green dog blitz).
Pre-Snap Recognition (Rat vs. Lab Motions):
Rat (R): Running back motions wide right outside the boundary receiver.
Lab (L): Running back motions wide left outside the boundary receiver.
Read: If a linebacker tracks the back out wide, it is Man coverage (Cover 1). If an outside cornerback widens to take the back and the linebacker only slides/bumps inside, it is Zone coverage (Cover 3).

title: Core NFL Schemes & Systems (Extracted Source)
full_text:
Cover 2 (Two-High, 5-Under Zone):
Shell: Safeties split deep halves ("wider than the widest, deeper than the deepest").
Underneath Zones: 5 underneath players: 2 Cornerbacks in the flats, 2 outside Linebackers in hook-curl zones, 1 Middle Linebacker in the middle-hook zone.
Jam Technique: Cornerbacks must physically jam and re-route the #1 outside receiver inside to disrupt timing and protect the vertical seam; free releases allow offenses to split the deep half safety.
Variations: Firmer Cover 2 (corners lock in the flat regardless) vs. Floated Cover 2 (corners sink underneath intermediate routes based on boundary releases).
Cover 3 (Three-Deep, 4-Under Zone):
Shell: Free Safety takes the deep middle third (leaning 60/40 to passing strength); both outside Cornerbacks defend deep outside thirds, keeping all vertical threats in front.
Underneath Landmarks: 4 underneath defenders:
2 Flat/Curl-Flat defenders buzz to the field numbers at 6 to 8 yards depth (if the QB looks away, they "melt" inside).
2 Hook defenders drop to landmarks 1 yard outside the NFL hash marks, reading the quarterback's eyes.
Weaknesses: Vulnerable in the flats to quick outs/hitches ("free access" because corners bail to deep thirds) and 4-vertical concepts stretching 3 deep defenders across 4 zones.
Cover 4 / Quarters (Pattern-Match Rules):
Setup: 4 deep quarters, 3 underneath defenders (2 quarters-flat defenders and 1 Mike linebacker).
Corner Responsibilities: Play man-to-man against the #1 receiver unless #1 runs underneath/shallow. Corners align inside-out (trusting DB speed on outside routes while protecting the inside) or outside-in (preventing deep outs).
Box & Triangle Match Structure:
The Box (Passing Strength):
Apex/Overhang Defender: Reads #2 receiver. If #2 goes out, matches to the flat; if #2 goes vertical, carries him to the safety; if #2 goes in, delivers him to the Mike.
Safety: Reads #2. If #2 goes vertical, locks him man-to-man. If #2 goes out, anticipates #1 coming deep/inside and brackets the post/dig. If #2 goes in, shades middle to rob crossers.
Mike Linebacker: Takes #3 (often RB). If #3 goes vertical, matches vertically; if #3 goes out, makes a "push" call to slide the Apex to #3 in the flat while Mike takes #2.
The Triangle (Weak Side):
Will Linebacker: Part of the run fit. Cannot chase routes into the flat.
Corner: Traps down on #2 if #2 breaks to the flat; if #2 is vertical, carries #1 deep.

title: Core NFL Schemes & Systems (Extracted Source)
full_text:
Weak Safety: If #2 is vertical, takes him deep. If #2 breaks out, traps #1 deep over the top.
Split-Field Concepts & Pressure Formations:
Cover 6 (Quarter-Quarter-Half): Plays Cover 4 (Quarters) to the passing strength and Cover 2 (Half-field safety and flat corner) to the weak side. Mike/Will carries the #3 receiver if he goes vertical.
Cover 9: Inverted Cover 6. Plays Quarters to the weak side (neutralizing isolated elite receivers like stacked weak-side threats) and Cover 2 to the strong side.
Cover 0 (Bluff & Amoeba Pressures): Puts 7 or 8 defenders walked up on the line of scrimmage with DBs backed off. Guarantees a free rusher if all rush. Teams often execute "Drop-8" or bail into Tampa 2 / Cover 3 post-snap with interior defenders dropping into "rat zones" to muddy throwing lanes.
Offensive Line Mechanics & Protection Rules
Pass-Blocking Technique & Fundamentals:
Tempo in the Set: Reading pass rusher's pre-snap stance. If the rusher is standing straight up, he must "load and go," giving the tackle time to pace his kick-slide; setting too wide or over-setting leaves the inside B-gap vulnerable.
Hand Placement & Punch: Bisect the defender's frame, then bisect his inside half again to target the armpit. Thumbs up, locking hands inside the chest plate to avoid holding penalties while anchoring against bull rushes.
Protection Schemes & Slide Rules:
5-0 / Big on Big (BOB): 5 offensive linemen lock in man-to-man matchups on 5 rushers. Susceptible to defensive line games, stunts, and twists.
Full Slide: Entire line slides one gap in a single direction; running back or fullback takes the backside edge rusher. Easiest to install for 3-step drops and play-action, but exposes running backs against physical edge defenders.
Half Slide (Jet / Turnback / 2-Jet & 3-Jet):
2-Jet: Slide protection to the left.
3-Jet: Slide protection to the right (slide moves away from the call number).
Guard and tackle on the man side lock up man-to-man on interior DL. The center and backside linemen slide into gap-zone assignments starting from the identified "Mike."
The first uncovered offensive lineman initiates the slide.
"One You, Two Me" Rule: Running back checks the Mike first. If Mike rushes, the back takes him; if a second linebacker blitzes, the quarterback must throw "hot."
Overload Pressure Adjustments:
4-Weak Blitz: 4 rushers come from the weak side. Addressed via:
Tom Call: Tells the running back to cross the formation to the weak side (leaves Mike/Sam unaccounted for).

title: Core NFL Schemes & Systems (Extracted Source)
full_text:
Fan Call: Pushes the offensive tackle out wide to take the edge rusher while the back fills the interior gap.
Hot Routes & Sight Adjustments: Receiver automatically alters route into vacated blitz space.
4-Strong Blitz: Addressed via:
Joker / Opposite Call: Flips the slide direction so linemen slide strong.
Stay Call: Keeps an extra blocker (Tight End or Fullback) in the protection, sacrificing an eligible receiver.
Play-Action & Rollout Mechanics:
Fake Power Protection: Pulls a backside guard to sell run-action to freeze linebackers while opening clean throwing lanes behind them.
Boot Action vs. Naked Boot:
Boot Action: An offensive lineman, tight end, or back crosses the formation against the fake to secure the edge for the rolling quarterback.
Naked Boot: The entire line flows in one direction; the quarterback rolls out with zero backside protection and must freeze the edge defender with the fake.
Sprint / Rollout Protection: Linemen slide toward the sprint side; backside tackle hooks the defensive end to prevent pursuit from behind.
Offensive Formations, Terminology & Route Systems
Personnel & Route Lettering:
Letter Designations:
H: Halfback / primary running back.
Y: Primary inline tight end.
Z: Flanker / play-side receiver (usually lines up off the line of scrimmage).
X: Split end / weak-side receiver (lines up on the line of scrimmage, away from the call).
F: Multi-purpose skill player (Fullback, slot receiver, or second tight end).
21 Personnel Formations (2 RBs, 1 TE, 2 WRs):
Backfield Sets:
Split Right/Left: H behind the weak tackle, F behind the strong tackle.
I Right/Left: F and H aligned in a straight line behind the QB (F at 4 yards, H at 8 yards).
Strong Right/Left: F offsets to the strong side between guard and tackle.
Weak Right/Left: F offsets to the weak side away from the tight end.
Receiver Modifiers (Moving Z and X away from the call):
Slot: Z aligns inside X on the weak side.
Zoom: X aligns inside Z on the weak side.
Star: X takes a tight 3-yard split from the tackle; Z aligns inside X.
Sun: X takes a tight 3-yard split; Z aligns outside X.
12 Personnel Formations (1 RB, 2 TEs, 2 WRs) – The "S-Words":
In S-words, Y and Z go to the call; F and X go away from the call.
Solo Right: Y inline to the right with Z split wide; F inline to the left with X split wide.
Classy Tag: Reduces splits of X and Z to tight 3-yard alignments.
Snug Right: Both Y and F align off the line of scrimmage; Z and X compress inside into 3-to-4-yard splits.

title: Core NFL Schemes & Systems (Extracted Source)
full_text:
Special Right: Y aligns 1 yard deep and 1 yard outside Z; F aligns 1 yard deep and 1 yard outside X.
Sink Right: Both Y and F sink into the backfield as fullbacks, creating a 3-back set.
Sprout Right: Y flexes wide outside Z; F flexes wide outside X.
Trips Formations (3 Receivers to the Call) – The "T-Words":
In T-words, Y, F, and Z go to the call; X goes away from the call.
Trips Right: Y is inline on the ball; F is in the slot off the ball; Z is outside off the ball.
Trough Right: "TE Get Off" – Y aligns off the line of scrimmage; Z aligns on the ball.
Trout Right: Y detaches from the offensive line into a 3-to-4-yard split with F and Z.
Trump Right: "M = Middle" – Y aligns in the middle between F and Z.
Trio Right: "O = Outside" – Y aligns as the outermost receiver with F and Z inside.
Passing Concepts & Progression Architecture:
Air Coryell Route Numbering: 3-digit calls dictate routes for X, Y, and Z on the route tree (e.g., 8 = Post, 9 = Go/Fade, 6 = 8–12 yard Dig). Mills concept runs a post from the outside receiver paired with a dig from the tight end to hold the deep safety.
Mesh (Air Raid / West Coast): Two receivers cross at 3–5 yards depth, setting natural rub picks against man coverage; running back releases into the flat as a checkdown.
Smash Concept: Outside receiver runs a 5-yard hitch/curl while the inside slot receiver runs an 8-to-12-yard corner route. High-lows the Cover 2 flat cornerback.
Dagger Concept: Inside receiver runs a vertical seam to clear deep safeties; outside receiver breaks on a 15-yard dig into the vacated middle.
Y-Cross: Inside receiver/tight end runs a 15–18 yard deep crosser behind linebackers; cleared by vertical clear-out routes outside.
Double China: Both outside receivers run 5-yard "China" in-routes while an inside receiver runs a corner route; creates inside-out conflict for red-zone defenders.
Ghost (Erhardt-Perkins): Independent route concept featuring a Go (Z), Flat (H), and Hitch (Y). Can be run out of Trips, Bunch, or Doubles by coaching route rules by position rather than formation diagrams.
Situational Down & Distance Football Metrics
1st Down Operations:
1st & 10: Goal is 4–6 yards to establish 2-down series management. Offenses convert on 1st down immediately 20–25% of the time, but convert the full series ~75% of the time. Defenses remain in base looks.
1st & Short (1–5 yards): Immediate conversion rate is ~60%; overall series conversion rate jumps to ~90%. Prime down for deep play-action shots due to minimal penalty for incompletion.

title: Core NFL Schemes & Systems (Extracted Source)
full_text:
1st & Long (15+ yards): Often resulting from penalties. Immediate conversion drops to 10–12%; series survival rate falls to 30–35%. Heavy reliance on quick screens and safe checkdowns to regain field position.
2nd Down Operations:
2nd & Short (1–3 yards): Highest offensive flexibility. Low-risk/high-reward deep shots or perimeter runs.
2nd & Medium (4–6 yards): Playbook completely balanced between inside runs and quick game. Conversion on the down sits around 40%; full-series conversion rate is ~75%.
2nd & Long (7–12 yards): Damage control. Goal is recovering at least 50% of needed yardage to create manageable 3rd downs; series survival rate sits at 55–60%.
2nd & Very Long (13+ yards): Often triggered by sacks. Defenses bring heavy heat; counter-punished with draw plays and screen passes.
3rd Down Operations:
3rd & Short (1–3 yards): Power football. ~70% run frequency against loaded 8-to-9-man fronts.
3rd & Medium (4–6 yards): Heavy zone-blitz down. Offenses utilize quick slants, rub-crossers, and option routes.
3rd & Long (7–12 yards): Long-developing route trees against exotic pressure looks; conversion rates fall to 20–25%.
3rd & Very Long (13+ yards): Sub-10% conversion rate. Offenses emphasize ball security and field position over aggressive conversion attempts.
4th Down Operations:
4th & Inches: Dominated by quarterback sneaks and power wedge runs; high analytical conversion rate.
4th & Short (1–4 yards): Offenses counter stacked run fronts with quick slants and RPO flat releases.
4th & Medium (5–9 yards): ~40% conversion rate; relies on pre-snap shift/motion to diagnose coverage shells and deliver timing-based throws.
4th & Long (10+ yards): 15–20% conversion rate; maximum blitz defense against deep protection structures.

Study Data: Researchers examined 878 deceased former NFL players (died between 2016 and 2021) and found at least 1 in 4 had CTE.
Selection Bias / Context: Only 235 brains were actually donated to science by family members, and 215 of those tested positive for CTE (families who observed cognitive symptoms prior to death were significantly more likely to donate).
Historical Context: Players studied competed largely in the late 1980s and 1990s.
Rule & Safety Changes: Over 50 rule changes in the past two decades; the modified kickoff rule (preventing coverage players from moving until the ball is in play) reduced concussions by approximately 43%.

title: Core NFL Schemes & Systems (Extracted Source)
full_text:
Running Back (RB): Carries the football, reads running lanes, catches passes out of the backfield.
Fullback (FB): Lead run blocker in the hole against linebackers; occasionally runs or catches.
Wide Receiver (WR): Speed/agility perimeter or slot route runner creating separation to catch passes.
Offensive Tackle (OT): Edge protector against pass rushers; sets edge in run blocking with footwork and length.
Offensive Guard (OG): Interior protector against defensive tackles; pulls and opens interior run lanes.
Center (C): Snaps the ball, anchors the line, calls out protections and defensive fronts.
Tight End (TE): Hybrid offensive lineman and wide receiver lining up inline, flexed, or in the slot.
Defensive Positions:
Defensive Tackle (DT): Interior lineman penetrating interior gaps to stop inside runs and collapse the pocket.
Defensive End (DE): Edge lineman rushing the passer and setting the edge against outside runs.
EDGE: Hybrid designation combining 4-3 Defensive End and 3-4 Outside Linebacker responsibilities.
Linebacker (ILB / OLB): Second-level defenders filling run gaps, covering tight ends/running backs, and blitzing.
Cornerback (CB): Perimeter coverage specialist matching outside wide receivers in man or zone.
Free Safety (FS): Deep middle centerfielder; typically positioned to the weak side to read the quarterback's eyes.
Strong Safety (SS): Positioned toward the tight end / strong side to provide box run support and match tight ends.
Special Teams:
Kicker (K): Field goals (3 points), extra points (1 point), and kickoffs.
Punter (P): Punts on 4th down to pin the opponent deep and minimize return yardage.
Holder: Catches the long snap and places/spins the ball for the kicker (almost always the punter or backup QB).
Long Snapper (LS): Snaps the football accurately over extended distance under pressure.
Return Specialist (KR / PR): Fields kickoffs/punts; usually an active cornerback, running back, or wide receiver.
Historical Formations & Play-Design Case Studies
The T-Formation (1940 Bears vs. Redskins):
Chicago demolished Washington 73–0 in the 1940 NFL Championship Game, ending the single-wing era and establishing modern under-center play.
Structure: Quarterback under center with 3 backs aligned behind him in a horizontal line forming a "T" (Fullback centered, two Halfbacks flanking).
Options: Hand off to the fullback up the middle, pitch to either halfback outside, or QB keeper.

title: Excluded from this feed (2026-10-11)
full_text:
# Excluded from this feed (2026-10-11)

## Conversation with Muse AI_10-12-2026_1791774180.txt

**Excluded by the overnight engineering run, not silently dropped.**

Two independent reasons, either one sufficient:

1. **It carries live credentials.** GitHub push protection rejected the first two
   attempts to push this feed with GH013 (repository rule violations) pointing at
   this exact row: a GitHub personal access token, a GCP API key bound to a
   service account, and further entries its classifier did not enumerate. A
   targeted local scrub removed 6 token-shaped strings and the push was still
   refused, which means the transcript contains credential families the local
   patterns do not model. The repo's own pre-commit secret scanner passed this
   file ("no secrets detected") both times, so it is not a detector worth
   trusting for this class of content.
2. **It is a 4.85 MB raw conversation transcript** — roughly 5% of the entire
   feed in a single row, and it duplicates material already on disk at its
   source path. A feed is a derived corpus, not a mirror of the workspace.

The source file is left in place and untouched. Only its inclusion in the
committed feed is declined.

**Action for the owner:** the credentials in that transcript are live strings
that were pasted into a chat log. Rotate them. A chat log is not a secret store,
and re-ingesting transcripts verbatim will keep re-introducing this.

# Excluded from this feed (2026-10-11)

## Conversation with Muse AI_10-12-2026_1791774180.txt

**Excluded by the overnight engineering run, not silently dropped.**

Two independent reasons, either one sufficient:

1. **It carries live credentials.** GitHub push protection rejected the first two
   attempts to push this feed with GH013 (repository rule violations) pointing at
   this exact row: a GitHub personal access token, a GCP API key bound to a
   service account, and further entries its classifier did not enumerate. A
   targeted local scrub removed 6 token-shaped strings and the push was still
   refused, which means the transcript contains credential families the local
   patterns do not model. The repo's own pre-commit secret scanner passed this
   file ("no secrets detected") both times, so it is not a detector worth
   trusting for this class of content.
2. **It is a 4.85 MB raw conversation transcript** — roughly 5% of the entire
   feed in a single row, and it duplicates material already on disk at its
   source path. A feed is a derived corpus, not a mirror of the workspace.

The source file is left in place and untouched. Only its inclusion in the
committed feed is declined.

**Action for the owner:** the credentials in that transcript are live strings
that were pasted into a chat log. Rotate them. A chat log is not a secret store,
and re-ingesting transcripts verbatim will keep re-introducing this.

## Theme 1 — Game State & Leverage (10 records)

### Record 1.1 — @EaglesXsandOs — 4 Feb 2025
- Source: https://x.com/EaglesXsandOs/status/1886882341584560226
- Post: EPA does not reweight for opponent or in-game situation. Key line: "a 10-yard gain from the 25-yard line in a tie game vs. the Chiefs in the 4th Quarter is weighted the same as in the 3rd Q of a 35-point blowout vs. the Panthers." Follow-up: "Not all 5 yard gains are created equally."
- THE SITUATION: A 10-yard gain, scored by EPA.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Score margin, quarter, and opponent strength. A tie game in Q4 vs Kansas City is a high-leverage snap; the same gain in a 35-point blowout vs Carolina is near-zero leverage. Flat EPA scores them identically.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Separate EPA (point value of the state change) from leverage/WPA (what the state change is worth in win probability). Weight plays by game state when the target is winning or team strength, not by yards or raw EPA alone.

### Record 1.2 — @ScottKacsmar — 3 Jan 2025
- Source: https://x.com/ScottKacsmar/status/1875030492480692271
- Post: "The sneak TD can be +0.03 on 1st down up to +3.45 (!) on 4th down." A 4-yard gain on 1st-and-10 at your own 30 can be about −0.05 EPA; a 5-yard gain on 2nd-and-6 can also be negative.
- THE SITUATION: Short-yardage gains near the goal line and on early downs.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The down. The finisher on a late down absorbs credit the early-down runners created; early-down gains below the success baseline can be negative EPA even while gaining yards.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: The price of a yard is set by down and distance. Never credit a play's yards without the state it started in; short-of-the-sticks gains late in a series are worth far more than the same yards early.

### Record 1.3 — @zxcvbnmwill — 6 Mar 2026
- Source: https://x.com/zxcvbnmwill/status/2029984303828947170
- Post: 3rd-and-4 from your own 45 is about 1.53 expected points; 1st-and-10 at the 50 is about 2.69, "so a 6 yard play is worth 1.16 EPA."
- THE SITUATION: A 6-yard gain on 3rd down.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The gain converts the down. Its value is EP(after) − EP(before) = 1.16, not "6 yards."
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Value is the change in state, not the yardage. Any feature built on raw yards without the before/after state is measuring the wrong thing.

### Record 1.4 — @galenhall — 29 Sep 2026
- Source: https://x.com/galenhall/status/2104758740624797737
- Post: "Starting on your own 2 yard line is worth −.65, starting on your 31 … is worth 1.51." From the 2, even a failed 4th down gains about 2.16 expected points of field position — "almost as much as making the field goal" — so roughly a 17% TD rate breaks even.
- THE SITUATION: A drive starting inside your own 5; a 4th-down decision near your own goal line.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Field position is nonlinear. The failure state (opponent pinned deep after your failed attempt, or you after a punt exchange) is itself valuable, which crushes the break-even conversion rate far below 50%.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Near the goal lines, price the failure state, not just the conversion. Red-zone and backed-up states need their own baselines; a flat model mis-ranks both plays and decisions there.

### Record 1.5 — @ArkansasQuant — 11 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/ArkansasQuant/status/2109155529931280671
- Post: Late, one-score, 4th-and-long: teams that went for it won 9% of the time, 17% when starting in their own territory. Teams that punted won 2–7%, "depending on timeouts and clock."
- THE SITUATION: Late-game 4th-and-long, down one score.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The alternative's win rate. 9% sounds hopeless until the punt's 2–7% is next to it; timeouts and clock move both numbers.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Evaluate decisions by the delta versus the alternative, never by the absolute success rate. Leverage is a gap, not a level.

### Record 1.6 — @BenjaminSolak — 4 Nov 2024
- Source: https://x.com/BenjaminSolak/status/1853242268800733468
- Post: Overtime, 4th-and-1: the Next Gen Stats model recommended Seattle go — "The increase in win probability was 14.5%." "That's an enormous delta. It was an obvious go spot."
- THE SITUATION: 4th-and-1 in overtime.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Overtime compresses the state space — possessions are the game. A fast opponent score afterward is evidence FOR going (the punt would have surrendered the same possession), not against it.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Judge decisions by the ex-ante WP delta (+14.5%), not by the outcome that followed. Resulting is a training-data poison: a correct go that fails is still a correct go.

### Record 1.7 — @Timo_NFL — 21 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/Timo_NFL/status/2112794793772192033
- Post: Down 3 at the 2 with 1 second left collapses to immediate win or loss, versus a kick that sends you to overtime. A strong team converting ~51% might still prefer OT at ~55%; a bad defense flips it. Separate case: up 4, 4th down, 2:30 left, opponent out of timeouts — a field goal leaves a live game; a conversion can end it.
- THE SITUATION: Endgame 4th-down choices at both ends — trailing at the goal line, and leading late.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Team strength and defensive quality flip the preferred branch; timeouts determine whether the "safe" kick actually ends the game or hands the ball back.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Edge states (1 second left, kneel-out clocks, OT) are separate regimes, not the tail of the mid-game distribution. The same nominal choice is a different decision depending on which team you are.

### Record 1.8 — @bburkeESPN — 8 Sep 2025
- Source: https://x.com/bburkeESPN/status/1965115599228637192
- Post: "If you have a game state of score, time, down, distance, etc 's', then WP(s) tells you the chance of winning given that state." Going for it is an expected value: success probability × WP after success, plus failure probability × WP after failure.
- THE SITUATION: Any 4th-down (or two-point) decision.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The decision is an expectation over branches, not a conversion-rate lookup.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Decision rule — compute p × WP(success) + (1−p) × WP(failure) and compare it to WP(kick/punt). "Punt" is never a default; it is one branch among three, priced like the others.

### Record 1.9 — @tejfbanalytics — 15 Jan 2023
- Source: https://x.com/tejfbanalytics/status/1614654125316407301
- Post: One game, cumulative leverage: the Chargers had −13.1% win probability added on 4th downs, "mostly from kicking FG's on 4th-and-goal from the +4, 4th-and-goal from the +5 and 4th-and-3 from the +22." The Jaguars had +24.0% by staying aggressive.
- THE SITUATION: A single playoff game's worth of 4th-down decisions.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Individually "safe" kicks compounded into −13.1% WPA. Decision quality is visible in the sum, not in any one call's outcome.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Track cumulative decision WPA. A coach/team decision tendency is a measurable, persistent quantity — small per-play leaks are a real signal, not noise.

### Record 1.10 — @nfl4thbot — 19 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/nfl4thbot/status/2111977339873620380
- Post: Dallas, 4th-and-4 at the Green Bay 47, Q1 12:01, 0–0: coaches were predicted to punt (85%), but the model's pick was go for it, at +4.0% win probability.
- THE SITUATION: A neutral, early, scoreless 4th-and-medium at midfield.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Leverage exists in the first quarter too. +4.0% WP in Q1 is the same kind of object as +14.5% in overtime, at lower magnitude.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Do not treat early-game decisions as low-stakes by default. Price every 4th down in WP; the coach's conservative lean is not evidence the model is wrong.

### Theme 1 teaching points (from Grok's extraction)
- State, not the box score, is the unit: a play's worth is WP(after) − WP(before), or EP(after) − EP(before).
- Split expected points from win probability: down/distance/yard line set EP; score margin, clock, timeouts, quarter set how points convert to WP.
- Garbage time should be down-weighted for "who is good," not deleted from play value.
- Edge states break average models: kneel-out, 1-second-left, and overtime are not the same distribution as mid-game plays.

## Theme 2 — Game Script (12 records)

### Record 2.1 — @dwainmcfarland — 24 Oct 2022
- Source: https://x.com/dwainmcfarland/status/1584361724123447296
- Post: The Falcons trailed by 7+ on every snap and still dropped back on only 45% of plays, versus a league average of 72% in that spot.
- THE SITUATION: A team trailing all game, and its pass rate.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The league's script response (72%) is a baseline, not a law. This offense refused the script — team philosophy is a separate parameter from score state.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Learn a team-specific offset from the script-conditioned expectation. Score changes the play call in a predictable direction, but the size of the shift is a team trait.

### Record 2.2 — @LateRoundQB — 20 Nov 2017
- Source: https://x.com/LateRoundQB/status/932714807576399873
- Post: Lions and Vikings ranked top-10 in pace in a neutral game script (margin within 6). The Lions had the highest pass-to-rush ratio in football in that neutral script (1.93).
- THE SITUATION: Comparing team pace and pass tendency.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The comparison is only meaningful inside neutral script. Neutral script is the identity baseline; everything else is score effects.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Estimate pace, pass rate, and efficiency in close games first (margin within ~6, or WP roughly 20–80%). That is the team prior; extreme scripts are a separate state.

### Record 2.3 — @grok — 13 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/grok/status/2110143602475090202
- Post: Chargers at −8.6 PROE (3rd-most run-oriented). Raw split was almost even (147 rushes, 144 passes), but they had been trailing often, so the negative PROE means they ran more than the situations called for.
- THE SITUATION: A near-50/50 raw run/pass split.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: They trailed often, when the expected split tilts heavily pass. Raw rate and script-adjusted rate tell opposite stories about the same team.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Train on residuals versus expected pass rate given score, down, and distance (PROE), not on raw attempt shares. (Provenance note: this post is from X's own AI account summarizing the metric — treat as a secondary source.)

### Record 2.4 — @PurpyNFL — 17 Nov 2025
- Source: https://x.com/PurpyNFL/status/1990414391620125139
- Post: Vikings posted a −14% pass rate over expected. With that same game script, historical teams would have passed a lot more.
- THE SITUATION: A box score that looks pass-heavy.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Conditioned on the script they actually faced, they were run-heavy. The box score and the script-adjusted read point in opposite directions.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Any feature built from attempt counts must be script-adjusted before it enters a model, or it encodes the schedule of scores the team happened to face.

### Record 2.5 — @PurpyNFL — 8 Dec 2025
- Source: https://x.com/PurpyNFL/status/1998052431138074861
- Post: Vikings' PROE was 0% in one game, meaning they were more pass-happy than their own recent baseline once script was accounted for. Kneel-downs and sack/scramble coding also distort raw run/pass counts.
- THE SITUATION: A single game's run/pass accounting.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Coding artifacts — kneels, sacks, scrambles — move the raw count without reflecting a play call.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Exclude or reclassify kneel-downs, sacks, and scrambles before estimating script effects or team tendencies.

### Record 2.6 — @bjT98504 — 16 Sep 2026
- Source: https://x.com/bjT98504/status/2100272656029278660
- Post: When leading, teams run more. Clock-killing 2-yard runs are low-EPA, so a defense can look fine in EPA while giving up large rush totals in lead-protection scripts.
- THE SITUATION: A defense's rushing yards allowed vs its EPA allowed.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Leading runs are a different play type — low-EPA by design. The two defensive metrics diverge when opponents spend long stretches protecting a lead.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Condition run-defense evaluation on score and leverage, or the ranking will track opponent script rather than defensive quality.

### Record 2.7 — @Moneylinehacks — 1 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/Moneylinehacks/status/2105472478789472359
- Post: Rushing volume and covering the spread move together because leading teams run. A back's yardage and his team's side of the score are not independent.
- THE SITUATION: Correlating a running back's volume with team success.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The causality runs through the scoreboard. Leaders run more; the carries are partly an effect of winning, not a cause.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Do not treat rush or pass attempts as exogenous inputs when predicting points, spreads, or player yardage. Volume and team success are jointly determined by script.

### Record 2.8 — @LinkofSunshine — 28 Sep 2026
- Source: https://x.com/LinkofSunshine/status/2104659075506270564
- Post: Teams pass more when they are losing, which is why naive correlations between pass volume and outcomes break.
- THE SITUATION: A naive pass-volume/outcome correlation.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Script is a confounder, not noise. The losing causes the passing at least as much as the passing relates to losing.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Any pass-volume feature must carry the score state with it, or the model will learn the arrow of causality backwards.

### Record 2.9 — @hawkblogger — 17 Oct 2025
- Source: https://x.com/hawkblogger/status/1979308402619867353
- Post: Seahawks had the 2nd-fewest plays in the NFL when trailing, but led the league at 8.7 yards per play and a 9.0% TD rate on those 89 plays.
- THE SITUATION: A team's efficiency while trailing.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The sample is 89 plays — small, desperate, against defenses that have changed shape. Extreme trailing efficiency is not interchangeable with neutral-script efficiency.

### Record 2.10 — @NFLSnapIQ — 8 Oct 2026

- Post: A very low early-down PROE may be real philosophy or just score and injuries. The useful split is neutral-game-script only.

- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Without the neutral-script split, scheme and circumstance are indistinguishable.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: The neutral-script early-down split is the diagnostic view. Build it before drawing any conclusion about coaching philosophy.

### Record 2.11 — @BAI8app — 11 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/BAI8app/status/2109371470493155784
- Post: A lopsided PROE is more about coaching than matchup until you split neutral-script early downs from the rest.
- THE SITUATION: A season-total PROE number.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The season total is a mixture of regimes weighted by how often the team was in each. Matchup, scheme, and script are blended.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Do not average across states. Reweight to a common script distribution before ranking teams or feeding a predictive feature.

### Record 2.12 — @RoyRobi73192051 — 11 Sep 2026
- Source: https://x.com/RoyRobi73192051/status/2098428592409465260
- Post: Plain statement of the base rule: teams pass more when playing from behind.
- THE SITUATION: The foundational script regularity.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: None — this is the prior the other records refine.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Encode the base rule as the expectation; measure every team and game as a deviation from it.

### Theme 2 teaching points (from Grok's extraction)
- Pace is endogenous to the score: trailing speeds the game up, leading slows it down. Play counts and target opportunity are outcomes of script, not fixed inputs.
- Defense scheme is a function of score too: protecting a lead invites lighter boxes and softer coverage; chasing a deficit invites stacked boxes and pressure.
- A season-long pass rate, rush total, or EPA/play is a mixture of neutral, leading, and trailing regimes — reweight before comparing.

## Theme 3 — Situational Splits (12 records)

### Record 3.1 — @SharpFootball — 13 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/SharpFootball/status/2110075345227370707
- Post: Red-zone touchdown rate this season ranges from 87.5% (San Francisco) to 42.9% (Chicago), with most teams clustered between roughly 50% and 70%.
- THE SITUATION: A drive reaching the opponent's 20.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The red zone is a separate state with huge team dispersion. The same offense that moves the ball between the 20s can be a bottom-tier finisher.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Define the red zone as its own state (inside the 20, goal-to-go nested inside it) and score the drive outcome — TD vs FG vs nothing — separately from the yards earned getting there.

### Record 3.2 — @GridironInfo_ — 15 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/GridironInfo_/status/2110788330166083977
- Post: Defines red-zone efficiency as EPA per play once inside the opponent's 20. In 2026, San Francisco's offense was the most efficient there; Jacksonville's defense the stingiest.
- THE SITUATION: Measuring red-zone performance.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Per-play efficiency inside the 20 is a different quantity from season-long EPA; the leaderboard does not carry over.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Keep red-zone EPA as a split feature for both offense and defense; never let full-field EPA stand in for it.

### Record 3.3 — @SharpFootball — 13 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/SharpFootball/status/2110064523553972365
- Post: Baltimore early downs in the red zone: +0.67 EPA per dropback (4th) and +0.32 per rush (4th). On 3rd down in field-goal range: −0.57 EPA per play, worst in the NFL.
- THE SITUATION: One team's situational splits.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Early-down red-zone strength and 3rd-down field-goal-range failure coexist in the same offense. The down split reverses the conclusion.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Within the red zone, split by down. An aggregate red-zone number can hide the exact down where the offense breaks.

### Record 3.4 — @TheJetPress — 19 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/TheJetPress/status/2112259194736742466
- Post: Jets red-zone offense: 31st in EPA/play, 2.0 yards per carry (26th), 2.88 yards per attempt (28th), 31st in success rate — explosives outside the red zone were masking the finishing problem.
- THE SITUATION: An offense with real explosive-play production.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Between-the-20s explosives flattered the offense; inside the 20 it is near the league's worst on every measure.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Full-field explosiveness does not imply finishing ability. Model the red zone as a distinct regime with its own team ratings.

### Record 3.5 — @dmlr53 — 29 Sep 2026
- Source: https://x.com/dmlr53/status/2105024578036900188
- Post: Starting a drive inside your own 5 carries about −0.5 to −0.8 expected points. A failed conversion there hands the opponent a far better state than the raw yards suggest.
- THE SITUATION: A backed-up drive start (inside own 5–10).
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The starting state is already negative. A 30-yard gain from the own 10 is worth less than a short-yardage score from midfield.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Backed-up is a negative-EP state; value plays from it in EP/EPA, never raw yards, or the model overvalues empty yardage from bad field position.

- Post: NFL teams were converting fourth downs at 58.3%, the highest rate in NFL history.
- THE SITUATION: The league-wide 4th-down base rate.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The base rate has moved. A static "punt on fourth" prior built on older football is outdated.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Fourth-down conversion priors must be era-current and distance-specific; stale priors systematically under-price going for it.

### Record 3.7 — @thatcaden_ — 19 Feb 2023

- Post: League fourth-and-15 conversion rate cited at 21.9%.
- THE SITUATION: A very long fourth down.

- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The state changed mid-window. What began as clock management re-entered a live, high-leverage problem.

- THE SITUATION: A young QB's red-zone passing line.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The compressed field changes the completion/TD/INT profile completely versus his open-field numbers; the split, not the aggregate, describes how he plays where it tightens.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Player efficiency features must be state-split. A QB's red-zone TD/INT profile is a separate quantity from his overall line and can diverge sharply.

### Theme 3 teaching points (from Grok's extraction)
- Prevent defense inflates volume and suppresses explosives: yards and completions against prevent overstate offensive quality; down-weight them, and weight scoring rate and explosive rate instead.
- Leverage-adjusted EPA (plays that can still swing the game count more) is more predictive than raw EPA.
- Production against backups in a blowout should not update a player or team prior at full weight.

## Theme 4 — Coaching Decisions in Context (8 records)

### Record 4.1 — @RyanPaganetti — 21 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/RyanPaganetti/status/2112949460733165950
- Post: Facing 4th-and-2.5 in a tie from their own 46 with about 2 minutes left, the Ravens took a delay of game and punted. ESPN graded it an 8.6-point win-probability mistake. Converting would win ~71%, failing ~29%; estimated conversion odds 55–60%, so going for it was roughly a 55% win chance vs about 46% for the punt.
- THE SITUATION: Tie game, ~2:00 left, 4th-and-short at midfield.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Trusting the defense does not flip the call — a failed attempt still leaves paths to win, while a conversion makes them heavy favorites. The delay-of-game penalty was a decision cost on top of the punt itself.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Price the full WP of go vs punt with branch values (WP after success ≈ 71%, after failure ≈ 29%), not conversion rate alone. A modest conversion chance still wins when the alternative hands the opponent a favored drive.

### Record 4.2 — @BenjaminSolak — 11 Nov 2024
- Source: https://x.com/BenjaminSolak/status/1855833141803372852
- Post: Texans tied 23–23, 4th-and-4 on the Lions' 40, 1:56 remaining. Next Gen Stats win probability: punt 41%, field-goal attempt 39%, go for it 52%. "Was a clear go spot. Big error late for the Texans."
- THE SITUATION: Tie game, under 2 minutes, 4th-and-4 in opponent territory.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: All three branches priced: the kick was actually the worst option (39%), below even the punt. "Safe" and "correct" diverged by 13 points of WP.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Always price all three branches. In long-field-goal range late in a tie, the field goal can be dominated by both alternatives.

### Record 4.3 — @billbarnwell — 8 Sep 2024
- Source: https://x.com/billbarnwell/status/1832911439561982390
- Post: "This punt has basically gone out of the game — trailing by one TD or less on fourth-and-1 from the opponent's 40–49 yard line, teams have gone for it 63 out of 64 times over the last five years."
- THE SITUATION: 4th-and-1, opponent's 40–49, trailing by one score or less.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The league's revealed base rate in this exact narrow bin is 63/64 go. A punt here is a 1-in-64 outlier, not a judgment call.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Historical base rates in narrow state bins are strong priors. When a coach deviates from a near-unanimous bin, the burden of proof is on the deviation.

### Record 4.4 — @NextGenStats — 10 Jan 2022
- Source: https://x.com/NextGenStats/status/1480383946718203905
- Post: Chargers' decision to go for it on 4th-and-1 from their own 18 was optimal on the NGS Decision Guide: win % if go 36%, if punt 35%, recommendation go by 1.4%.
- THE SITUATION: 4th-and-1 from your own 18 — the deepest "never go" territory in conventional wisdom.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Field position thresholds are not absolute. When the punt's expected net is small, even a backed-up 4th-and-1 can be a (slight) go.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: No state is categorically off-limits to the EV computation. Compute the branches everywhere; let the numbers, not field-position folklore, draw the lines.

### Record 4.5 — @BenjaminSolak — 10 Sep 2026
- Source: https://x.com/BenjaminSolak/status/2097885845046919677
- Post: Next Gen Stats called 4th-and-9 from the opponent's 47 a strong go. "If you punt, you need to force a 3-and-out to get the ball back. If you go for it and fail… you need to force a 3-and-out to get the ball back anyway."
- THE SITUATION: 4th-and-9, late, needing the ball back.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The defensive requirement after a punt and after a failed attempt is the same (a 3-and-out). The punt buys almost nothing except worse field position on the failure branch.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: When both branches require the same defensive outcome, the go branch weakly dominates. Compare what each branch actually changes, not the labels "aggressive" vs "safe."

### Record 4.6 — @MikeReiss — 11 Sep 2023
- Source: https://x.com/MikeReiss/status/1701068291953823848
- Post: Belichick going for it on 4th-and-3 from the Eagles' 17, trailing 22–14 with 9:39 left, agreed with by ESPN Analytics: WP going for it 21.4%, kicking 20.8%.
- THE SITUATION: Down 8, 9:39 left, 4th-and-3 at the opponent's 17.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Inside the red zone the kick is nearly automatic points, yet the go still edged it — because down 8, the touchdown's value toward tying outweighs the certain 3.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Score margin interacts with the kick/go choice: a field goal that leaves you still trailing by two scores is worth less than its points. Model the margin after each branch, not just the points.

### Record 4.7 — @Timo_NFL — 21 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/Timo_NFL/status/2112794822490612072
- Post: 4th down, 2:30 left, no opponent timeouts, up by 4. Kick a field goal to go up 7 and play defense (OT if they score), or go for it and end the game immediately a significant share of the time.
- THE SITUATION: Leading by 4 late, opponent out of timeouts, 4th down in field-goal range.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The field goal does not end the game — it creates a new one (a tying drive, then OT). The conversion ends it on the spot a meaningful fraction of the time.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Score, clock, and opponent timeouts interact. "Take the points" is not a terminal state; price the game that follows the kick.

### Record 4.8 — @nfl4thbot — 19 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/nfl4thbot/status/2111977339873620380
- Post: DAL ball, 4th-and-4 at the GB 47, Q1 12:01, 0–0. Predicted coach action punt (85%), but the model's pick is go for it (+4.0% win probability).
- THE SITUATION: Scoreless first quarter, midfield, 4th-and-medium.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The model-vs-coach disagreement is itself quantified (+4.0% WP). Neutral early spots still carry decision leverage.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: A coach's conservative lean is not automatically justified by information the model lacks. Several-point WP edges are rarely overturned by personnel adjustments (backup QB, kicker form) alone — but personnel should still shift the conversion/make estimates that feed the calculation.

### Theme 4 teaching points (from Grok's extraction)
- "You need a stop either way" logic favors going when a failed attempt and a punt leave the same defensive requirement.
- Be careful at the edges of the state space (kneel-out clocks, very late, extreme deficits): models train

## 2. Deep Mathematical Extraction: Giuseppe A. Paleologo ("Gappy"), *From Regression to Transformers* (`Oct 31, 2026`)

### 2.1 Book Architecture (17 Chapters + 2 Appendices)
- **Part I — Foundations (Ch. 1–3):**
  - *Ch. 1: Statistical Learning* (Risk decomposition, Bayes predictor, No-Free-Lunch lower bound, empirical risk minimization, structural hierarchy: Linear $\to$ Fixed Basis $\to$ RKHS $\to$ Deep Networks $\to$ Attention).
  - *Ch. 2: Linear Prediction* (Population $L^2$ projection, OLS normal equations, Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem & residualization procedure, QR/SVD numerical geometry, Inverse-Wishart exact out-of-sample risk).
  - *Ch. 3: Generalization and Regularization* (Uniform laws, Rademacher complexity, Symmetrization, Massart finite-class bound, Martingale Azuma–Hoeffding walk-forward selection allowance, Linear smoothers, $\operatorname{df}(\lambda)$ vs. $d_{\text{var}}(\lambda)$, Ridge regression & spectral shrinkage).
- **Part II — Fixed Nonlinear Expansions and Kernels (Ch. 4–6):**
  - *Ch. 4: Splines and Basis Expansions* (Truncated power vs. B-splines, natural cubic splines, roughness penalty $\int (f'')^2$, Generalized Representer Theorem with unpenalized null space $\mathcal{Z}$, Demmler–Reinsch basis, P-splines, tensor-product vs. additive GAMs, Unified Spectral Filter Table).
  - *Ch. 5: Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces* (Riesz representation, evaluation functionals, Moore–Aronszajn theorem, Mercer expansion & feature map, Representer theorem, Kernel Ridge Regression, GP posterior equivalence, source condition $m = T^r g$ & effective dimension $\mathcal{N}(\lambda)$ minimax rates).
  - *Ch. 6: Kernel Approximation and Random Features* (Nyström low-rank approximation, Bochner's theorem & Random Fourier Features, sketching as randomized numerical linear algebra, double descent & benign overfitting).
- **Part III — Adaptive Nonlinear Predictors (Ch. 7–11):**
  - *Ch. 7: Single-Index Models, Projection Pursuit, and Classical Perceptrons* (Ridge functions, Barron's theorem).
  - *Ch. 8: Multilayer Perceptrons and Representation Learning* (Piecewise linear regions, backpropagation via reverse-mode AD, residual connections).
  - *Ch. 9: Optimization, Implicit Regularization, and Scaling Limits* (Gradient flow, early stopping spectral filter $1 - e^{-dt}$, Neural Tangent Kernel vs. feature-learning/mean-field regime).
  - *Ch. 10: Structured Architectures Before Attention* (Weight sharing, equivariance, CNNs, RNNs, LSTMs/GRUs).
  - *Ch. 11: Autoregressive Sequence Modeling* (Chain rule of probability, next-token cross-entropy, exposure bias, teacher forcing).
- **Part IV — Attention and Transformers (Ch. 12–16):**
  - *Ch. 12: Attention as Data-Dependent Kernel Smoothing* (Nadaraya–Watson estimator, learned query-key bilinear forms, $\sqrt{d_k}$ variance scaling, multi-head subspace projections, effective sample size $n_{\text{eff}} = (\sum_j a_j^2)^{-1}$).

   Under Gaussian covariates $X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{\Sigma})$ with $n > p + 1$, via the Inverse-Wishart expectation $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{W}^{-1}] = \frac{1}{n-p-1}\mathbf{I}_p$:
   $$\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_n}\big[\|\hat{f}_n - m\|_{L^2(P_X)}^2\big] = \frac{\sigma^2 p}{n - p - 1}$$

4. **Frisch–Waugh–Lovell (FWL) Orthogonal Partialling Out (Theorem 2.1 & Procedure 2.1):**

### Architect: Fable 5.1 · 2026-09-15 · supersedes "The Honest Map"

Every number here was measured this session, read-only, with the command recorded in
`scratchpad/FINDINGS.md` (F1–F19). Nothing below is an opinion about the football or the
market; the opinions are only about what to do.

---

## CONTEXT — the five facts that decide everything

1. **The NFL game market is closed.** ~190 specifications tested out of sample. The closing line
   is efficient (home covers 49.05% on n=7,081, 27 seasons). No defensive trait is mispriced
   (14 tests, none reach |z|=1). Published edges decay after publication (wind: real for 20
   years, dead by 2025). Our own team model hit 49.83% ATS on 895 held-out games.
   **Nobody spends another hour trying to beat NFL sides or totals with public data.**

2. **Our engine has negative standalone skill and a real orthogonal signal.** Head-to-head on
   540 identical picks: model Brier 0.251, market 0.220, a constant 0.248. But corr(model,
   outcome) = +0.146 while corr(model, market) = +0.128. **At 10% weight blended toward the
   market it beats the market out of sample** (0.20818 vs 0.20905; football 0.18825 vs 0.18946).
   That is the one lever on the engine, and it is a calibration gain, not an edge.

3. **The product loses money and the record is baseball.** Only computable market: 180–44,
   80.36%, **−2.88% ROI** (break-even at −373 is 82.12%). Record is **72.5% MLB, 3.1% NFL**;
   **86% of the NFL record is preseason**; regular-season NFL = **11 picks**. Spreads/totals:
   1,459 settled, **zero** stored prices, ~46.5% win rate.

4. **The only validated NFL model is props.** Brier skill 4.2% over climatology, 0 decile
   inversions, 12,571 out-of-sample predictions. Blocked by: `PickType` has no prop value and
   `@@unique([gameId,pickType])`; ingest fetches 2 of ~13 markets at a credit cap of 8; the
   prop archive has **zero readers**; `/fantasy/props` is 12 fictional players on a normal CDF.

5. **Zero customers.** 2 users (one is a Stripe test), 2 checkout attempts ever (last 08-19,
   three weeks *before* the 503 began), 1 waitlist lead, 0 product events. The constraint is
   demand. And **the repo's problem is not missing capability** — 22 of 25 "advanced" techniques
   already exist; `pfr_adv_stats`, fixture tombstoning, in-play disclosure, the Pinnacle
   archive were all *built and never wired*.

---

## PRODUCT DEFINITION — locked, so nobody re-derives it

**Galaxy Sports Edge is an NFL-first product that publishes three things:**

1. **NFL player props** — the validated model, graded against posted lines.
2. **Market-anchored NFL game probabilities** — the engine shrunk 90% toward the market, with
   honest calibration and a vig-free exchange reference. Sold as *calibration*, never as edge.
3. **The public record of what does not work** — the reliability table, the 190 dead
   hypotheses, the decay curves. The only position in this market that cannot be copied by a
   competitor with something to hide.

**It stops publishing:** MLB spreads and totals (45.5%/45.4%), NFL preseason, soccer
moneylines, and any row with no book price. Volume that loses is not volume.

---

## THE PLAN — five phases, each ends in something a human can see

Rules for the executing model: ≤5 files per task, one commit per task, verify block before
every commit (`npm run typecheck && npm run lint && npx vitest run <file>`), never touch the
frozen paths (schema, migrations, `.github/`, `scripts/guardrails/`, `.claude/`, `.env*`,
lockfile). Never flip an env flag. Never bump MODEL_VERSION. Report `NOT RUN` rather than
invent a result.

### Phase 0 — Stop lying, stop bleeding (days 1–2)

| # | change | files | verify |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.1 | **Land PR #819.** Merge `origin/main`; conflicts are exactly `AGENTS.md` and `apps/web/__tests__/preview-legacy-redirect.test.tsx`. CI is green on the head. | 2 | `git merge-tree` clean, CI green, PR mergeable |
| 0.2 | **Render the in-play disclosure.** Four producers, zero renderers (Devin was right and it's wider). Render `policy.inPlayNote` on `/clv` `ClvScoreboard` when `inPlayExcluded > 0`; same for the calibration surfaces. Add a page test. | `apps/web/app/clv/page.tsx` + calibration renderers + 1 test | test asserts the count appears |
| 0.3 | **`/gsn` failure says it failed.** Remove `SAMPLE_TRANSMISSION` from the fallback path in `lib/gsn/build-transmission.ts:38-44,:125-131`. | 1 | no invented counts render on empty/error |
| 0.4 | **`/performance` judged at the real bar.** Pass `threshold={0.524}` at `page.tsx:385`; split bettable vs model-signal lanes; keep model-signal rows in the record. | 2 | page shows both lanes at 0.524 |
| 0.5 | **Gate preseason at mint.** No preseason gate exists anywhere on the publish path (`settle-sport.ts:33-36` deliberately *fetches* it). Add a season-type check in `process-sport.ts` before mint; NFL preseason rows are withheld. Withhold-only → no MODEL_VERSION bump. | 1–2 | test: a preseason fixture mints no pick |
| 0.6 | **Close the soccer leak.** `isThreeWayMoneylineSport` (`scoring.ts:1116`) is correct and applied at `:1225`, yet 42 book-priced MLS MLs minted under v5.2.7 through 09-10. A second mint path bypasses it. Find every site that creates `pickType: MONEYLINE` and assert the guard at each. Do **not** re-grade the 29 draws — `settlement.ts:94` grades them correctly for a 3-way market; the defect was publishing them. | 1–3 | test: soccer sport key mints no ML through any path |
| 0.7 | **Fix the selection-string price.** `"Columbus Crew SC ML (+102)"` locked at −135; `(-19084)` is not a price. The card must render `clvLockPrice`, never a string-embedded number. | 1 | test pins card price == lock price |

### Phase 1 — Wire what is already built (week 1)

| # | change | files | verify |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | **Fill `pfr_adv_stats` from nflverse.** PFR scraping is `forbidden`; the registry says "use nflverse's `pfr_advstats` release." `lib/ingestion/pfr-adv-stats.ts` is written and tested with zero importers. Point it at the nflverse release, schedule it beside `refresh-player-stats`. This is the founder's own football signal (broken tackles, yards after contact). | 2 | table > 0 rows; cron entry resolves |
| 1.2 | **Tombstone fixture twins.** `findTwinCandidate` detects; `mergedIntoGameId` has no writer. Every NFL game this week is 2 rows (11 books / 0 books), neither tombstoned. Write the alias in the ingestion path the design already specifies (`game-identity.ts:95-99`). | 1–2 | this week's 16 NFL games → 16 canonical rows |
| 1.3 | **Widen prop ingest.** `NFL_EVENT_ODDS_MARKETS` from 2 to every market the engine scores (pass yds/tds/comp/int, rush yds/att/td, rec/rec yds/rec td, anytime td, sacks — verify keys against the Odds API docs, do not guess). Credit cap is a founder env. | 1 | prop rows land for ≥8 markets |
| 1.4 | **Build the prop reader.** `decodePropMarket` has one caller: its own test. Write `OddsLineSnapshot → RateSample` and the `player_game_stats` outcome join (keyed `(playerId, season, week)`, no `gameId` — the game→week map is part of the work). | 2–3 | a graded prop sample exists |
| 1.5 | **Kalshi via PredExon, not direct.** Kalshi Trade API is `paid-required` (Dev Agreement §3). PredExon is `use-with-caution`, commercial-use true, founder holds the key, `PREDEXON_INGEST` default OFF. Wire the reader; **founder flips the flag**. This is the second book for `MIN_BOOKMAKERS=2` and a vig-free CLV reference at 1-cent spreads. Note the API renamed price fields to `*_dollars`/`*_fp`. | 2 | NFL games carry a PredExon/Kalshi price |
| 1.6 | **Unlink the fiction.** 125 of 158 public pages unreachable; 0 of 12 Fantasy tools on live data; `/fantasy/nba` is titled "Fictional… Validator Demo" in the nav. Remove from nav/footer (code stays). Fantasy 12 → 3. Fix the 12 label/page mismatches by renaming the *label*. | nav.tsx, footer.tsx, mobile-nav.tsx | 37 labels → ≤12; every label matches its H1 |

### Phase 2 — The holdout, permanently (week 1–2)

The 500-adjustments failure has one cause: every adjustment improved the training score
(0.24476→0.23828→0.23680→0.23676) while the holdout degraded (0.25010→0.24756→0.25547→0.28754).
Without a holdout they are indistinguishable.

| # | change | verify |
|---|---|---|
| 2.1 | `packages/verifier`: a **frozen holdout** (every settled pick from a fixed date forward, never trained on), a **scorecard** (Brier + log-loss vs `marketFairProb` on identical rows), and a **duel** (candidate must beat the market-anchored baseline on the holdout). No pre-registration ceremony, no four gates — one harness, one number. | re-grade v5.0.0→v5.2.7: all score worse than market on the holdout, as measured |
| 2.2 | **Rule, enforced in CI:** no MODEL_VERSION bump ships without a passing scorecard on the frozen holdout. `model-freeze.mjs` already guards the bump; the scorecard becomes its precondition. (`scripts/guardrails/` is frozen — the *founder* lands this hook.) | founder-landed |
| 2.3 | **First candidate through the harness: shrinkage.** `p = market + 0.10·(model − market)`. Measured 0.20818 vs 0.20905 holdout; football 0.18825 vs 0.18946. P(better) 0.75–0.87 — suggestive, not established. Score it on the frozen holdout. If it passes, it is a v5.2.8 **founder** proposal with the measurement attached. | scorecard |

#### 2.4 The candidate queue — every idea from the dumps, sequenced, none written off

The founder's standard is "10 things that improve 0.2% is real movement." That standard is
only meetable through 2.1: each item below is one script, one pre-registered margin, one
number on the frozen holdout, logged in the fact-graph. Items are grouped by what blocks them
**today**, not by whether anyone likes them.

**A. Testable this week — data already in nflverse or our DB. Run in this order (cheapest,
most decision-relevant first). Each is a 2.1 candidate; a pass is a v5.2.8 line item.**

| # | candidate | data | status | note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | **Birthday + former-team target share** (founder's own example) | nflverse `rosters` (birth_date, team history) + pbp targets | **never run** | Estimand: residual target share on (birthday ∨ former-team) games vs the player's trailing-5 DYN baseline. Pooled mean residual, cluster-robust by player. This is the founder's "unseen factor" test and it costs one afternoon. |
| A2 | Shrinkage weight `w` (F18) | our settled picks + `marketFairProb` | **passed, holdout** | The first positive in ~190 specs. Goes first through 2.1 to confirm it survives the frozen split. |
| A3 | Referee tendencies (Vinovich under, Hussey home, Eck favorite) | nflverse `games.csv` has `referee` | never run | Discover ≤2019 / validate 2020+. Kill if |z|<1 on the validate era. |
| A4 | Eastward travel ≥2 zones, afternoon kickoff (Fodor & Krieger spec) | nflverse stadium/location + kickoff | partial (F12 tested west-early and east-late, not this spec) | Run the exact published spec, then the 2020+ decay check. |
| A5 | Wind/precip on totals (Borghesi) | nflverse `temp`,`wind`,`roof` | **measured: decayed to ~0 by 2025** | Re-run yearly; it is a 30-second script. Not dead forever, dead now. |
| A6 | Permutation entropy of within-drive play calling (W8) | pbp | never run | vs `pass_oe`, ≥0.02 R² margin. |
| A7 | Intrinsic dimension of play-call manifold (W7) | pbp | never run | vs distinct-play-type count. |
| A8 | Boltzmann-informed recalibration of our own `p` | our picks | never run | A transform, not a feature; scored on holdout Brier vs isotonic. |
| A9 | DFA scaling exponent of EPA sequences (W6) | pbp | never run | Low prior (Koopman p=0.89). Cheap; run anyway. |
| A10 | Wasserstein barycenter distance (W5) | pbp | never run | Low prior (W2 was field-position in disguise). |
| A11 | HMM form regimes, pooled fit + shuffle gate (T3) | pbp | never run | Report K* under AIC and BIC both. |
| A12 | Prelec 4th-down weighting (IRL) | pbp | never run | Not a pick improvement; a coaching-behavior estimand. Runs last in this group. |
| A13 | Persistent homology (T7, Null A + Null B) | pbp | never run | Published prior is null. Single shot, no rescue. |

Already measured and dead on the holdout, so **not** in the queue unless a new spec is stated:
rest (r=0.0084, n=2,953), intransitivity (sign opposite), Moskowitz blowout fade (50.49%),
coach revenge (n=70), divisional-rematch under, first-meeting-loser (52.07% < 52.38%; the
Autopsy's arithmetic on this one was wrong). The team model itself: 49.83% ATS on 895 held-out
games — that is the honest ceiling on public-data game sides, and it is why A1–A13 are
features for **props and calibration**, not new side picks.

**B. Blocked on data we do not have — not written off; each names the acquisition that
unblocks it.**

| candidate | needs | nearest path |
|---|---|---|
| Betfair order-flow imbalance, WoM, iceberg detection | exchange L2 stream | No US access. Kalshi via PredExon (1.5) is the only exchange feed we can legally read; forward-only from flip date. |
| Prelec near-expiry distortion, FLB child-market tails | in-play prediction-market prices | Kalshi forward-only (65 settled, 49 preseason). Pre-register before scoring; earliest read Week 8. |
| Open-to-close line movement (Claremont AUC 0.702→0.730) | opening lines | oddsmagnet totals usable (90.3%), spreads not (19.4%). Kalshi opens from 1.5. |
| Props regression-to-stable-metrics, snap-count-on-return | prop lines + graded outcomes | Phase 1.3/1.4. This is the highest-ceiling item in the dumps and it is already the Phase 3 program. |
| Vector-field potentials, DYN separation features, coverage-split man/zone, Weibull AFT in-play | player tracking | No public NFL tracking data. NGS is aggregates; `pfr_advstats` (1.1) is the closest we get. |
| Critical slowing down, wearables, biometrics | athlete sensor data | Does not exist outside teams. |

**C. Infrastructure, not prediction — real, and Phase 5, because it multiplies a product that
must exist first.** Phase VI's 20 repos (Ghost/Listmonk/Dub/Mautic/n8n/PostHog…), Phase VII's
viral mechanics, the Neon Auth swap. Deploying an attribution stack in front of zero customers
and a 49.8% side model attributes nothing.

**What the queue changes:** the previous lead ran ~190 specs, got one positive, and the other
ideas went into "explicitly out." That is what "writing things off" looks like. Under 2.4 every
item has a status, a data dependency, and a slot; the only way off the list is a number on the
frozen holdout or a named data gap.

### Phase 3 — Props becomes a product (weeks 2–4) — the only untested market

Sequenced so nothing irreversible happens before the measurement:

1. Phase 1.3 + 1.4 accumulate a graded sample (~250/week at full-slate ingest).
2. **Grade the HB engine against posted prop lines through the Phase 2 harness**, target
   n≈500, power certificate stated *before* looking. Skill is 4.2% and over-confident above the
   median; the honest prior is "maybe."
3. **Only on a passing scorecard**: founder migration — `PickType` gains a prop value and
   `@@unique([gameId,pickType])` is relaxed to admit player rows. Schema is law-2 frozen; this
   is a founder-authorized change and nothing before step 2 touches it.
4. Replace `/fantasy/props` (12 invented players) with the real board.

If step 2 fails, three weeks were spent closing the last open question honestly — and that
result is publishable under product #3.

### Phase 4 — Publish what doesn't work (parallel, week 2+)

One script, public data, reproducible: the reliability table (stuff rate +0.68, success +0.63,
pressure +0.43, explosive-allowed −0.04), the market-gap table (every trait priced at z<1), the
decay curves (wind 2023→2025), the 190 dead hypotheses with their out-of-sample numbers.
Nobody in this market publishes this because nobody can afford to. It requires no edge and
cannot be copied by a competitor with something to hide.

### Phase 5 — The river (after a human arrives)

Checkout fix (founder env, #822) → `track()` wired (22 events defined, 0 dispatched) → one
non-Google sign-in (email OTP; **not** a Neon Auth swap — that's Vite/React-Router and an
auth-stack change, founder decision) → email capture on `/` and under the `/picks` paywall →
delete the affiliate code that contradicts the published pledge (ruling F-6). **No new revenue
surface until this one takes a dollar.** Expect no dollars until Phase 4 puts a human on the site.

---

## FOUNDER DECISIONS — yours, not an agent's

1. **Rotate the two Neon connection strings pasted in chat.** Today.
2. `PREDEXON_INGEST=true` (1.5) and `EVENT_ODDS_CREDIT_CAP` raised (1.3).
3. Checkout: `PRICING_PHASE=FOUNDING` or six new Stripe Prices (#822).
4. The CI precondition hook (2.2) — `scripts/guardrails/` is frozen for agents.
5. Shrinkage as v5.2.8 (2.3), on the scorecard.
6. The props schema migration (Phase 3 step 3), on the scorecard.
7. Amputate the fantasy suite or merely unlink it (1.6 unlinks; deletion is yours).
8. **Stop feeding external research dumps into the project until Phases 0–2 ship.** Four of
   the last six proposals were already tested and dead; every citation predated 2012.

---

## EXPLICITLY OUT — only three things, everything else is in the 2.4 queue

- **Beating NFL sides/totals as the product goal.** Measured closed on 895 held-out games
  (49.83% ATS). Side-market *features* still run through 2.4 as calibration/props inputs; what
  is out is selling a side pick as an edge.
- Re-grading the 29 soccer draws — correctly graded for a 3-way market; the fix is upstream (0.6).
- Any MODEL_VERSION change from an agent session.

Everything that used to sit here (Kalshi order flow, Prelec, vector fields, TDA, Weibull AFT,
tracking-data features) is now in 2.4 §B with the data acquisition that unblocks it named.

---

## VERIFICATION — how the founder knows each phase landed

- **P0:** #819 merged; `/clv` shows the exclusion count; `/gsn` never fabricates; `/performance`
  shows two lanes at 0.524; a preseason fixture and a soccer key mint no pick; card price ==
  lock price.
- **P1:** `pfr_adv_stats > 0`; this week's NFL games are 16 rows not 32; ≥8 prop markets
  landing; `decodePropMarket` has a production caller; PredExon prices on NFL games; nav ≤12
  labels, each matching its page.
- **P2:** the harness re-grades v5.0.0→v5.2.7 and none beat the market on the frozen holdout —
  if any does, the harness is wrong and gets fixed before it grades anything else. Then A1–A13
  each have a row in the fact-graph with a holdout number and a verdict; A1 (birthday/former
  team) and A2 (shrinkage) are the first two rows.
- **P3:** a graded prop sample with a pre-stated power certificate and a scorecard verdict.
- **P4:** the reliability table reproduces from one script and matches FINDINGS.md.

## What I will not claim

I did not find an edge in NFL game markets and I am telling you not to look for one there
again. I found that your engine carries a real signal it has been drowning by trusting itself
too much, that your only validated model has no product around it, that your football read was
right about the game and already in the price, and that the premier product has eleven real
picks. That is the whole picture. It is smaller than the site suggests and more honest than
anything a competitor publishes, and the plan above is built on it rather than around it."}

title: append_day_feed.py
full_text:
"""Append a day's research-bucket files to the dated trainer feed.

The mind's trainer feed (brain/feeds/<date>/trainer_feed.jsonl) is the
trainer-ready corpus: one JSON record per document with its source, category,
path, and full text. prepare_feed.py built the 2026-10-11/13 feeds from fixed
dir lists; the mind guardian appends what IT routes from the watch roots. Files
that land directly under docs/<bucket>/research/<date>/ (live-ingest pilots,
for example) had no path into the feed until this script.

Dedupe is by `path`: a file already present in the feed is skipped, so running
this repeatedly is safe.

Usage
-----
    python brain/feeds/append_day_feed.py --date 2026-10-13 \
        --dirs docs/data-sources/research/2026-10-13/weather-pilot \
               docs/data-sources/research/2026-10-13/news-rss \
               docs/data-sources/research/2026-10-13/kalshi \
               docs/data-sources/research/2026-10-13/injuries
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path

REPO_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
FEED_EXTS = ["*.md", "*.json", "*.txt", "*.csv", "*.xml"]


def load_existing_paths(feed_path: Path) -> set:
    paths = set()
    if not feed_path.exists():
        return paths
    with open(feed_path, "r", encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore") as f:
        for line in f:
            line = line.strip()
            if not line:
                continue
            try:
                rec = json.loads(line)
                p = rec.get("path")
                if isinstance(p, str):
                    paths.add(p)
            except json.JSONDecodeError:
                continue
    return paths


def main() -> int:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Append day files to the dated trainer feed (dedupe by path).")
    ap.add_argument("--date", required=True, help="Feed date bucket, e.g. 2026-10-13")
    ap.add_argument("--dirs", nargs="+", required=True, help="Directories (repo-relative or absolute) to append")
    ap.add_argument("--dry-run", action="store_true")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    feed_path = REPO_ROOT / "brain" / "feeds" / args.date / "trainer_feed.jsonl"
    feed_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    existing = load_existing_paths(feed_path)
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()

    added, skipped_dupe, failed = 0, 0, []

import os, glob, json

output_feed = r'c:\Users\Garrett\Sports\brain\feeds\2026-10-11\trainer_feed.jsonl'
os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(output_feed), exist_ok=True)

docs_dirs = [
    r'c:\Users\Garrett\Sports\docs\engine\research\2026-10-11',
    r'c:\Users\Garrett\Sports\docs\dfs\research\2026-10-11',
    r'c:\Users\Garrett\Sports\docs\props\research\2026-10-11',
    r'c:\Users\Garrett\Sports\docs\predictions\research\2026-10-11',
    r'c:\Users\Garrett\Sports\docs\data-sources\research\2026-10-11'
]

entries = 0
with open(output_feed, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as out:
    for d in docs_dirs:
        for ext in ['*.md', '*.txt', '*.json', '*.csv', '*.html']:
            for fp in glob.glob(os.path.join(d, ext)):
                try:
                    with open(fp, 'r', encoding='utf-8', errors='ignore') as f:
                        content = f.read()
                    rec = {
                        'source': os.path.basename(fp),
                        'category': os.path.basename(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(fp))),
                        'path': fp,
                        'text': content
                    }
                    out.write(json.dumps(rec) + '\n')
                    entries += 1
                except Exception as e:
                    print(f'Error reading {fp}: {e}')

print(f'Synthesized {entries} trainer-ready mind feed documents into {output_feed}')
